explanation.summary: Pharmacokinetic mismatch is the central reasoning step: naloxone (half-life ~60 minutes) reverses opioid receptor occupancy briefly, while methadone (half-life ~24 hours, can extend to 59 hours due to autoinduction and tissue redistribution) continues to bind. After bolus, naloxone is cleared while methadone is still toxic. AU practice is naloxone INFUSION at two-thirds the cumulative effective bolus per hour, titrated to RR >=12 and adequate airway maintenance. Continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours given methadone's prolonged effect. Buprenorphine overdose may NOT respond to naloxone due to high receptor affinity. Always consider co-ingestion: benzodiazepine (synergistic respiratory depression but flumazenil rarely indicated) and paracetamol (delayed hepatotoxicity).
key_points: Naloxone t1/2 ~60 min; methadone t1/2 ~24 h (up to 59 h)
AU practice: naloxone infusion at 2/3 effective bolus dose per hour
Titrate to RR >=12 and airway maintenance, not full reversal
Buprenorphine overdose may not respond to naloxone (high affinity)
Observe at least 24 hours for methadone overdose
explanation.pearls: Avoid over-aggressive naloxone in chronic opioid-dependent patients - precipitated withdrawal is unpleasant, increases aspiration risk, and may not be needed. Aim for RR >=12 and airway maintenance, not awake-and-talking.

options.rationale: MECHANISM: naloxone is a competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist with a short half-life (~60 minutes). Methadone has a half-life of ~24 hours (8-59 hour range). The bolus reverses receptor occupancy briefly; as naloxone redistributes and is cleared, methadone re-binds receptors and re-sedation follows. AU practice (eTG Toxicology): commence naloxone infusion at two-thirds the cumulative effective bolus dose per hour. So if 400 microgram bolus produced response, infuse 0.4 mg/h (267 microgram/h rounded). Titrate to RR >=12 and adequate consciousness for airway. Source: eTG Toxicology; NSW Poisons Information Centre.
This is the opposite of correct - methadone is the toxin causing sedation. Giving more methadone deepens toxicity. Source: eTG.
Flumazenil reversal in patients with chronic benzodiazepine use risks seizures; it is rarely indicated in mixed-overdose patients especially with opioid co-ingestion. Source: NSW PIC.
Intubation is appropriate in failure of medical reversal, but the standard pathway is naloxone infusion first - intubation is reserved for failure of infusion to maintain airway. Source: eTG.
Methadone was taken hours earlier and the patient has reduced GCS - charcoal is contraindicated due to aspiration risk and is past its absorption window. Source: eTG.

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis is one of the most important psychiatric mimics. It typically affects young women and presents in stereotyped phases: viral prodrome -> psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, psychosis, mood lability, behavioural change) -> seizures and movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias, chorea) -> autonomic instability + reduced consciousness. CSF anti-NMDA antibodies are diagnostic. EEG delta brushes are pathognomic. In women aged 18-35, approximately half have an underlying ovarian teratoma producing the antigen - imaging and tumour removal is curative alongside immunotherapy (first-line steroids + IVIG or plasmapheresis; second-line rituximab + cyclophosphamide). Prognosis is good with early treatment. Cognitive recovery may take 12-24 months.
key_points: Classic phases: prodrome -> psych -> seizures + dyskinesia -> autonomic
CSF anti-NMDA antibody is diagnostic
EEG delta brushes are pathognomic
~50% of young women have ovarian teratoma - REMOVE the tumour
First-line immunotherapy: steroids + IVIG or plasmapheresis
explanation.pearls: Any first-episode psychosis in a young woman with new seizures, movement disorder, dysautonomia, or refractory presentation should trigger urgent LP for NMDA antibodies. Antipsychotics worsen the movement disorder and may precipitate NMS-like reactions.

options.rationale: NMS presents with rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, raised CK - not orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetoid movements, seizures, or anti-NMDA antibody positivity in CSF. The serology and EEG findings are diagnostic. Source: eTG Neurology.

ANTIBODY PATTERN: CSF anti-NMDA-receptor antibodies are diagnostic of anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis. Classic clinical phases: prodromal viral-like illness -> psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, psychosis, mood lability) -> seizures + orofacial dyskinesias + choreoathetoid movements -> autonomic instability + dyskinesias. EEG delta brushes are pathognomic. In young women, ~50 percent have an underlying ovarian teratoma producing the antigen - urgent abdominal/pelvic imaging (transabdominal/transvaginal USS + CT/MRI) and tumour removal is the curative step alongside immunotherapy (steroids + IVIG or plasmapheresis as first line; rituximab/cyclophosphamide as second line). Source: ANZAN; Australian Encephalitis Network; eTG Neurology.

ADEM is a post-infectious demyelinating disease with multifocal neurology and characteristic MRI white-matter lesions; the antibody and EEG findings here are diagnostic of NMDA-receptor encephalitis. Source: ANZAN.

Anti-Hu paraneoplastic encephalitis is associated with small-cell lung cancer in older smokers; demographics, antibody profile, and CT chest are not appropriate first investigation in a 24-year-old woman with NMDA-positive CSF. Source: ANZAN.
Synthetic cannabinoid psychosis does not produce CSF antibody positivity, EEG delta brushes, or orofacial dyskinesias as a constellation. Source: NSW Health.

explanation.summary: The mechanism-counter-mechanism logic: methamphetamine causes massive monoamine release with both alpha-1 (vasoconstriction, coronary spasm) and beta-1 (chronotropy, contractility) stimulation. The dangerous component in ACS is alpha-1 coronary vasoconstriction. Pure beta-blockade leaves alpha-1 unopposed which can worsen spasm; benzodiazepines lower central sympathetic outflow indirectly, GTN relieves spasm directly, and phentolamine provides pure alpha-1 blockade if needed. Beta-blockade alone is therefore contraindicated.
key_points: Sympathomimetic ACS first-line: benzodiazepines + GTN
Avoid pure beta-blockade; labetalol acceptable if beta-blocker essential
Phentolamine for refractory alpha-mediated HTN
Cooling for hyperthermia >39 degrees Celsius
Consult NSW PIC 13 11 26 early
explanation.pearls: The unopposed-alpha concern is best supported in cocaine ACS but extended to amphetamine by Australian guidelines. If the patient needs a beta-blocker for tachyarrhythmia, labetalol is the agent of choice because it has alpha-1 blockade built in.

options.rationale: In sympathomimetic-induced coronary vasospasm, nitrates relieve epicardial spasm directly and lower BP via venodilation without unopposed alpha effects. Australian toxicology guidance (NSW PIC, eTG) endorses benzodiazepines first, then GTN and phentolamine for ongoing hypertension or chest pain in cocaine/amphetamine ACS. Beta-blockers are avoided because of the theoretical risk of unopposed alpha-mediated coronary vasoconstriction.

Non-selective and selective beta-blockade is relatively contraindicated in sympathomimetic ACS because of the unopposed-alpha hypothesis; in Australian practice labetalol (mixed alpha-beta) is preferred over pure beta-blockade if a beta-blocker is essential. (Source: eTG).
Same concern as metoprolol; oral route also inappropriate in acute coronary syndrome with active hypertension. (Source: AMH).
Adrenaline would worsen the sympathomimetic state catastrophically; not indicated. (Source: ARC Guidelines).
Non-dihydropyridine CCB has negative inotropic effect risky in ACS with possible LV strain; not first-line. (Source: eTG).

explanation.summary: Clozapine's adverse-effect profile is broad and side-effect-specific monitoring schedules are mandatory in Australian practice. Mapping the presentation back to the side effect determines whether the drug must be stopped or continued. Acute chest pain + tachycardia + troponin elevation + dyspnoea in a clozapine patient is myocarditis until proven otherwise; mandatory cessation, cardiology consult, echocardiogram + cardiac MRI confirm. Other key clozapine adverse effects with their monitoring: agranulocytosis (FBC weekly 18 weeks then monthly), seizure (EEG/dose review at high doses), GI hypomotility (constipation history at each visit), metabolic syndrome (HbA1c + lipids 3-monthly first year), pulmonary embolism (high index of suspicion), sialorrhoea (clinical), hypotension (BP at each visit).
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis: peaks 14-21 days but possible later; mandatory cessation
Workup: ECG + troponin + CRP + NT-proBNP + echocardiogram + cardiac MRI
Smoking induces CYP1A2 - smoking cessation can double clozapine plasma level
Mandatory FBC monitoring: weekly x18 weeks, fortnightly x18 weeks, then monthly indefinitely
Re-challenge after myocarditis is not generally recommended in Australia
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation in a clozapine patient is a pharmacokinetic event - plasma level can double within 1-2 weeks. Always consult before any smoking change, including admission to a non-smoking ward.

options.rationale: Neutrophil count is 4.8 (well above the 1.5 mandatory cessation threshold); agranulocytosis is not occurring. The presentation does not fit; agranulocytosis typically presents with sepsis from infection, not chest pain and troponin rise. Source: Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol.

Clozapine-induced myocarditis occurs in 0.7-3 percent of patients, peaks 14-21 days after initiation but can occur later (especially with smoking-related metabolism changes). Presentation: tachycardia + chest pain + dyspnoea + raised troponin + raised CRP/NT-proBNP in a clozapine patient is myocarditis until proven otherwise. Mandatory cessation; cardiology review; echocardiogram for LVEF assessment; cardiac MRI for confirmation. Re-challenge generally not recommended. Source: RANZCP Clozapine Position Statement; Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol.

Metabolic syndrome is a recognised clozapine effect but does not present acutely with chest pain and raised troponin in a young patient. The acute presentation demands cardiac evaluation. Source: RANZCP.
Sialorrhoea is a common clozapine side effect but is unrelated to acute cardiac presentation. Source: AMH.
Gastrointestinal hypomotility is a serious clozapine effect but does not explain tachycardia + troponin + dyspnoea; the presentation is cardiac. Source: RANZCP.

explanation.summary: Choosing a regimen means weighing teratogenicity (favours lamotrigine, quetiapine over valproate, carbamazepine, lithium), efficacy in bipolar maintenance (favours lithium, valproate, quetiapine, lamotrigine, olanzapine), breastfeeding compatibility (favours lamotrigine, quetiapine, sertraline, olanzapine; avoid lithium, valproate, carbamazepine), and monitoring complexity (favours quetiapine, lamotrigine over lithium). Quetiapine satisfies all four; lamotrigine is reasonable for bipolar depression maintenance but less effective for mania prevention. Patient autonomy and shared decision-making frame the discussion: each option's evidence and trade-off should be discussed explicitly.
key_points: Valproate: absolutely avoid in women of reproductive age unless no alternative
Lithium: most efficacious but intensive monitoring; not first-line in BF
Quetiapine: best balance of efficacy, safety, BF compatibility, simplicity
Lamotrigine: best for bipolar depression maintenance; titration risk of SJS/TEN
Sudden discontinuation of mood stabiliser in pregnancy: relapse risk approaches 80% in 6 months
explanation.pearls: When discussing pregnancy planning in any woman of reproductive age on valproate, document the discussion explicitly - PBS access in Australia now requires a pregnancy-prevention attestation.

options.rationale: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy at any gestation (neural-tube defects, autism, lower IQ) and is single-strongest absolute contraindication in the Australian Pregnancy Category D listings for bipolar. Restarting is wrong. Source: RANZCP Perinatal Position Statement; AMH.

Quetiapine satisfies all four constraints: teratogenic risk is among the lowest of mood stabilisers/atypical antipsychotics in pregnancy (Pregnancy Category B3), has good evidence for bipolar maintenance, is breastfeeding-compatible (low RID typically <1 percent), and requires minimal additional monitoring beyond standard antenatal. Lithium is more efficacious but requires intensive monitoring (TFT, renal, lithium level), 12-week fetal echo for Ebstein anomaly, and is excreted in breast milk at significant levels. Source: RANZCP Perinatal Position Statement; Bipolar Disorder Australian Treatment Guide; LactMed.

Lithium is highly effective and reasonable in pregnancy if antenatal monitoring is feasible, but her plan needs minimal monitoring complexity AND breastfeeding compatibility - lithium requires intensive monitoring and is not first-line for breastfeeding women (high RID, neonatal toxicity risk). Source: RANZCP.
Carbamazepine is teratogenic (NTD, craniofacial defects) and is no longer recommended for bipolar in women of reproductive age in Australian guidance. Source: RANZCP; AMH.

Wait-and-see strategy in a patient with two prior manic admissions and one suicide attempt is unsafe - relapse risk during pregnancy off all maintenance approaches 80 percent in 6 months. Source: RANZCP.

explanation.summary: Severe AN with medical instability + treatment refusal is one of the few situations where the medical and mental health systems intersect operationally. MARSIPAN-AU (Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa - Australia/New Zealand) gives objective criteria for medical admission: BMI <14, HR <40, postural BP drop >20 mmHg, T <35.5, glucose <3, K <2.5, P <0.4, ECG QTc >500 or rhythm abnormality. When the patient refuses, NSW MHA 2007 Section 14 mental illness criteria (with eating disorder substantially impairing decision-making capacity around feeding) provides involuntary admission authority - even where surface capacity appears intact. Refeeding starts at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with pre-treatment phosphate + thiamine and progresses over 5-7 days under daily electrolyte monitoring. The principle: capacity to refuse weight restoration is not equivalent to capacity to refuse life-saving treatment for the underlying disorder.
key_points: MARSIPAN-AU admission triggers: BMI<14, HR<40, postural drop>20, T<35.5, gluc<3, K<2.5, QTc>500
NSW MHA 2007 Section 14 covers severe AN with treatment refusal
Refeed start: 5-10 kcal/kg/day, titrate over 5-7 days
Pre-treatment: phosphate + thiamine before any kcal
Cardiac monitoring mandatory: QTc, bradycardia, arrhythmia
explanation.pearls: Aboriginal Mental Health Worker referral is essential when the patient identifies as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander; cultural-safety governance under NSW MHA 2007 includes consultation with the patient's preferred community supports.

options.rationale: MARSIPAN-AU criteria for mandatory medical admission are met (BMI <14, HR <40, postural BP drop >20 mmHg systolic, T <35.5, glucose <3, K <2.5 [borderline], QTc >500 ms). Discharge would be negligent regardless of stated capacity, because severe AN classically presents with intact superficial reasoning but a circumscribed inability to weight-restore. NSW MHA Section 14 mental illness criteria can be met for severe AN where the eating disorder substantially impairs judgment. Source: MARSIPAN-AU; NSW MHA 2007.

Combined trigger: ALL MARSIPAN-AU admission criteria are met (BMI 13.5, HR 38, postural BP drop, T 35.2, glucose 2.8, QTc 510). Under NSW MHA 2007, severe AN with refusal of care meets Schedule 1 criteria when the eating disorder is judged to substantially impair the patient's ability to make safe treatment decisions about feeding/weight restoration. Refeeding starts low (5-10 kcal/kg/day; progress per protocol over 5-7 days) to prevent refeeding syndrome; phosphate and thiamine pre-treatment are mandatory; cardiac monitoring for QTc and arrhythmia. Family is consulted; the eating-disorder service is involved early. Source: MARSIPAN-AU; NSW MHA 2007; RANZCP Eating Disorders Position.

Starting at 30 kcal/kg/day in severe AN triggers refeeding syndrome (intracellular phosphate/magnesium/potassium shift causing arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy). MARSIPAN-AU protocol starts at 5-10 kcal/kg/day and titrates. The patient is also refusing care - voluntary admission cannot be assumed. Source: MARSIPAN-AU.

Guardianship orders take days to weeks; her condition is acutely life-threatening. NSW MHA 2007 provides immediate involuntary admission authority for psychiatric emergencies. Guardianship may be a longer-term consideration. Source: NSW MHA 2007.

Sedation and intubation are inappropriate in an alert cooperative-to-discussion patient. TPN is reserved for failed enteral nutrition; oral or NG is preferred. A rate of 25 kcal/kg/day on day 1 risks refeeding syndrome. Source: MARSIPAN-AU.

explanation.summary: Lithium is purely renally cleared. Its handling follows sodium: it is freely filtered and ~80 percent is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by sodium-coupled mechanisms. Anything that reduces GFR (NSAID afferent constriction, ACEI efferent dilation in low-perfusion states) or upregulates proximal sodium reabsorption (volume depletion, low-salt diet, thiazide) causes lithium reabsorption to climb and serum levels to rise. The narrow therapeutic index (0.6-1.0 mmol/L; toxicity 1.5+; severe 2.5+) and the neurotoxic accumulation (substitutes for sodium in CNS Na-coupled transport, accumulates in Purkinje cells and basal ganglia) produce the classic cerebellar + extrapyramidal syndrome. Management: stop lithium, stop the precipitant (NSAID, ACEI), aggressive IV crystalloid to restore renal lithium clearance, haemodialysis when level >4.0 mmol/L acute or >2.5 with neurological signs (lithium has small Vd, dialyses readily).
key_points: Lithium = 100% renal clearance; never hepatic
High-risk triple interaction: lithium + NSAID + ACEI (or diuretic)
Therapeutic 0.6-1.0; toxicity >1.5; severe >2.5
Dialysis indications: level >4 acute, or >2.5 with neuro signs, or AKI
Long-term lithium adverse: nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, renal interstitial fibrosis
explanation.pearls: When commencing any new medication for a patient on lithium, ask: does this drug change renal sodium handling? If yes, monitor lithium level within 1-2 weeks. The typical scenario is a patient with new-onset hypertension started on an ACEI without lithium re-monitoring.

options.rationale: Lithium is not metabolised by CYP450 (it is purely renally excreted). CYP enzyme interactions are not the mechanism. The other half of the option (Na-K ATPase + Purkinje cell effect) is partially correct as a mechanism, but the predictability claim is wrong. Source: AMH; eTG Toxicology.

MECHANISM: lithium is freely filtered at the glomerulus and reabsorbed in the proximal tubule via sodium-coupled transporters. Anything that reduces GFR (NSAIDs via prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar constriction, ACEIs via efferent arteriolar dilation) OR increases proximal sodium reabsorption (dehydration, low-salt diet, thiazides) causes lithium reabsorption to rise and serum level to climb. Cerebellar and basal ganglia neurons accumulate lithium because it substitutes for sodium in active transport. The triple combination of lithium + ACEI + NSAID is a well-recognised prescribing hazard in Australian general practice. Source: AMH; eTG Toxicology; Murray's Toxicology Handbook.
Lithium is NOT hepatically metabolised - it is purely renally excreted unchanged. CYP3A4 is irrelevant. Source: AMH.
Lithium actually INCREASES PTH (causes hyperparathyroidism over years), producing hypercalcaemia not hypocalcaemia. Tetany is not the clinical picture described. Source: AMH.
Lithium is not an antimuscarinic. Anticholinergic toxidrome is different (hot, dry, flushed, mydriasis, ileus) and not the cerebellar-extrapyramidal picture described. Source: eTG Toxicology.

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium therapy requires structured surveillance for renal, thyroid and parathyroid effects. Once a patient is stable, lithium level, U&E, TSH and corrected calcium are checked every 3 to 6 months. An eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m^2 warrants nephrology input to weigh ongoing lithium against relapse risk. Abrupt cessation or aggressive dose reduction is reserved for clear toxicity or rapid renal decline.
key_points: Routine lithium monitoring is lithium level, U&E, TSH and calcium every 3 to 6 months when stable
Refer to nephrology when eGFR is below 60 or declines rapidly
Avoid combined ACE inhibitor plus ARB therapy
Lithium nephropathy is usually a clinical diagnosis without biopsy
explanation.pearls: Nephrology referral threshold: eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m^2 OR decline greater than 4 mL/min per year.

options.rationale: Long-term lithium requires lithium level, U&E, TSH and calcium every 3 to 6 months once stable; eGFR below 60 warrants nephrology input for shared decision-making about continuation. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

Stable bipolar I on therapeutic lithium with stage 2 CKD does not mandate cessation; abrupt switch risks relapse and valproate carries its own monitoring burden. Continue with closer surveillance unless eGFR falls below 45 or declines by more than 4 mL/min/year. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

Halving a therapeutic dose risks subtherapeutic levels and mood relapse without clear renal benefit; dose reduction is reserved for levels above the target range or symptomatic toxicity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)
Adding a second renin-angiotensin blocker is not indicated and ARB plus ACE inhibitor combination increases acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia risk. (Source: KHA-CARI: CKD management)

Slow eGFR decline with minimal albuminuria does not meet criteria for urgent imaging or biopsy; lithium nephropathy is a clinical diagnosis with stable trajectory in most patients. (Source: KHA-CARI: CKD management)

explanation.summary: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism affects up to 1 in 5 patients on long-term therapy and is more common in women, especially with positive TPO antibodies. The standard approach is to treat with levothyroxine rather than to discontinue lithium, particularly in patients at high relapse risk. In a woman planning pregnancy, achieving euthyroid status before conception reduces fetal neurodevelopmental risk. Lithium itself is teratogenic but the absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is lower than historically taught and continuation may be appropriate with shared decision-making.
key_points: Lithium hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine, not by stopping lithium
Target TSH below 2.5 mIU/L preconception and in first trimester
TPO antibody positivity predicts lithium hypothyroidism
High relapse risk bipolar warrants continuation through pregnancy planning
explanation.pearls: Levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily is a reasonable starting dose in non-pregnant adults; titrate by TSH at 6 weeks.

options.rationale: Sudden lithium cessation in a high relapse risk patient is associated with manic recurrence; lithium nephrotoxicity is not the issue here and hypothyroidism is correctable. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is managed with thyroxine replacement rather than lithium withdrawal in a stable bipolar patient at high relapse risk; pregnancy planning increases the imperative for euthyroid status before conception. (Source: AMH: Levothyroxine)
Carbimazole is used for hyperthyroidism; the patient has biochemical hypothyroidism and thyroxine is required. (Source: AMH: Thyroid disorders)
Reducing lithium in a high relapse risk patient risks decompensation; subtherapeutic dosing is not justified by hypothyroidism which is independently treated. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

Delay risks worsening hypothyroidism through pregnancy planning and conception; TSH above 4 in a woman planning pregnancy with positive TPO antibody warrants treatment now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotic metabolic monitoring follows a structured schedule, especially in the first year. Weight, waist, blood pressure, fasting glucose and lipids are checked at baseline, 3 months, then 3 to 6 monthly. Olanzapine carries the highest metabolic burden alongside clozapine. Lifestyle intervention is first line for weight gain before adjunct metformin or antipsychotic switch.
key_points: Baseline, 3 month then 3 to 6 monthly metabolic monitoring during the first year
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic risk
Metformin is second line for antipsychotic weight gain after lifestyle fails
Switch to a lower metabolic burden agent is reserved for established harm
explanation.pearls: Metformin can be added if weight gain exceeds 5% over 3 months despite lifestyle and the patient is otherwise well controlled on antipsychotic.

options.rationale: While lifestyle counselling is correct, a single recheck at 6 months delays detection of rapid metabolic decline during the first year on a high-risk antipsychotic. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

Premature switching after only 3 months of effective treatment risks relapse; metabolic side effects should first be addressed with lifestyle and surveillance, with switch reserved for established intolerance or inefficacy. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

First year on a metabolically active antipsychotic requires 3-monthly metabolic monitoring including weight, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose and lipids; lifestyle intervention is first line for weight gain at this stage. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

Metformin for antipsychotic weight gain is considered when lifestyle measures fail and after at least 3 to 6 months; HbA1c 5.8% does not meet diabetes criteria and lifestyle is the first step. (Source: AMH: Metformin)

Risperidone is also metabolically active and may worsen prolactin; statin therapy is not indicated by current lipid profile or absolute cardiovascular risk in a 24-year-old. (Source: AMH: Antipsychotics)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia from risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride is managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing agent such as aripiprazole, quetiapine or olanzapine. Aripiprazole has the most evidence for prolactin reduction without antipsychotic withdrawal. Dopamine agonists are avoided where possible because they may precipitate psychotic relapse. Persistent symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia causes bone density loss in both sexes.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are high-prolactin agents
Aripiprazole is the prolactin-sparing switch of choice
Dopamine agonists risk psychotic relapse
Long-term hyperprolactinaemia causes osteoporosis
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive aripiprazole 5 to 10 mg added to risperidone is an alternative when switching is not possible; partial dopamine agonism normalises prolactin in many patients.

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists antagonise antipsychotic action and risk psychotic relapse; they are not first line for antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia. (Source: AMH: Cabergoline)
Dose reduction in a stable patient risks relapse and rarely normalises prolactin from this range; switch to a prolactin-sparing agent is preferred. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)
Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea is not acceptable to leave untreated due to bone density loss and quality of life impact. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)
Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing and often partially reverses antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia; switch is preferred over add-on cabergoline. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

Abrupt antipsychotic cessation risks rebound and psychotic relapse; quetiapine is reasonable but cross-titration is needed, and gynaecology referral is unnecessary if antipsychotic switch resolves the prolactin. (Source: AMH: Antipsychotics)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD in Australia is a long-acting stimulant, with lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate as preferred options. ECG and cardiovascular history are checked before initiation but routine cardiac imaging is not required without risk factors. Austroads guidance supports driving on stimulants when symptoms are controlled and there is no impairment, because treated ADHD has lower crash rates than untreated. Atomoxetine, guanfacine and bupropion are non-stimulant options reserved for stimulant failure, substance misuse risk or contraindications.
key_points: Lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate are first-line for adult ADHD
ECG and BP at baseline; no routine cardiac imaging without risk factors
Treated ADHD has lower crash risk than untreated
Atomoxetine is second line
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine starting dose 30 mg morning; titrate weekly to 50 to 70 mg based on response and tolerability.

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second line for adults and licence surrender is not required for legally prescribed stimulants. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)
Guanfacine is third line for adult ADHD and there is no 6-week driving ban; only sedation while titrating should be considered. (Source: AMH: Guanfacine)
Bupropion is not approved for adult ADHD in Australia and the premise that ADHD rarely requires medication is incorrect. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)

Dexamfetamine is a reasonable agent but the advice on police disclosure is incorrect; patients only need to comply with general driving licence and medical reporting rules. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)
Lisdexamfetamine is first line for adult ADHD per RANZCP guidance and Austroads recognises that treated ADHD is associated with lower crash risk than untreated ADHD. (Source: RANZCP CPG: ADHD)

explanation.summary: Nicotine withdrawal begins within hours of the last cigarette and peaks over the first two to three days, producing irritability, restlessness, poor concentration and craving. Australian smoke-free health care policy requires that nicotine replacement be offered to every admitted smoker; a 21 mg 24-hour patch suits a smoker of more than 10 cigarettes daily, with gum, lozenge, inhaler or mouth spray for breakthrough craving. Withdrawal is distressing but not medically dangerous, which is why benzodiazepines have no role. In context: an admission is a high-yield cessation opportunity, since perioperative abstinence of even a few weeks reduces wound infection and respiratory complications, and a patient stabilised on replacement in hospital can be discharged onto a full cessation plan.
key_points: Offer nicotine replacement to every smoker admitted to hospital, on admission
21 mg/24 hour patch for more than 10 cigarettes daily, plus a short-acting form as required
Benzodiazepines treat alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, not nicotine withdrawal
Unrecognised nicotine withdrawal is a common cause of inpatient agitation and self-discharge
explanation.pearls: Perioperative smoking abstinence for as little as four weeks lowers wound and respiratory complication rates, so the preoperative admission is a genuine treatment opportunity rather than a courtesy.

sources.label: NSW Health Smoke-free Health Care Policy

options.rationale: A heavy smoker admitted to a smoke-free facility needs nicotine replacement offered on admission; a 24-hour patch with an oral short-acting form controls withdrawal agitation and supports a postoperative quit attempt. (Source: NSW Health Smoke-free Health Care Policy)
source_refs: NSW Health Smoke-free Health Care Policy

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines treat alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, where autonomic instability and seizure risk are real. They do not treat nicotine withdrawal and add sedation and delirium risk before surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Varenicline suits a planned outpatient quit attempt with a nominated quit date a week ahead. It does not relieve withdrawal symptoms today and is not the acute inpatient answer. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

Leave to smoke would only be considered for a competent patient who declines nicotine replacement and is safe to mobilise. He has an unstabilised tibial fracture and untreated withdrawal. (Source: NSW Health Smoke-free Health Care Policy)
source_refs: NSW Health Smoke-free Health Care Policy

options.rationale: Deferral is reasonable only where a patient is nil by mouth and declines a patch. Untreated withdrawal drives agitation, hypertension and self-discharge in the preoperative period. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Droperidol 10 mg IM is the first-line parenteral sedative for severe acute behavioural disturbance in Australian emergency departments based on the DORM and DORM II studies. It offers fast onset, predictable duration and a favourable safety profile when QT prolongation risk factors are absent. Second-line options include olanzapine IM or midazolam IM, and ketamine is reserved for refractory cases. Continuous monitoring of airway, oxygenation and circulation begins as soon as feasible after sedation.
key_points: Droperidol 10 mg IM is first line for severe ABD in Australian EDs
Onset 10 to 20 minutes, repeat in 15 minutes if needed
Olanzapine IM avoided within 1 hour of benzodiazepines
Ketamine reserved for failure of standard sedation
explanation.pearls: Monitor for respiratory depression and check ECG once safe; QTc above 500 ms or known long QT favours olanzapine over droperidol.

options.rationale: Midazolam alone is associated with greater respiratory depression than droperidol in this setting and is second line in current Australian ED practice. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

Droperidol 10 mg IM is first-line for severe acute behavioural disturbance in Australian emergency practice; onset 10 to 20 minutes and good safety profile in agitated patients without known long QT. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

The haloperidol plus lorazepam combination is widely used internationally but has slower onset than droperidol monotherapy; current Australian guidance preferences droperidol. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

Olanzapine IM is an option but reserved when droperidol is contraindicated; combined olanzapine plus benzodiazepine within 1 hour increases hypotension and oversedation risk. (Source: AMH: Olanzapine IM)

Ketamine is reserved for failure of first and second line sedation; routine first-use ketamine in an undifferentiated patient is not standard and risks laryngospasm without airway preparation. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

explanation.summary: Severe sympathomimetic toxidrome with hyperthermia above 39, severe lactic acidaemia, rhabdomyolysis and airway compromise mandates definitive airway control rather than further procedural sedation. Ketamine RSI is preferred over suxamethonium because suxamethonium can exacerbate hyperkalaemia in rhabdomyolysis and induces sympathetic surge. Active cooling with cold IV fluids and exposure is the principal disease-modifying intervention; hyperthermia drives multi-organ failure. Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia and NMS, not psychostimulant toxicity.
key_points: Hyperthermia above 39 in sympathomimetic toxidrome warrants immediate cooling and airway control
Ketamine RSI preferred over suxamethonium with rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia
Dantrolene has no role in psychostimulant hyperthermia
Repeated sedation without airway control wastes resuscitation time
explanation.pearls: Cold IV crystalloid at 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes plus surface cooling can drop temperature by 1 degree per 30 minutes; target below 38.5 within 1 hour.

options.rationale: IM ketamine in this patient is acceptable as a rescue strategy but defers definitive airway control in a patient with active aspiration and severe acidaemia; the team is already preparing intubation, and IV access exists. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

Third dose of droperidol with benzodiazepine in an unstable patient with airway compromise wastes time and risks dropping BP without addressing temperature; intubation is required. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

Sympathomimetic toxidrome with hyperthermia above 39, rhabdomyolysis, acidaemia and airway compromise meets criteria for definitive airway control; ketamine RSI avoids sympathetic surge from suxamethonium and active cooling addresses the principal driver of mortality. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)
Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia and NMS, not sympathomimetic hyperthermia which responds to sedation, paralysis and external cooling; airway must be secured first. (Source: AMH: Dantrolene)
Suxamethonium without sedation is inhumane; further hyperkalaemia in rhabdomyolysis is dangerous; charcoal is not indicated for sympathomimetic intoxication. (Source: AMH: Suxamethonium)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is diagnosed clinically using Bush-Francis criteria and confirmed by a lorazepam challenge. Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV given over a few minutes with reassessment at 10 to 15 minutes is both diagnostic and the first treatment step. A clear response supports scheduled lorazepam 6 to 24 mg daily titrated to effect. Antipsychotics, especially high-potency first generation agents, can worsen catatonia and precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS and should be withheld until catatonia resolves. ECT is highly effective second-line treatment.
key_points: Bush-Francis is the standard catatonia rating tool
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia
ECT is second line and definitive treatment for refractory cases
explanation.pearls: Scheduled lorazepam doses of 6 to 24 mg per day are often tolerated without sedation when catatonia is active because of altered GABA tone.

options.rationale: Restarting an antipsychotic without first addressing catatonia risks precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome; lorazepam is required first. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)
Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS, especially in malignant catatonia; first-generation high-potency agents are particularly avoided. (Source: AMH: Haloperidol)
ECT is second line after lorazepam fails, although highly effective in malignant catatonia; a trial of lorazepam should normally precede ECT. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)

Lorazepam challenge with 1 to 2 mg IV is the diagnostic and initial therapeutic step for catatonia; a 50 percent reduction in Bush-Francis score within 10 to 15 minutes is supportive and guides ongoing scheduled lorazepam. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)
Amantadine is third line after lorazepam and ECT; structural imaging has already been done and contrast is not indicated for catatonia workup at this stage. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic anticonvulsant and is associated with major malformations in about 10 percent of exposed pregnancies and neurodevelopmental impairment in up to 40 percent. The TGA in 2023 introduced Pregnancy Prevention Program requirements for valproate, including documented annual counselling, effective contraception and acknowledgement forms for women of reproductive potential. Switching is considered when pregnancy is planned but must be done in a stable patient with bridging therapy. Lamotrigine and lithium are commonly used alternatives.
key_points: Valproate has 10 percent malformation risk and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk
TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program mandates annual documented counselling and contraception
Folic acid does not negate valproate teratogenicity
Switch to lamotrigine or lithium when planning pregnancy in stable bipolar
explanation.pearls: Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) such as etonogestrel implant or copper IUD is preferred for women on valproate due to user-independent reliability.

options.rationale: Polycystic ovary morphology is a recognised valproate effect but routine annual ultrasound surveillance is not standard; teratogenic counselling cannot wait. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

Premature switch may destabilise bipolar; condom-only contraception is not reliable enough for a teratogenic medication; counselling and effective contraception should come first. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

Folic acid does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity meaningfully and effective contraception is required during valproate exposure regardless of pregnancy plans. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)
Abrupt cessation risks relapse and quetiapine is not equivalent to valproate for bipolar maintenance; managed switch is appropriate but only after counselling. (Source: AMH: Sodium valproate)

Valproate carries up to 10 percent major congenital malformation risk and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk; Australian guidance mandates documented teratogenic counselling and reliable contraception for women of reproductive potential, with consideration of switch when planning pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: The NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD recommends structured psychological therapy such as DBT, MBT or schema-focused therapy as first-line treatment, particularly with recurrent self-harm. DBT has the strongest evidence and reduces self-harm, suicide attempts and inpatient days. Medication is reserved for clearly identified comorbid disorders and is not the primary treatment for BPD itself. Prolonged inpatient admission is generally avoided due to risk of regression and dependency.
key_points: DBT, MBT and schema-focused therapy are first-line for BPD
Pharmacotherapy is for comorbid conditions, not BPD per se
Avoid prolonged inpatient admission
Standard CBT and supportive counselling are less effective
explanation.pearls: Standard DBT comprises weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group, phone coaching and therapist consultation team for at least 12 months.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: DBT is the most evidence-based first-line treatment for BPD with recurrent self-harm, with reductions in self-harm, suicide attempts and hospitalisation in randomised trials. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Medication is not first-line for BPD and quetiapine is not indicated for emotion dysregulation alone; psychological therapy is the primary treatment. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Standard CBT is less effective for BPD than structured therapies (DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy); 12 sessions is also too short. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Inpatient admission is generally avoided in BPD outside of brief crisis admission; involuntary admission and routine pharmacotherapy worsen long-term outcomes. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: SSRI is not first-line for BPD without comorbid major depression; supportive counselling is less effective than structured BPD-specific therapy. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

explanation.summary: TCA toxicity causes sodium and potassium channel blockade leading to QRS widening, prolonged QT and ventricular arrhythmia, plus anticholinergic features and seizures. Indications for sodium bicarbonate include QRS above 100 ms, terminal R in aVR greater than 3 mm, ventricular dysrhythmia or hypotension. Standard regimen is 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus followed by infusion to target pH 7.5. Avoid class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics; treat seizures with benzodiazepines; intralipid is reserved for refractory arrest.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms is the trigger for sodium bicarbonate in TCA toxicity
Target arterial pH 7.5 with bicarbonate infusion
Avoid amiodarone, lidocaine and procainamide
Intralipid is rescue therapy in refractory arrest
explanation.pearls: Bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus, repeat every 5 minutes if QRS remains widened, then infusion at 100 to 150 mmol in 1 L D5W at 250 mL/h.

options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose or TCA toxicity due to seizure precipitation; the drowsiness here is anticholinergic plus TCA, not benzodiazepine. (Source: AMH: Flumazenil)

QRS above 100 ms in TCA toxicity is an indication for sodium bicarbonate; bolus 1 to 2 mmol/kg with reassessment is the standard antidote and reduces cardiotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Activated charcoal in a drowsy patient without secured airway risks aspiration; benzodiazepines treat established seizures but bicarbonate is the priority for cardiotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Magnesium has no evidence in TCA toxicity and amiodarone can worsen sodium channel blockade; class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Intralipid is rescue therapy in refractory TCA cardiac arrest; not first line; sodium bicarbonate precedes it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis in DSM-5-TR based on clinical signs such as Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, tremor entrainment and dissociative seizure features. Psychological stressor is no longer required for diagnosis. Communication of the diagnosis using clear language and pathophysiological explanation improves outcomes. First-line treatment involves physiotherapy for motor FND and CBT for cognitive aspects; antidepressants are reserved for comorbid mood or anxiety disorders.
key_points: FND is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical signs
Psychological stressor is no longer a DSM-5-TR diagnostic requirement
Repeated investigations reinforce illness; collaborative explanation is first step
Physiotherapy and CBT are mainstay treatments
explanation.pearls: Hoover sign: passive hip extension power on the weak side is restored when the patient is asked to flex the contralateral hip against resistance, indicating selective central engagement.

options.rationale: Repeated negative investigations reinforce the sick role and delay treatment; FND is a positive diagnosis not requiring exclusion of all alternatives. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Somatic Symptom Disorders)

Malingering requires intentional production of symptoms for external gain; the patient cannot consciously generate a positive Hoover sign and presence of secondary gain does not establish intentionality. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Factitious disorder requires conscious deception without external gain; positive clinical signs and absence of evidence of deception point to FND. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

FND in DSM-5-TR is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical signs such as Hoover sign and tremor entrainment; it does not require exclusion of all organic disease nor evidence of psychological stressor. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Somatic Symptom Disorders)
GAD does not cause focal weakness with positive Hoover sign; SSRI is not first-line treatment for FND without comorbid anxiety. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Somatic Symptom Disorders)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome risk is highest in BMI under 14, weight loss greater than 15 percent in 3 months, minimal intake for more than 10 days and pre-existing electrolyte derangement. ANZAED guidance recommends starting at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day in highest-risk patients with daily electrolyte monitoring and pre-emptive replacement of phosphate, magnesium and potassium. Thiamine 100 to 300 mg IV daily for 3 to 5 days precedes carbohydrate to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy. Calorie titration upwards is guided by electrolyte stability and clinical tolerance.
key_points: BMI under 14 is highest refeeding risk - start 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day
Pre-emptive phosphate, magnesium and potassium replacement
Thiamine before glucose load
Daily electrolyte monitoring in first week of refeeding
explanation.pearls: Phosphate falls 1 to 3 days into refeeding; check daily and replace IV if below 0.6 mmol/L or symptomatic at any level.

options.rationale: 30 kcal/kg/day at this BMI exceeds safe starting rate per ANZAED guidance and risks severe refeeding hypophosphataemia; starting rate should be 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day in highest-risk patients. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

Delaying nutrition does not prevent refeeding syndrome; structured low-rate feeding with concurrent electrolyte replacement is the standard approach with daily electrolyte monitoring. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)
Enteral is preferred over parenteral when the gut works; beta blockade in extreme bradycardia of anorexia is dangerous and contraindicated. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)
Ad libitum feeding in severe anorexia risks rapid refeeding syndrome and is not standard; structured low-rate refeeding with daily electrolytes is required. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

BMI under 14 with hypophosphataemia and bradycardia is highest refeeding risk; start at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day, replace electrolytes pre-emptively and give thiamine 100 to 300 mg IV daily for the first 3 to 5 days. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treated primarily with structured evidence-based psychological therapies. Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) has the strongest evidence base, with mentalisation-based therapy and schema-focused therapy as effective alternatives. Pharmacotherapy is symptom-targeted, short-term, and reserved for crisis or comorbidity; no medication is licensed for BPD itself. Prolonged inpatient care is avoided. Crisis plans, care coordination and skills coaching access are key adjuncts.
key_points: DBT is the most evidence-based first-line therapy
MBT and schema-focused therapy are effective alternatives
No medication is first-line for BPD itself
Avoid prolonged inpatient care
explanation.pearls: DBT consists of weekly individual therapy plus group skills training across mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, typically over 12 months.

options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy is first-line in BPD; DBT has the strongest evidence base, with mentalisation-based therapy and schema-focused therapy as alternatives. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)
Antipsychotics are not first-line and are reserved for short-term symptom-targeted use (transient psychotic phenomena, severe anger); psychotherapy comes first. (Source: NICE BPD Guideline)

Antidepressants are not first-line for BPD without comorbid major depression; symptom-targeted prescribing in BPD has limited evidence and may delay psychotherapy access. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)
Supportive therapy alone is inferior to structured therapies designed for BPD such as DBT, MBT or schema-focused therapy. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)
Prolonged inpatient care is not recommended in BPD and can worsen outcomes; community-based structured therapy is the standard. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)

explanation.summary: First-line treatment for adult PTSD is trauma-focused psychological therapy, with prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy or EMDR carrying the strongest evidence. Where therapy is unavailable, unacceptable to the patient, or insufficient, SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine are first-line pharmacotherapies. Watchful waiting is for the first 4 weeks post-trauma only. Prazosin and atypical antipsychotics are adjunctive options for specific symptoms.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first line
SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine when psychotherapy unavailable
Watchful waiting only in the first 4 weeks post-trauma
Avoid benzodiazepines for PTSD
explanation.pearls: Prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy show effect sizes around 1.0; benefit usually emerges within 8 to 12 weekly sessions.

options.rationale: SSRIs are effective but psychological therapy is preferred first-line where available and acceptable; this patient prefers therapy and meets criteria for it. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

Trauma-focused CBT (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) and EMDR are first-line treatments for PTSD with the strongest evidence; psychological therapy is preferred over pharmacotherapy where accessible. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Prazosin can target nightmares but is adjunctive, not first-line for PTSD as a whole; trauma-focused therapy addresses the broader syndrome. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Active PTSD at 6 months post-trauma warrants treatment now; watchful waiting is appropriate only in the first 4 weeks post-trauma. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Quetiapine is not first-line for PTSD and exposes the patient to metabolic and movement side effects without addressing trauma memory processing. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Autism in adult women is frequently missed because of camouflaging or masking behaviour, internalising symptoms, restricted interests in socially typical topics, and overlapping diagnoses such as anxiety, eating disorders and BPD. Formal assessment uses the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2), Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) and developmental history with collateral informants. Diagnosis enables NDIS access, autism-specific supports and reframing of previous diagnoses.
key_points: Adult women with ASD often masked or misdiagnosed
Sensory sensitivity, narrow interests, and burnout cues to assessment
Gold-standard assessment uses ADOS-2 plus developmental history
Diagnosis enables NDIS support and reframing
explanation.pearls: RAADS-R cutoff above 65 and AQ-50 above 32 in adults are suggestive but not diagnostic; formal multidisciplinary assessment is needed.

sources.label: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults
National Guideline for ASD Assessment Australia

options.rationale: Adult diagnosis of autism in women is increasingly recognised due to masking and previous misdiagnosis; this presentation warrants formal assessment. (Source: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

options.rationale: Antidepressants address comorbid anxiety but do not constitute assessment for autism, which would change formulation and support needs. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

options.rationale: Suggestive screening scores plus presenting features warrant formal multidisciplinary assessment using gold-standard tools (ADOS-2, ADI-R or developmental history with collateral); adult women often receive late diagnoses due to masking. (Source: National Guideline for ASD Assessment Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for ASD Assessment Australia

options.rationale: Sensory sensitivity, masking and restricted interests are not core BPD features; misattribution to BPD is a common pitfall in autistic women. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

options.rationale: Self-directed reading does not substitute for assessment; missing the diagnosis prolongs distress and burnout and delays NDIS access. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, within an illness that also includes a major mood episode (manic for bipolar type, depressive for depressive type) over a substantial portion of the total illness duration. Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms occurring only during mood episodes. Differentiating the two has prognostic and treatment implications: schizoaffective typically requires both antipsychotic and mood stabiliser long term.
key_points: Schizoaffective: psychosis 2+ weeks without mood symptoms in same illness
Bipolar with psychosis: psychosis only during mood episode
Schizoaffective treatment: antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser
Long-term prognosis intermediate between schizophrenia and bipolar
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine plus lithium is a common Australian first-line combination for schizoaffective bipolar type; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistance.

options.rationale: Psychosis predates the mood episode by 5 weeks, which does not fit mood-congruent psychotic bipolar; schizoaffective should be considered. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)
Schizophreniform does not account for clearly demarcated mood episode; the presence of a 3-week manic episode within the psychotic illness shifts the formulation. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)
Urine drug screen is negative and the presentation extends over 8 weeks beyond plausible intoxication or withdrawal; substance-induced disorder is unlikely. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

Psychotic symptoms persisting at least 2 weeks without mood symptoms within an illness that includes a 3-week manic episode meets schizoaffective bipolar criteria; antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser is first line. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)
Brief psychotic disorder is limited to less than 1 month; 8 weeks of symptoms and a co-occurring mood episode rule it out. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed positively using rule-in neurological signs (Hoover sign for limb weakness, tremor entrainment, dissociative seizure features on video EEG with preserved consciousness) rather than by exclusion. Patient explanation using the positive signs themselves and referral to FND-experienced physiotherapy and psychological therapy form the core management. Malingering and factitious disorder require evidence of intentional symptom production with or without external incentives, which is uncommon and not implied by clinical examination findings.
key_points: FND is a positive rule-in diagnosis using neurological signs
Patient explanation grounded in the positive signs is key to engagement
FND-specific physiotherapy and psychological therapy are first line
Malingering needs evidence of external incentive
explanation.pearls: FND has a similar prevalence to multiple sclerosis in neurology clinics; early diagnosis and FND-specific physio improve recovery, especially within the first 6 months.

options.rationale: Malingering requires external incentive (e.g. compensation, legal advantage); none is identified, and the patient is distressed and wishes to return to work, against malingering. (Source: DSM-5-TR; AAN FND Guidance)

Factitious disorder involves intentional symptom production for the sick role; positive rule-in signs of FND such as Hoover sign suggest a positive diagnosis of FND, not factitious. (Source: AAN FND Guidance)
SSD requires excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to somatic symptoms; the central feature here is positive rule-in motor signs, consistent with FND rather than SSD. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Stroke has been excluded by MRI and CTA; secondary prevention is not warranted and labelling stroke risks unnecessary medication. (Source: NHMRC Stroke Guidelines)

FND is diagnosed positively from rule-in signs such as Hoover sign and tremor entrainment, not by exclusion; explaining the diagnosis using the positive signs plus referral to FND-experienced physiotherapy is first-line. (Source: AAN FND Guidance)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is precipitated by carbohydrate reintroduction in severe malnutrition; insulin surge drives intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium causing severe hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmia, cardiac failure and Wernicke encephalopathy. Australian guidance for high-risk eating disorder admissions starts at 20 kcal/kg/day, escalates over 7 to 10 days, prescribes prophylactic thiamine 300 mg daily, phosphate replacement, and daily monitoring of phosphate, magnesium, potassium and ECG. ECG monitoring is essential as QTc prolongation and arrhythmia are leading causes of death.
key_points: Start refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day in high-risk patients
Prophylactic thiamine 300 mg daily and phosphate replacement
Daily electrolytes and ECG for 7 to 10 days
Avoid parenteral nutrition when gut functional
explanation.pearls: Phosphate below 0.6 mmol/L during refeeding warrants IV phosphate replacement (e.g. 30 mmol over 12 hours) and slowing calorie escalation.

options.rationale: Severe malnutrition with BMI under 14 and 2 months of low intake meets very high refeeding-risk criteria; prophylactic thiamine, phosphate replacement and daily electrolyte monitoring for 7 to 10 days are standard. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

Insulin is not used in refeeding; insulin surge from carbohydrate reintroduction is the underlying mechanism of refeeding syndrome and pharmacological insulin worsens this. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

Rapid escalation in severe malnutrition causes refeeding syndrome (severe hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmia, Wernicke); slow escalation with daily monitoring is standard. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)
Withholding nutrition prolongs starvation; refeeding is started cautiously with electrolyte replacement and thiamine before the first calories. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

Parenteral nutrition increases line infection and metabolic complication risk; enteral feeding is preferred when the gut is functional, even in severe malnutrition. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR, hypotension and seizure risk. QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR above 3 mm predicts arrhythmia and seizures. First-line treatment is IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeated to maintain QRS below 100 ms and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55, alongside airway protection and benzodiazepines for seizures. Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Hypertonic saline is an alternative source of sodium load when bicarbonate excess limits use.
key_points: Terminal R in aVR above 3 mm or QRS above 100 ms = sodium channel toxicity
Bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV first line
Avoid class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics and flumazenil
Lipid emulsion for refractory collapse
explanation.pearls: Aim arterial pH between 7.45 and 7.55 with serial bicarbonate boluses; sodium load and alkalinisation both reduce sodium channel blockade.

options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to standard measures including sodium bicarbonate; first-line for TCA-induced QRS widening is bicarbonate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR above 3 mm in TCA overdose indicates sodium-channel blockade with high risk of seizures and arrhythmia; IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg with airway protection is first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures; benzodiazepines are not the toxin here. (Source: AMH: Flumazenil)

Sinus tachycardia with QRS widening from sodium channel blockade does not require cardioversion; class Ic and Ia antiarrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Charcoal in a patient with GCS 9 without secured airway risks aspiration; airway protection precedes decontamination, and bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with proven superiority in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Initiation requires gradual titration starting at 12.5 mg evening day 1, then 25 mg day 2, increasing by 25 to 50 mg per day to a target of 300 to 450 mg by 3 to 4 weeks. Weekly FBC monitoring for the first 18 weeks then monthly captures clozapine-induced neutropenia (peak risk weeks 6 to 18). Weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks screens for myocarditis. Patients must be on a clozapine patient monitoring system. Seizure threshold lowered: avoid drugs and triggers.
key_points: Initiation: 12.5 mg day 1, titrate by 25 to 50 mg per day
Weekly FBC for 18 weeks, monthly thereafter
Weekly troponin and CRP first 4 weeks for myocarditis
Target 300 to 450 mg per day by 3 to 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation can double clozapine plasma levels via CYP1A2 induction loss; warn patients and adjust dose monitoring if smoking status changes.

options.rationale: Starting at therapeutic dose causes severe orthostasis, sedation, seizures and arrhythmia; gradual titration is mandatory. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as failure of 2 adequate antipsychotic trials; further antipsychotic delay clozapine, which is the only agent with proven superior efficacy in this group. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

Starting at 100 mg twice daily exceeds safe initiation rates and risks orthostasis, sedation and seizure; monthly FBC misses the high-risk neutropenia window in weeks 6 to 18. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)
Starting dose is too rapid and monthly FBC misses the high-risk neutropenia period; weekly FBC for 18 weeks is the Australian standard. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

Australian clozapine titration begins at 12.5 mg with gradual upward titration to therapeutic dose over 2 to 4 weeks; weekly FBC monitoring is mandatory for 18 weeks then monthly, with troponin and CRP weekly for first 4 weeks for myocarditis surveillance. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome is most pronounced with olanzapine and clozapine. RANZCP monitoring schedule: weight, waist, BP, fasting lipids and glucose, HbA1c at baseline, 3 months, 6 months and annually. New onset metabolic disease (type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension) is managed in parallel with antipsychotic optimisation: lifestyle (diet, exercise, smoking cessation), metformin first-line for diabetes (also has modest antipsychotic-associated weight benefit), statin per absolute CV risk, antihypertensive per BP. Switch to a lower-risk antipsychotic (aripiprazole, lurasidone) is considered if disease is severe and switch is acceptable to the patient.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine highest metabolic risk
RANZCP monitoring: baseline, 3 months, 6 months, annual
Metformin first-line for new T2DM; statin per CV risk
Switch to aripiprazole or lurasidone if severe and acceptable
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 to 2000 mg daily reduces antipsychotic-induced weight gain by 3 to 5 kg over 12 weeks even without diabetes; consider in patients with greater than 7 percent weight gain on antipsychotic.

options.rationale: HbA1c 7.4 with symptomatic hyperglycaemia warrants pharmacotherapy initiation per Australian diabetes guidance; deferral risks complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Abrupt switch risks relapse and discontinuation syndrome; first-generation antipsychotics carry higher extrapyramidal burden and are not the standard substitute. (Source: RANZCP Metabolic Monitoring)

Olanzapine has the highest metabolic risk among antipsychotics; switching is one option but in a patient stable for 18 months on a single agent, initiating metformin while continuing the antipsychotic is reasonable per Australian psychiatric metabolic guidance, with antipsychotic switch as a parallel consideration. (Source: RANZCP Metabolic Monitoring)

Clozapine has higher metabolic risk than olanzapine and is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; switching solely for metabolic reasons worsens not improves the metabolic phenotype. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)
Stopping antipsychotic in stable schizophrenia carries a 70 percent 1-year relapse rate; CBT is adjunctive not substitutive. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor disturbance with mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia and stupor. DSM-5 requires 3 or more of 12 features. Causes include mood disorders (most common in Australia), psychosis, autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic and toxic. Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is both diagnostic challenge (response in 70 to 80 percent within 30 to 60 minutes) and therapeutic; titrate to effect, often 8 to 24 mg daily. ECT is highly effective and indicated for lorazepam non-response or malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, rigidity, hyperthermia).
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is diagnostic and therapeutic
70 to 80 percent partial response within 60 minutes
Avoid antipsychotics (worsen or precipitate NMS)
ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia includes fever, autonomic instability and rigidity overlapping clinically with NMS; both are treated with urgent ECT plus benzodiazepines and stopping the offending drug.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and increase risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome; lorazepam is the established first-line challenge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is the standard catatonia challenge: 70 to 80 percent of catatonia responds at least partially within 10 to 60 minutes, supporting both diagnosis and treatment plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Untreated catatonia carries risk of dehydration, venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and aspiration pneumonia; immediate intervention rather than withdrawal observation is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is generally reserved for lorazepam-refractory or life-threatening cases (malignant catatonia, NMS-like presentation); lorazepam trial is first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Supportive measures (DVT prophylaxis, hydration) are important adjuncts but are not the primary intervention; lorazepam challenge should not be deferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation in psychiatric patients is safe and improves both physical and mental health. First-line pharmacotherapies are varenicline, combination NRT (patch plus short-acting), or bupropion. Varenicline is the single most effective agent. The EAGLES trial established safety in stable schizophrenia, depression and other psychiatric conditions, leading to removal of the FDA black box warning in 2016. Standard varenicline titration: 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily, set quit date at day 8, continue for 12 weeks. Bupropion is avoided in seizure disorder, eating disorders and abrupt alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
key_points: Varenicline most effective single agent for cessation
EAGLES trial: safe in stable psychiatric disease
Bupropion lowers seizure threshold
Combine pharmacotherapy with behavioural support
explanation.pearls: Smoking induces CYP1A2 metabolism; quit reduces clozapine and olanzapine clearance and may require 30 to 50 percent dose reduction over 1 to 4 weeks.

options.rationale: Patch monotherapy was tried last year and failed at week 4; escalation to varenicline or combination NRT is more effective. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

The black box warning was removed in 2016 after the EAGLES trial showed no excess neuropsychiatric harm; bupropion lowers seizure threshold and is less effective than varenicline. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy and is safe in stable psychiatric disease per the EAGLES trial; standard titration over 7 days reaches 1 mg twice daily. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)
Behavioural support alone has lower quit rates than combined behavioural plus pharmacotherapy; both are recommended together. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

Nortriptyline is second-line for smoking cessation with cardiac and anticholinergic risks; varenicline is first-line in motivated patients without contraindication. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian PTSD guidance recommends trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first-line treatment, with 8 to 12 sessions. Pharmacotherapy (SSRI: sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine) is reserved for patients declining or unable to access therapy, or as adjunct when therapy is insufficient. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated. Antipsychotics are not first-line. Comorbid substance use (especially alcohol) requires concurrent management; complete sobriety is not required to commence therapy. Co-occurring depression, dissociation and chronic pain are common and addressed simultaneously.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR is first-line
SSRI as adjunct or when therapy unavailable
Benzodiazepines contraindicated (impair extinction)
Concurrent management of comorbid alcohol use
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1 to 10 mg nocte has evidence for reducing trauma nightmares and is included as second-line adjunct in Australian guidance for nightmare-predominant PTSD.

options.rationale: Cannabidiol is not established first-line for PTSD; trauma-focused CBT or EMDR with concurrent alcohol use management is first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

SSRIs are recommended but psychological therapy is the preferred first-line; pharmacotherapy is offered when therapy is unavailable or insufficient, not as a substitute. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)
Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD; they impair fear extinction learning, are addictive and risk worsening avoidance. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)
Atypical antipsychotics are not first-line and risk metabolic harm; trauma-focused psychological therapy is the cornerstone of PTSD treatment. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

Australian PTSD guidance places trauma-focused CBT (or EMDR) as first-line, with concurrent management of comorbid alcohol use as adjunct; SSRI is added if therapy alone is insufficient or unavailable. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises when carbohydrate-rich nutrition triggers intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium in a chronically starved patient, causing arrhythmia, heart failure, seizure, rhabdomyolysis and death. High-risk features include BMI under 16, weight loss over 15 percent, minimal intake for 10 days, or pre-existing electrolyte abnormality. Management: thiamine 100 to 300 mg daily IV or oral starting before any feeds; correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphataemia and hypocalcaemia before and during refeeding; commence feeds at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring; ramp up over 7 to 10 days. Inpatient medical admission for BMI under 14, bradycardia under 40, hypotension, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia or syncope.
key_points: Thiamine 100 to 300 mg before any feed
Correct phosphate, potassium, magnesium pre-emptively
Start feeds 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day, ramp over 7 to 10 days
BMI under 14 + bradycardia requires inpatient admission
explanation.pearls: Hypophosphataemia below 0.5 mmol/L during refeeding triples mortality risk; replace IV phosphate (e.g. potassium phosphate 20 mmol over 6 hours) before increasing calories further.

options.rationale: High-calorie initiation in severely underweight patients precipitates refeeding syndrome; start at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day and correct electrolytes first. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)
BMI under 14 with bradycardia and hypotension requires inpatient medical stabilisation; community care is unsafe at this severity. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

Carbohydrate-rich rehydration without thiamine and electrolyte correction precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and severe refeeding syndrome; controlled feeding with thiamine is preferred. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

Severe anorexia with electrolyte derangement and bradycardia mandates pre-emptive electrolyte correction, thiamine before any carbohydrate, and cautious caloric ramp from 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

Parenteral nutrition is reserved for failure of enteral access and carries higher refeeding risk if initiated at full caloric load; enteral or oral feeding with cautious ramp is preferred. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring follows a structured schedule: baseline (weight, waist, BP, FBC, UEC, LFTs, fasting lipids, fasting glucose or HbA1c, prolactin, ECG), then weight and BP weekly for the first 4 weeks, weight and BP at 12 weeks, then fasting biochemistry at 12 weeks, 6 months and annually. Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole and lurasidone the lowest. Intervention triggers include weight gain over 5 percent, waist increase over 5 cm, new dyslipidaemia, prediabetes (HbA1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent) or diabetes (HbA1c above 6.5 percent), and warrant lifestyle counselling and consideration of switching to a lower-risk agent.
key_points: Baseline plus 12 weeks plus 6 months plus annual biochemistry
Olanzapine and clozapine highest metabolic risk
Switch trigger: weight above 5 percent gain or new dyslipidaemia or dysglycaemia
Prolactin only if clinical symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia
explanation.pearls: Adding metformin 500 mg twice daily reduces antipsychotic-induced weight gain and improves insulin sensitivity in patients with significant weight gain who must remain on the offending agent.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.rationale: Fasting lipids are part of the 12-week panel not deferred to annual review; metabolic effects emerge within weeks and require early detection for intervention. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.rationale: Olanzapine therapeutic drug monitoring is reserved for non-response, toxicity or adherence concerns; routine monitoring is metabolic biochemistry rather than serum drug levels. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.rationale: Routine ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated; baseline and 12-week ECG are sufficient unless QTc prolongation, syncope or family sudden death history exists. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
