source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.rationale: Antipsychotic 12-week metabolic monitoring includes fasting lipids, glucose, weight, blood pressure, waist, prolactin and ECG QTc; this is the time point for the first post-initiation set of bloods. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.rationale: Routine EEG and MRI are not part of antipsychotic monitoring; they are reserved for atypical presentations, new neurological signs or specific clinical suspicion. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

explanation.summary: Lithium long-term monitoring includes lithium concentration (target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance, 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for acute mania, taken 12 hours post-dose), renal function (U, E, creatinine, eGFR), thyroid function (TSH, free T4 if abnormal) and calcium (lithium causes hyperparathyroidism in around 5 to 10 percent of long-term users). Frequency is 3-monthly for the first 6 months then 6-monthly to 12-monthly for stable patients. ECG at baseline. Toxicity risk increases with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, dehydration and reduced renal function; review medications and fluid status at every visit.
key_points: Annual lithium, UEC, eGFR, TSH, calcium for stable patients
Maintenance target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L 12 hours post-dose
NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides raise lithium concentration
Hyperparathyroidism prevalence 5 to 10 percent in long-term lithium
explanation.pearls: An eGFR fall over 25 percent within a year on lithium warrants nephrology review and consideration of switching to valproate or lamotrigine; nephropathy may progress despite lithium cessation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Bipolar guidelines

options.rationale: Lithium 12-month review covers lithium concentration plus renal function, thyroid function and calcium to detect nephropathy, hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism as long-term adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Annual review includes lithium, U and E, eGFR, TSH and calcium together; lithium concentration alone misses the cumulative organ-specific toxicities that emerge over time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

FBC and LFTs are not specifically affected by lithium; renal function, thyroid function and calcium are the lithium-specific surveillance tests required annually. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Routine echocardiogram is not part of lithium monitoring; ECG at baseline is recommended but ongoing cardiac imaging is reserved for symptoms or specific risk factors. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Annual review is mandatory regardless of clinical stability because lithium nephropathy and hypothyroidism develop insidiously over years; deferring misses early intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, and the Australian Medicines Handbook lists a current or previous eating disorder, a seizure disorder, central nervous system tumour, and abrupt withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines among its contraindications; concurrent monoamine oxidase inhibitor use is another. Hypokalaemia from purging and heavy weekend drinking compound the risk. Combination nicotine replacement, a 24-hour patch matched to her cigarette intake plus an oral short-acting form for breakthrough craving, is effective and carries no seizure risk, and behavioural support is added regardless of the agent chosen. In context: choosing a cessation agent is a safety screen before an efficacy decision, so the eating disorder history, seizure history, pregnancy status and current medicines are established before the prescription is written.
key_points: Bupropion is contraindicated with current or past eating disorder and with seizure risk
Abrupt alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal is a further contraindication
Combination nicotine replacement is the safe effective alternative here
Screen for these before choosing an agent, not after the first seizure
explanation.pearls: Purging-related hypokalaemia and binge drinking each lower the seizure threshold on their own, so the contraindication is not a formality in this presentation.

options.rationale: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated with a current or past eating disorder and with heavy alcohol use. Combination nicotine replacement carries none of that risk and is effective. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)
This is the standard schedule for a smoker with no seizure risk factors, no eating disorder and no hazardous drinking. Her history makes the seizure risk unacceptable. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)
Waiting out hazardous drinking addresses one contraindication only; the eating disorder remains an absolute one regardless of how long she abstains from alcohol. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)

Nortriptyline is an unsubsidised later-line option when first-line agents have failed or are unsuitable, and it too lowers the seizure threshold and is dangerous in overdose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Deferral would be right only if a cessation attempt were destabilising her eating disorder treatment. Nicotine replacement is safe alongside it and her motivation is now. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 criteria: five or more inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (over six for under 17), symptoms present in two or more settings, evidence symptoms began before age 12, and significant functional impairment with other causes excluded. Workup includes childhood collateral (school reports, parents), adult self-report scales (Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, Connors), psychiatric history, substance use review and basic biochemistry to exclude differentials. Stimulant prescription in Australia is restricted to authorised psychiatrists, paediatricians and selected other specialists under state-based authority schedules. GP shared-care arrangements are common after stabilisation.
key_points: DSM-5 requires childhood onset before age 12
Specialist diagnostic assessment in Australia before stimulant prescription
Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale is a validated screening tool
Comorbidity with anxiety, depression and substance use is common
explanation.pearls: Stimulant prescribing in Australia requires individual state-based authority approval which is renewed annually; GPs may continue prescribing under shared care after specialist initiation in most jurisdictions.

sources.label: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Stimulant prescription is restricted to authorised paediatric, psychiatric or other authorised prescribers in Australia and cannot be initiated empirically without specialist diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Routine imaging and polysomnography are not required for adult ADHD diagnosis; they are reserved for atypical presentations such as new-onset symptoms or focal neurology. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Empirical antidepressant treatment without diagnosis risks missing primary ADHD and delays correct treatment; specialist diagnostic assessment should occur first. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Adult ADHD is a recognised diagnosis when childhood symptoms can be demonstrated to predate age 12; dismissing the presentation denies access to evidence-based treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires specialist assessment including DSM-5 criteria, childhood symptom evidence (school reports, parental collateral), adult symptom scales and exclusion of differentials. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: PTSD first-line treatment is trauma-focused psychological therapy: trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing. Both have strong evidence for symptom reduction over 8 to 12 weekly sessions. Pharmacotherapy (SSRI sertraline, paroxetine or fluoxetine) is reserved for patients who decline or cannot access psychological therapy, who have inadequate response, or who have comorbid depression. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated as they impair extinction learning and worsen long-term outcomes. Prazosin is an evidence-based adjunctive treatment for distressing nightmares.
key_points: First-line: TF-CBT or EMDR for 8 to 12 sessions
Sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine: SSRIs as second-line
Benzodiazepines contraindicated in PTSD
Prazosin adjunctive for distressing nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1 mg nocte titrated weekly to 5 to 10 mg specifically reduces PTSD trauma nightmares; first-dose hypotension warrants supine titration and warning patients about postural symptoms.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.rationale: SSRIs are effective but trauma-focused psychological therapies have superior evidence as first-line; pharmacotherapy is reserved for inadequate response or patient preference. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.rationale: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are the first-line psychological treatments for PTSD with the strongest evidence base for symptom reduction and sustained remission. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not recommended in PTSD as they impair extinction learning and worsen long-term outcomes; prazosin alone is reserved for nightmare reduction adjunctively. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling is less effective than trauma-focused therapy and does not address core PTSD symptoms; first-line trauma-focused therapy should be offered. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for risk to self or others, severe functional decompensation or treatment failure; outpatient trauma-focused therapy is first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is best treated with structured evidence-based psychological therapy. Dialectical behaviour therapy (12 months of weekly individual therapy plus group skills training) has the strongest evidence and is first-line where available. Other evidence-based therapies include mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy and transference-focused psychotherapy. No medication is licensed for borderline personality disorder; pharmacotherapy targets comorbid depression, anxiety, ADHD or PTSD when present. Crisis admissions are used briefly for imminent suicide risk only; planned brief admissions during crises help avoid prolonged admissions that risk worsening dependence and identity confusion.
key_points: DBT first-line evidence-based therapy for BPD
Mentalisation-based therapy and schema therapy are alternatives
No first-line pharmacotherapy approved for core symptoms
Brief crisis admissions only; avoid prolonged inpatient stays
explanation.pearls: Dialectical behaviour therapy includes mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness skills modules; commitment to the full 12-month structure is the strongest predictor of outcome.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: No medication has approval or strong evidence as first-line treatment for borderline personality disorder; structured psychological therapy is the cornerstone of management. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: Routine admission for self-harm in borderline personality disorder reinforces the behaviour and worsens long-term outcomes; brief crisis admissions are used only when imminent risk warrants. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: ECT is reserved for severe treatment-resistant depression or catatonia; it has no role in core borderline personality disorder treatment without comorbid mood diagnosis. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: Dialectical behaviour therapy has the strongest evidence base for reducing self-harm, hospital admissions and treatment dropout in borderline personality disorder over a 12-month program. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling has not reduced her self-harm or admissions; evidence-based structured therapy such as DBT, mentalisation-based therapy or schema therapy is indicated. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

explanation.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy is first-line treatment for severe depression with psychotic features, severe melancholia, catatonia, nutritional compromise, severe suicidality or treatment resistance. Response rates are 70 to 80 percent in psychotic depression. Standard course is 6 to 12 bilateral or right unilateral treatments over 3 to 4 weeks. Capacity for informed consent must be assessed; involuntary ECT is allowed only via specific tribunal processes under each state Mental Health Act. Common adverse effects include transient cognitive impairment (anterograde amnesia for events during the course, gradually resolving), headache and nausea. Mortality risk is similar to general anaesthesia for minor procedures.
key_points: ECT first-line for psychotic, melancholic or treatment-resistant depression
Response 70 to 80 percent in psychotic depression
6 to 12 treatments over 3 to 4 weeks
Capacity assessment mandatory; tribunal pathway for involuntary
explanation.pearls: Right unilateral ultra-brief pulse ECT delivers similar efficacy to bilateral ECT with less cognitive impairment when titrated to seizure threshold and dosed at 6 to 8 times threshold.

sources.label: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines

options.rationale: ECT is first-line for severe melancholic depression with psychotic features, treatment resistance, or where rapid response is needed for nutritional or suicide risk; response rates are 70 to 80 percent. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines

options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is a reasonable strategy in less severe treatment-resistant depression; here the urgency of malnutrition and psychotic depression warrants ECT first-line. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines

options.rationale: TMS is reserved for moderate non-psychotic depression and has lower response rates than ECT in severe psychotic melancholic depression; ECT is first-line in this presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines

options.rationale: Severe psychotic melancholic depression with nutritional compromise does not respond adequately to psychological therapy alone; biological treatment is urgent. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines

options.rationale: Severe melancholic depression with nutritional failure requires urgent intervention; further waiting risks aspiration, severe dehydration and completed suicide. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy professional practice guidelines

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR schizoaffective disorder requires an uninterrupted period of illness in which a major mood episode (manic or depressive) is concurrent with the criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia; delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime duration of the illness; and mood episodes present for the majority of total illness duration. Bipolar disorder with psychotic features differs in that psychosis only occurs during mood episodes. Schizophrenia differs in that mood episodes are brief relative to total illness. Treatment of schizoaffective disorder combines antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser; paliperidone is the only antipsychotic with regulatory approval specifically for schizoaffective disorder in many jurisdictions.
key_points: Schizoaffective requires 2 or more weeks of psychosis without mood episode
Mood episodes present majority of total illness duration
Bipolar with psychosis: psychosis only during mood episodes
Schizophrenia: mood episodes brief relative to total illness
explanation.pearls: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for schizoaffective disorder with treatment-resistant psychosis or persistent suicidality and may be combined with lithium or valproate for mood symptoms.

options.rationale: Bipolar disorder with psychosis requires psychotic symptoms to occur only during mood episodes; his persistent psychosis during a euthymic 12-month interval excludes this. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

Schizophrenia requires mood episodes to be brief relative to total illness duration; his recurrent meeting-criteria manic episodes exclude primary schizophrenia. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

Schizoaffective disorder requires psychotic symptoms for at least 2 weeks without prominent mood symptoms, with mood episodes present for the majority of total illness; this fits the collateral history. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

Negative drug screen and absence of substance-use history with documented inter-episode psychosis over 12 months exclude substance-induced primary diagnosis. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

Delusional disorder excludes prominent hallucinations or disorganised speech; his auditory hallucinations and disorganisation exclude this diagnostic category. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR delusional disorder requires one or more delusions for 1 month or longer, never met criterion A for schizophrenia (which requires two of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised behaviour, negative symptoms with at least one of the first three), functioning not markedly impaired outside the delusion, and symptoms not better explained by another mental, medical or substance condition. Subtypes are erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, persecutory, somatic and mixed. Treatment uses antipsychotic monotherapy (response rates 50 percent), and adjunctive cognitive behavioural therapy. Engagement is often poor because the patient does not recognise illness.
key_points: Delusional disorder: isolated non-bizarre delusions over 1 month
Schizophrenia: 2 or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganisation, negative
Brief psychotic: under 1 month with full return to baseline
Schizophreniform: criterion A symptoms for 1 to 6 months
explanation.pearls: Folie a deux (shared delusional disorder) develops when a partner of a primary delusional patient comes to share the delusion; separation from the primary patient often resolves the delusion in the secondary partner without medication.

options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires either hallucinations or disorganisation or negative symptoms in addition to delusions; his isolated delusion with preserved function does not meet criteria. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)
Brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms for under 1 month with full return to baseline; the four-year duration excludes this diagnosis. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

Schizophreniform requires criterion A of schizophrenia (delusions plus another psychotic symptom) for 1 to 6 months; his isolated delusion does not meet criterion A. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

OCD obsessions are recognised by the person as products of their own mind and resisted; his delusion is held with full conviction without resistance and excludes OCD with poor insight. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions over 1 month, no other criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia, preserved function apart from the delusion and exclusion of medical and substance causes. (Source: American Psychiatric Association: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR substance-induced psychotic disorder requires psychotic symptoms developing during or within 1 month of substance intoxication or withdrawal where the substance is capable of producing the symptoms, and where symptoms are not better explained by a primary psychotic disorder. Distinguishing features from primary psychosis are: clear temporal relationship to substance use, prior similar episodes resolving with abstinence, and symptom remission within days to weeks of abstinence. However, around 25 to 50 percent of patients diagnosed with methamphetamine-induced psychosis are later reclassified with primary psychotic disorder when symptoms persist. Observation over 1 to 4 weeks of confirmed abstinence is the most reliable way to separate the two.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis resolves within 1 to 4 weeks of abstinence
Persistent psychosis beyond abstinence indicates primary disorder
Brief antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine for acute safety
25 to 50 percent of methamphetamine psychosis is later reclassified
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine 10 mg orally is the preferred antipsychotic for acute methamphetamine psychosis due to sedative properties and benzodiazepine sparing; midazolam 2.5 to 5 mg IM can supplement for severe agitation.

options.rationale: Schizophrenia diagnosis requires symptoms outside the context of substance use and persistence after a period of abstinence; premature diagnosis misdirects long-term planning. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Substance-induced psychotic disorder with prior remission on abstinence and active intoxication suggests methamphetamine cause; observation over 1 to 4 weeks of abstinence clarifies primary versus substance-induced diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Symptomatic management with antipsychotic and benzodiazepine is needed for safety in agitation with psychosis; discharge without observation risks harm to self and others. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate antipsychotic trials; it has no first-line role in substance-induced or first-presentation psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Acute psychotic agitation requires psychiatric observation, antipsychotic and short-term benzodiazepine; transfer to residential detox alone misses safety needs and diagnostic clarification. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder shares phenomenology with primary schizophrenia. Diagnostic discrimination requires observing symptom course off cannabis: persistent psychosis beyond 4 weeks of abstinence suggests primary psychotic illness with cannabis as precipitant. Up to 50 percent of patients diagnosed with cannabis-induced psychosis are later reclassified as schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. Management is antipsychotic monotherapy (olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole as first-line) plus support for substance cessation through psychological therapy and contingency management. High-potency cannabis (THC content above 10 percent) and adolescent use significantly increase the risk of transition to primary psychotic illness.
key_points: Persistent psychosis beyond 4 weeks abstinence suggests primary disorder
Antipsychotic treatment required during active psychosis
Up to 50 percent reclassified as schizophrenia at follow up
High-potency cannabis (THC above 10 percent) increases risk
explanation.pearls: Cannabidiol (CBD) has shown modest antipsychotic effects in early trials but is not recommended over standard antipsychotics; recreational high-THC products with low CBD content carry the strongest psychosis association.

options.rationale: Persisting psychosis for 3 weeks already exceeds typical acute intoxication; safety risks and diagnostic uncertainty require admission and antipsychotic treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; first presentation cannabis psychosis is treated with a standard atypical antipsychotic such as olanzapine. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
Benzodiazepines control agitation but do not treat psychotic symptoms; antipsychotic medication is required for active psychosis lasting weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Cannabis-induced psychosis with persistent symptoms warrants antipsychotic and admission for safety and substance cessation; review at 4 weeks abstinent guides primary psychotic disorder diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Active psychosis requires immediate antipsychotic treatment; residential rehabilitation is not equipped for acute psychosis and delays appropriate management. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

explanation.summary: Valproate causes major congenital malformations in around 10 percent (neural tube defects, cardiac, craniofacial, urogenital), and neurodevelopmental impairment (autism spectrum, lower IQ) in around 30 to 40 percent of exposed pregnancies. Both effects are dose-related but no dose is safe. TGA, FDA and EMA have warned that valproate must not be used in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated and the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Program are met (effective contraception, annual review, signed acknowledgement of risks). Alternatives include lamotrigine, lithium (with monitoring), quetiapine, olanzapine, aripiprazole and carbamazepine (also teratogenic but less so).
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity: 10 percent major malformation, 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental
Pregnancy Prevention Program requires effective contraception and annual review
Alternatives: lamotrigine, lithium, quetiapine, olanzapine, aripiprazole
Folate 5 mg daily reduces but does not eliminate neural tube defect risk
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine requires slow titration over 6 weeks because of Stevens Johnson syndrome risk; combined oral contraceptive use halves lamotrigine concentration through enzyme induction so target lamotrigine dose may need adjustment.

sources.label: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.rationale: Valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless conditions of pregnancy prevention program are met; switch to safer agent plus effective contraception is recommended. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.rationale: Folate reduces but does not eliminate valproate-related neural tube defects; structural malformations and neurodevelopmental harms occur independent of folate supplementation. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.rationale: DMPA is effective contraception but does not address the high teratogenicity and cognitive risk; alternative mood stabiliser is the safer first-line strategy. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.rationale: Dose reduction does not eliminate teratogenicity at any dose; permanent sterilisation is not required, but effective reversible contraception or alternative drug is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.rationale: Mandatory contraception and teratogenicity counselling are required at every valproate prescribing visit; deferring the conversation is unsafe given the irreversible fetal risks. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes cardiotoxicity through sodium channel block (QRS prolongation, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia) and anticholinergic and alpha-adrenergic block. ECG predictors of toxicity are QRS over 100 ms (seizures and arrhythmias) and terminal R wave above 3 mm in aVR. First-line management is sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to narrow QRS toward 100 ms and target pH 7.45 to 7.55. Hyperventilation supplements alkalinisation in intubated patients. Refractory hypotension uses noradrenaline; refractory cardiotoxicity uses lipid emulsion as rescue. Class IA, IC, III antiarrhythmics, beta-blockers and physostigmine are contraindicated. Decontamination with charcoal is reserved for early presentation with airway protected.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms or aVR R above 3 mm: give sodium bicarbonate
Target pH 7.45 to 7.55 with bicarbonate boluses and hyperventilation
Lipid emulsion as rescue for refractory cardiotoxicity
Avoid antiarrhythmics, beta-blockers, physostigmine in TCA overdose
explanation.pearls: Terminal R wave above 3 mm in lead aVR is the most sensitive ECG predictor of seizures and ventricular arrhythmia in TCA overdose and warrants pre-emptive sodium bicarbonate even before QRS prolongation appears.

sources.label: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Toxicology

options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiotoxicity after sodium bicarbonate, hyperventilation and inotrope failure; it is not the first-line agent in TCA overdose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate cardiac arrest, seizures and bradyarrhythmia; sodium bicarbonate is the correct first-line treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

Sodium bicarbonate boluses for QRS prolongation above 100 ms in TCA overdose reduce cardiac sodium channel block by alkalinisation and sodium loading; target pH 7.45 to 7.55. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

Magnesium is used for torsades de pointes and refractory ventricular arrhythmia but is not the first-line treatment for TCA-related QRS prolongation; sodium bicarbonate is. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

Amiodarone and class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose because they prolong QRS further and may precipitate ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder (formerly conversion disorder) is a positive rule-in diagnosis based on clinical signs of internal inconsistency: Hoover sign (hip extension absent on direct testing but restored when contralateral hip flexion is tested against resistance), tubular visual field, give-way weakness, entrainment of tremor to externally cued frequency, and tremor or dystonia distractibility. FND is not a diagnosis of exclusion. Communication of the diagnosis emphasises positive signs and reversibility. First-line treatment is FND-specific physiotherapy and CBT with multidisciplinary input. Distinguishing features: conversion or FND is involuntary and the patient is distressed; factitious disorder is conscious symptom production for the sick role; malingering is conscious feigning for external gain.
key_points: FND is positive rule-in diagnosis using internal inconsistency signs
Hoover sign distinguishes functional from organic leg weakness
Treatment: FND-specific physiotherapy plus CBT
Distinguish involuntary FND from conscious factitious or malingering
explanation.pearls: Positive Hoover sign has a sensitivity of around 65 percent and specificity above 95 percent for functional leg weakness when carefully performed and is the single most useful bedside sign for this differential.

sources.label: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder

options.rationale: Malingering requires conscious feigning for external gain; her genuine distress and engagement with treatment make malingering unlikely without further evidence. (Source: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder

options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires conscious production of symptoms to assume the sick role without obvious external incentive; she does not deliberately produce symptoms. (Source: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder

options.rationale: Psychogenic stroke is not a DSM-5-TR diagnostic entity; functional neurological disorder is the correct term for positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency. (Source: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder

options.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder requires excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours about somatic symptoms over 6 months; her acute weakness with internal inconsistency signs is FND. (Source: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder

options.rationale: FND requires positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover, tubular field, give-way weakness) and is a positive rule-in diagnosis, not exclusion of organic disease. (Source: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder)
source_refs: Royal College of Physicians: Functional neurological disorder

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised by three or more of: stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerisms, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia and echopraxia. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale assists structured screening. Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV challenge produces dramatic improvement within minutes in 70 to 80 percent and confirms diagnosis; positive challenge guides scheduled lorazepam 6 to 24 mg per day. Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. ECT is highly effective and is first-line for malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, fever, rigidity) and for lorazepam non-response. Underlying causes include mood disorders, schizophrenia, autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA receptor), infections and medical conditions; workup proceeds in parallel with treatment.
key_points: Catatonia: 3 or more of 12 Bush-Francis signs
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV challenge diagnostic and therapeutic
Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS
ECT for malignant catatonia or lorazepam non-response
explanation.pearls: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with catatonia, orofacial dyskinesia, autonomic instability and seizures particularly in young women with ovarian teratomas; check CSF anti-NMDA antibodies when atypical features occur.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; first-line is lorazepam challenge followed by scheduled benzodiazepine therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment within 10 minutes confirms catatonia in 70 to 80 percent of cases and guides ongoing scheduled lorazepam therapy at 6 to 24 mg per day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

ECT is highly effective for catatonia but lorazepam trial is appropriate first-line in stable patients; ECT is reserved for malignant catatonia or lorazepam non-response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
Lithium does not treat acute catatonia; benzodiazepine therapy is first-line, with ECT for refractory cases regardless of underlying mood diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Polysomnography has no role in catatonia workup; MRI may be considered for atypical features but should not delay lorazepam challenge in classical catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance management follows a stepped approach: verbal de-escalation, environmental modification, and only then pharmacological tranquillisation. Australian first-line for IM route is olanzapine 10 mg (avoid combining with parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour due to respiratory depression risk) or droperidol 10 mg (Australian preference, IM or IV). Second-line is repeat olanzapine or addition of benzodiazepine after appropriate interval. Avoid IM olanzapine plus parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour. Continuous observation post-medication is mandatory: airway, breathing, vital signs and conscious state every 10 to 15 minutes for the first hour. Mechanical restraint is a last resort and the shortest duration appropriate.
key_points: Verbal de-escalation always first
IM olanzapine 10 mg or droperidol 10 mg first-line in Australia
Avoid IM olanzapine plus parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour
Continuous observation for 1 hour post-medication
explanation.pearls: Droperidol 10 mg IM has rapid onset (within 15 minutes), shorter duration than olanzapine and minimal QT effect at this dose despite the historical black-box warning; it is the Australian emergency department workhorse for acute behavioural disturbance.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: IV access is currently unavailable and forcible insertion in agitation is unsafe; IM route is preferred until the patient is safe to assess for IV cannulation. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: High-dose haloperidol with midazolam carries QT prolongation and respiratory depression risk; standard first-line single agent IM olanzapine is safer in unmonitored settings. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for prehospital and specialised settings with airway and full resuscitation capability; it is not first-line in ED ABD management protocols. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: IM olanzapine 10 mg is recommended Australian first-line for acute behavioural disturbance where IV access is unavailable; reassessment at 30 minutes guides further dosing. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: After failed verbal de-escalation with ongoing threats to staff safety, pharmacological tranquillisation is indicated; delaying medication risks staff and patient injury. (Source: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of acute behavioural disturbance

explanation.summary: Metabolic syndrome affects 30-50 percent of patients on second-generation antipsychotics, with olanzapine carrying the highest risk. Australian monitoring schedules recommend weight, waist, BP, fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, 3 months, then at least annually. Metformin is the first-line pharmacological adjunct for weight gain and dysglycaemia in patients who require continued antipsychotic therapy. Switching antipsychotics is preferred when psychiatrically safe, but past relapse on aripiprazole here makes maintaining olanzapine plus metformin the safer combination.
key_points: Olanzapine has the highest metabolic risk among atypicals
Annual fasting glucose, lipids, weight, waist for all patients on antipsychotics
Metformin first-line adjunct with 2-5 kg weight reduction
Past relapse on switching argues against repeating that strategy
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 mg twice daily started early in olanzapine treatment can prevent around half the expected weight gain at 12 months in first-episode psychosis, but onset of benefit is gradual and takes 8-12 weeks to plateau.

options.rationale: Lifestyle alone is insufficient when impaired fasting glucose and dyslipidaemia are already present; metformin augmentation is supported in AU practice for antipsychotic-related metabolic syndrome. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

Adjunct metformin reduces weight by 2-5 kg and improves glycaemic markers in patients with antipsychotic-associated metabolic syndrome without destabilising mental state, when continued antipsychotic efficacy is required. (Source: RANZCP; AMH)
The previous aripiprazole trial caused acute relapse with readmission; further switching risks decompensation in a patient with established efficacy on olanzapine. (Source: RANZCP)
Dose reduction risks psychotic relapse; GLP-1 RAs are not first-line in Australia for antipsychotic-associated weight gain and are unfunded for this indication. (Source: AMH)
Bariatric review is appropriate only after structured medical and pharmacological weight management has been trialled and failed. (Source: NHMRC Obesity Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires DSM-5 criteria including childhood onset before age 12, pervasive multi-setting impairment, and exclusion of better explanations. Substance use, mood, anxiety, and sleep disorders mimic and co-occur with ADHD; stabilising these first improves diagnostic accuracy. Only specific specialists (psychiatrists, paediatricians, neurologists) can initiate stimulant pharmacotherapy under PBS Authority. Stimulant choice and titration consider cardiovascular risk, substance use risk, and adherence patterns.
key_points: DSM-5: childhood-onset before age 12, multi-setting impairment
Collateral history (childhood) essential; ASRS alone is screening not diagnosis
Cannabis use disorder must be stabilised before stimulant trial
PBS Authority required: psychiatrists, paediatricians, neurologists only
explanation.pearls: ASRS-v1.1 Part A with four or more positive items has sensitivity around 68 percent for adult ADHD but specificity only around 80 percent, so a positive screen always requires formal diagnostic interview and childhood collateral.

options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires evidence of symptoms before age 12, multi-setting impairment, and exclusion of mimics such as substance use and mood disorders; cannabis stabilisation is needed because chronic use confounds diagnostic clarity. Only psychiatrists, paediatricians or neurologists can initiate stimulants under PBS Authority. (Source: RANZCP ADHD professional practice guideline; PBS)
Stimulant trials in active cannabis use risk masking the substance use disorder and are not diagnostic confirmation; stimulants must follow an established diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP)
EEG and MRI are not part of standard adult ADHD assessment; they are reserved for focal neurological signs or atypical features. (Source: RACGP)
Sertraline is not indicated for primary attentional symptoms; first-line ADHD pharmacotherapy is stimulants once diagnosis is established. (Source: AMH)
Neuropsychological testing supports but is not diagnostic alone; childhood history and collateral remain essential. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Tobacco smoke is a potent CYP1A2 inducer, accelerating clozapine clearance. On cessation, clozapine plasma concentrations rise by 50-70 percent within 2-4 weeks, risking sedation, hypotension, seizures, ileus and myocarditis. Australian practice is to anticipate clozapine dose reduction during cessation (typically 25-30 percent over 1-2 weeks), with clozapine-level monitoring at baseline, 1 week, 2 weeks, then monthly. Varenicline is first-line cessation pharmacotherapy with the highest quit rates; older neuropsychiatric concerns have been largely refuted by recent RCTs and post-marketing data.
key_points: CYP1A2 induction by smoking - clozapine clearance drops on cessation
Plasma clozapine rises 50-70 percent within 2-4 weeks of stopping
Anticipate 25-30 percent clozapine dose reduction
Varenicline first-line; NRT second-line; bupropion third (lowers seizure threshold)
explanation.pearls: Caffeine intake also affects clozapine via CYP1A2 - patients reducing or stopping caffeine simultaneously can compound the rise in clozapine levels; monitor caffeine intake at the cessation review.

options.rationale: Varenicline is effective, but clozapine levels rise 50-70 percent on smoking cessation due to loss of CYP1A2 induction; unchanged dosing risks toxicity (seizures, sedation, myocarditis). (Source: AMH; eTG Psychotropic)
NRT is appropriate, but the metabolic issue is the same: stopping smoking removes CYP1A2 induction and clozapine levels rise; dose adjustment is required. (Source: AMH)

Smoking cessation removes CYP1A2 induction; clozapine clearance falls and levels rise 50-70 percent. Stepwise dose reduction (typically 25-30 percent over 1-2 weeks) with serial level monitoring prevents toxicity while supporting cessation. Varenicline has the highest abstinence rate at 12 months in AU studies. (Source: AMH; eTG Psychotropic; RACGP Smoking Cessation)
Withholding effective pharmacotherapy from a motivated patient is not standard care; behavioural therapy alone has lower quit rates. (Source: RACGP)
Switching from an effective clozapine regimen risks relapse; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness and switching is rarely justified for smoking-cessation alone. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes mixed toxicity: sodium-channel blockade (QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR), anticholinergic effects (delirium, tachycardia, mydriasis, ileus), and seizures. QRS greater than 100 ms predicts seizures (15-30 percent risk) and greater than 160 ms predicts arrhythmia (50 percent risk). The cardiotoxic mechanism is shared with class IA antiarrhythmics; sodium bicarbonate alkalinises serum, increases extracellular sodium, and reduces drug-channel affinity, narrowing the QRS within minutes. Target pH 7.45-7.55. Activated charcoal is only useful within 1-2 hours of ingestion with a secured airway.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms = seizure risk; over 160 ms = arrhythmia risk
Terminal R wave aVR greater than 3 mm is specific for sodium-channel blockade
IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg, titrate to QRS and pH 7.45-7.55
Avoid physostigmine, flumazenil, class IA/III antiarrhythmics
explanation.pearls: Amitriptyline ingestion of 1 g (50 x 20 mg tablets) is potentially lethal in an adult of average weight; patients deteriorate rapidly within 2-6 hours of ingestion, so ED observation periods less than 6 hours are unsafe.

options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it precipitates asystole and seizures in the setting of sodium-channel blockade. (Source: AMH; eTG Toxicology)
Lipid emulsion is a salvage therapy reserved for refractory cardiac arrest or shock unresponsive to bicarbonate and standard measures, not first-line. (Source: NSW Health Toxicology)
Flumazenil is contraindicated here; it has no role in TCA toxicity and risks seizure precipitation. (Source: AMH)

QRS prolongation greater than 100 ms in TCA overdose indicates fast sodium-channel blockade; IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg corrects acidosis and provides sodium load, narrowing the QRS and stabilising cardiac sodium channels. Repeat boluses titrated to QRS narrowing and serum pH 7.45-7.55. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Magnesium is reserved for torsades de pointes; the threat here is broad-complex tachycardia from sodium-channel blockade, not QT-related torsades. (Source: ANZCOR)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor disturbance most commonly arising from mood, psychotic, or general medical conditions. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale of 3 or more of 14 screening items supports diagnosis; 14 or more total signals severe catatonia. Treatment is lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV, repeat to 6-hourly), with ECT for non-responders or malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and may precipitate NMS; they are withheld until catatonia resolves and the underlying psychosis is treated separately.
key_points: Bush-Francis 3 or more of 14 screening = supports catatonia
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV challenge first-line; 70-80 percent response
ECT if benzodiazepine fails or malignant catatonia
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolved
explanation.pearls: A negative lorazepam challenge does not rule out catatonia; the trial dose is too low for some patients, and scheduled lorazepam 1-2 mg every 4-6 hours often produces delayed response within 48 hours - escalate to ECT only after this trial.

options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV with response at 15 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia; response rate is 70-80 percent. If partial, repeat doses or scheduled lorazepam 6-hourly are titrated. (Source: RANZCP; eTG Psychotropic)
ECT is the next escalation if benzodiazepine challenge fails or in life-threatening malignant catatonia; a trial of benzodiazepines comes first when not malignant. (Source: RANZCP ECT guideline)
Antipsychotics in untreated catatonia risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome; further antipsychotic load is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)
Adds further antipsychotic load and is contraindicated; haloperidol is associated with NMS in catatonia. (Source: AMH)

Dantrolene is reserved for confirmed NMS; this patient's CK is mildly elevated but vitals and rigidity do not meet NMS criteria; catatonia and NMS may overlap but treatment of underlying catatonia comes first. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is the most common autoimmune encephalitis. The classic course is a prodromal viral-like illness followed by prominent psychiatric symptoms (mistaken for first-episode psychosis), then movement disorders, autonomic instability, seizures, and reduced consciousness. Diagnosis is by CSF IgG to NMDA-receptor antibody; serum antibody alone has lower sensitivity. First-line immunotherapy is IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days plus IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; second-line includes rituximab and cyclophosphamide. Ovarian teratoma is found in 30-40 percent of female patients; removal accelerates recovery. Delayed treatment correlates with worse long-term cognitive outcomes.
key_points: Psychiatric prodrome + movement disorder + seizures + autonomic instability = autoimmune encephalitis until proven otherwise
CSF anti-NMDAR antibody more sensitive than serum
First-line: high-dose IV methylpred plus IVIG or plasma exchange
Tumour search mandatory (ovarian teratoma in 30-40 percent of women)
explanation.pearls: Symptom-onset to first-line immunotherapy within 4 weeks is the single strongest predictor of full neurological recovery in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; delays beyond 4 weeks are associated with persistent cognitive deficit in 30-40 percent of patients.

options.rationale: Symptoms beyond psychosis (seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability) are not consistent with primary psychiatric illness; antipsychotic switching without organic workup misses an organic encephalitis. (Source: RANZCP)

NMS is plausible (rigidity, fever, CK) but the syndrome predates antipsychotic exposure and includes seizures, suggesting autoimmune encephalitis as primary, with NMS as a possible secondary diagnosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Symptomatic management without identifying the underlying cause delays disease-modifying therapy; outcomes worsen significantly with each week of treatment delay in anti-NMDAR encephalitis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)
ECT is reserved for treatment-resistant psychosis or catatonia after organic causes are excluded; in suspected autoimmune encephalitis it does not address the underlying disease. (Source: RANZCP)

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is the most common autoimmune encephalitis in young women, with psychiatric prodrome followed by seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, and reduced consciousness. CSF antibody testing confirms diagnosis; first-line treatment is IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days plus IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; ovarian teratoma (in 30-40 percent of women) is detected on pelvic imaging and removal accelerates recovery. (Source: BMJ Best Practice; ASCIA)

explanation.summary: First-line treatment for adult ADHD in AU is a long-acting stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine or extended release methylphenidate. Baseline assessment includes cardiovascular history, BP, ECG when indicated, and screening for substance use and psychosis risk. Titration with monitoring of BP, HR, sleep, appetite, and mood is standard. Driving counselling is important; ADHD itself impairs driving but stimulant treatment generally improves performance.
key_points: Long-acting stimulants first-line in adult ADHD
Baseline ECG if cardiovascular risk factors
Monitor BP, HR, sleep, appetite, mood at each titration step
Atomoxetine second-line for tics or substance risk
explanation.pearls: AU prescribers require state authority to initiate dexamfetamine or lisdexamfetamine; check the local Schedule 8 framework before starting therapy.

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line in adult ADHD reserved for stimulant intolerance, comorbid tic disorder, or substance misuse risk. (Source: RANZCP)
Modafinil is not registered for ADHD in AU and does not have an evidence base supporting first-line use in adult ADHD. (Source: AMH)
Bupropion is not approved for ADHD in AU and is only used off-label after stimulant failure. (Source: AMH)
Immediate release agents are second-line due to abuse potential and inconsistent symptom control between doses. (Source: RANZCP)
Long-acting stimulants are first-line in adult ADHD; lisdexamfetamine offers smooth release and lower abuse liability than immediate release agents. (Source: RANZCP ADHD; AMH)

explanation.summary: AU and international BPD guidance favours continuity of outpatient psychotherapy over inpatient admission for self-harm without imminent suicidal intent. Discharge with a brief safety plan, return precautions, and rapid follow-up by the treating team or service is supported. Pharmacotherapy targets specific comorbidities such as depression or anxiety rather than the personality disorder itself. Admission is reserved for high acute risk, escalating risk, severe comorbidity, or social vulnerability.
key_points: Continuity of outpatient psychotherapy preferred over admission
Brief safety plan and rapid follow-up within 48 hours
Pharmacotherapy targets comorbidities, not BPD itself
Admit only for high acute risk or escalating crisis
explanation.pearls: Brief admissions for BPD have been associated with reduced self-efficacy and increased re-presentation in AU cohorts; aim for community resilience-building rather than inpatient sanctuary unless safety cannot be maintained.

options.rationale: Continuity of established DBT with a brief crisis support plan is recommended over inpatient admission for self-harm in established BPD without imminent suicidal intent. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guidelines)
A brief follow-up review within days is recommended after self-harm to consolidate safety planning even if community follow-up is in place. (Source: NHMRC)
Voluntary admission for BPD self-harm without imminent suicidal intent is not supported and can reinforce avoidance of community skills practice. (Source: NHMRC)
Involuntary admission is not indicated when criteria are not met and disrupts established outpatient psychotherapy in BPD. (Source: NHMRC)
Pharmacotherapy is not the primary treatment for BPD self-harm; medication changes after a crisis presentation are discouraged in AU practice. (Source: NHMRC)

explanation.summary: Smoking prevalence in schizophrenia is over 50 percent and is the leading driver of cardiovascular mortality in this population. Varenicline and combination nicotine replacement are first-line pharmacotherapy with similar safety in stable mental illness as in the general population since the EAGLES trial. Behavioural support combined with pharmacotherapy doubles quit rates compared with either alone. Cytochrome P450 1A2 metabolism slows when smoking stops, which can increase clozapine and olanzapine plasma levels by up to 50 percent.
key_points: Varenicline safe in stable psychotic illness post-EAGLES
Combination NRT effective alternative
Behavioural support doubles quit rates
Clozapine and olanzapine levels rise on smoking cessation
explanation.pearls: When smokers on clozapine quit, reduce dose by 20 to 30 percent over the first 2 weeks and monitor levels and side effects; failure to do so risks sedation, seizure, and toxicity.

options.rationale: Dose escalation of aripiprazole is not an evidence-based smoking cessation strategy and risks increased side effects. (Source: RANZCP)
Varenicline is no longer contraindicated in psychotic disorders; the previous black box warning was removed after the EAGLES trial. (Source: AMH)

Varenicline is safe and effective in stable schizophrenia and is supported by AU smoking cessation guidance with routine monitoring for neuropsychiatric symptoms. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation; AMH)
Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and may interact with antipsychotic metabolism; varenicline is preferred when not contraindicated. (Source: AMH)
Inpatient nicotine detoxification is not standard in AU; outpatient pharmacotherapy with monitoring is the recommended approach. (Source: RACGP)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised by mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echo phenomena, and immobility. The lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg IV is the diagnostic and therapeutic first step; response within 10 minutes supports diagnosis and ongoing oral or IV lorazepam typically 6 to 16 mg daily. Antipsychotics should be ceased as they may precipitate or worsen catatonia and increase NMS risk. Refractory or malignant catatonia warrants urgent ECT.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV diagnostic and therapeutic
Ongoing lorazepam 6 to 16 mg daily commonly required
Cease antipsychotics in suspected catatonia
ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale of 2 or more items present for over 24 hours satisfies DSM-5 criteria for catatonia and supports proceeding to lorazepam trial.

options.rationale: Bromocriptine is not first-line for catatonia; lorazepam and ECT are the evidence-based treatments. (Source: RANZCP)
ECT is first-line for malignant or refractory catatonia and benzodiazepine non-responders; a lorazepam trial first is standard. (Source: RANZCP)
Dantrolene is reserved for NMS where temperature rises and rigidity dominate; the picture here lacks hyperthermia and severe rigidity. (Source: RANZCP)

A lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg IV is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia; a robust response within 10 minutes supports the diagnosis and guides ongoing therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)
Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS; they should be ceased or avoided when catatonia is suspected. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychosis typically resolves within days to weeks of cessation; persistence beyond a month supports an evolving primary psychotic disorder under DSM-5. Heavy use of high-potency cannabis approximately doubles lifetime risk of schizophrenia. Treatment with a second-generation antipsychotic, cannabis cessation support, and engagement with early psychosis services are central. Family history, premorbid functioning, and negative symptoms can all inform prognosis but none alone is diagnostic.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis typically resolves within a month of cessation
Persistence beyond a month suggests primary psychotic disorder
High-potency cannabis doubles schizophrenia risk
Family history raises risk but does not confirm diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Up to 50 percent of patients with cannabis-induced psychosis transition to a primary psychotic disorder within 3 years; early intervention services should follow these patients for at least 2 years.

options.rationale: DSM-5 distinguishes substance-induced psychosis from primary psychotic disorder by symptom resolution within about a month of substance cessation; persistence supports primary diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP First Episode Psychosis; DSM-5)
Negative symptoms can occur in both substance-induced and primary psychotic disorders during the acute phase. (Source: RANZCP)
Urine drug screen reflects recent use, not aetiology of psychotic symptoms, and is not a diagnostic gateway. (Source: RANZCP)
Temporal association alone does not exclude primary psychotic disorder; cannabis is both a trigger and risk factor for primary psychosis. (Source: RANZCP)
Family history raises risk but alone does not distinguish between substance-induced and primary psychosis. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Adult PTSD is treated first-line with a trauma-focused psychological therapy. The Phoenix Australia guidelines recommend TF-CBT and EMDR as comparable first-line options. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine, venlafaxine) are an alternative or adjunct, particularly for patients who decline psychotherapy or have prominent comorbid depression. Single-session debriefing is not recommended. Co-occurring substance use, depression, or chronic pain are addressed concurrently with PTSD treatment rather than sequentially.
key_points: TF-CBT and EMDR equally first-line for adult PTSD
SSRIs are alternative or adjunct treatment
Single-session debriefing not recommended
Treat comorbid depression or substance use concurrently
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1 to 4 mg nocte can reduce trauma related nightmares in PTSD where sleep disturbance dominates; consider adding when nightmares persist despite psychotherapy.

options.rationale: Head-to-head trials show comparable outcomes between TF-CBT and EMDR; neither is clearly superior. (Source: Phoenix Australia)
Supportive counselling is less effective than trauma-focused therapy for PTSD across severity levels. (Source: Phoenix Australia)
Both TF-CBT and EMDR are first-line for adult PTSD in AU; choice is guided by availability, clinician expertise, and patient preference. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD)
Trauma-focused psychological therapies are first-line; SSRIs are an alternative or adjunct, not the recommended first step. (Source: Phoenix Australia)
Single-session debriefing is not effective and may be harmful; structured trauma-focused therapy is recommended instead. (Source: Phoenix Australia)

explanation.summary: Varenicline and combination NRT (patch plus short-acting form) are the most effective pharmacotherapies for smoking cessation in adults. Varenicline is started one week before the quit date and continued for 12 weeks, with consideration of a 12-week maintenance course in high relapse risk. Combination NRT is a reasonable alternative for those who cannot take varenicline. Bupropion is third-line and contraindicated in seizure disorder. Behavioural support roughly doubles success rates of pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Varenicline and combination NRT are first-line
Start varenicline one week before the quit date
Treat for at least 12 weeks; consider maintenance
Add behavioural support to pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Varenicline achieves 6-month cessation around 25 percent versus 18 percent for single patch alone in heavy smokers; the FDA boxed warning for psychiatric effects was removed in 2016 after the EAGLES trial showed no excess risk.

options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest single-agent cessation efficacy and suits a planned quit attempt with no contraindications. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation; Therapeutic Guidelines)
Repeat patch monotherapy after prior failure has low success; escalation to varenicline or combination NRT is recommended. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)
Bupropion is third-line behind varenicline and combination NRT and is contraindicated in seizure disorder, but here varenicline is preferred. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)
E-cigarettes are not a first-line cessation strategy in Australia and are recommended only after registered therapies fail. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)
Behavioural advice alone is insufficient in a heavy smoker with prior failed attempts; pharmacotherapy adds substantial benefit. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Sertraline is the preferred first-line antidepressant in breastfeeding women because of the lowest measured infant serum concentrations among SSRIs. Paroxetine is an alternative. Fluoxetine has the longest half-life and active metabolite, leading to greater infant accumulation. Citalopram and escitalopram are acceptable alternatives if previously effective. Treatment should be combined with structured psychological therapy and a planned review at one and four weeks. Mothers should be reassured that breastfeeding does not need to be stopped.
key_points: Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in lactation
Fluoxetine accumulates more in breastfed infants
Add psychological therapy
Review at one and four weeks for response and tolerability
explanation.pearls: Infant serum sertraline levels are typically less than 2 percent of weight-adjusted maternal dose, which is the lowest of the SSRIs and underpins the COPE recommendation as first-line in lactation.

options.rationale: Fluoxetine has the longest half-life of the SSRIs and accumulates in breastfed infants more than alternatives. (Source: COPE; LactMed)
Citalopram is acceptable but has slightly higher infant exposure than sertraline and is not preferred first-line in lactation. (Source: COPE; LactMed)
Mirtazapine has less safety data in lactation and is not the preferred first-line agent for postnatal depression. (Source: COPE)
Sertraline has the lowest measured infant serum concentrations among SSRIs and is the preferred first-line agent in breastfeeding women. (Source: COPE; LactMed)
Venlafaxine has higher discontinuation symptoms and is not first-line in postnatal lactation. (Source: COPE)

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia with electrolyte derangement, bradycardia, and prolonged starvation is high risk for refeeding syndrome. ANZAED guidance starts feeds at 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine supplementation and daily monitoring of phosphate, magnesium, potassium, and glucose for the first week, with electrolyte replacement as needed. Bradycardia and orthostasis are markers of medical instability requiring inpatient monitoring. Psychological therapy and family work continue alongside medical stabilisation.
key_points: Start 20 kcal/kg/day, increase as electrolytes allow
Thiamine 300 mg IV before feeds in high-risk patients
Daily phosphate, magnesium, potassium, and glucose
Bradycardia and orthostasis are medical instability markers
explanation.pearls: Refeeding hypophosphataemia typically develops 24 to 72 hours after starting feeds; the threshold for replacement is phosphate under 0.6 mmol/L with IV potassium phosphate at about 0.3 mmol/kg over 6 hours.

options.rationale: Starting feeds at 5 kcal/kg/day is too restrictive and delays nutritional recovery; current ANZAED guidance starts higher with vigilance. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)
Starting feeds at 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and daily electrolyte monitoring is current ANZAED guidance for high-risk refeeding. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)
40 kcal/kg/day at BMI 13.6 with electrolyte derangement carries high refeeding risk; weekly bloods is insufficient. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)
TPN is reserved for failed enteral feeding or contraindications; oral or NG feeding is preferred. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)
High continuous feed without electrolyte and thiamine preloading risks refeeding syndrome and cardiac complications. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)

explanation.summary: Social and emotional wellbeing is the holistic framework for mental health in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, recognising connection to country, family, culture, spirituality, and community as integral. The first step in an engaged primary care assessment is partnership with an Aboriginal community-controlled health service and SEWB worker where available. Pharmacotherapy and psychological therapy can be added once a therapeutic relationship and cultural support are in place. Grief and loss responses, including Sorry Business, are part of cultural context and shape presentation.
key_points: SEWB framework rather than medical-model only
Partner with ACCHS and SEWB worker
Add pharmacotherapy and therapy once engaged
Recognise grief and loss in cultural context
explanation.pearls: The Kessler-5 is the validated screening tool for psychological distress in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations and replaces the K10 in this context; scores 12 or above warrant further SEWB assessment.

sources.label: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.rationale: Mainstream urgent referral is disproportionate without risk features and may worsen engagement with care. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy alone does not address social and emotional wellbeing or cultural context; partnership care is preferred. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.rationale: Six-week passive review without active engagement risks deterioration; supportive care should commence now. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.rationale: Self-help leaflets alone do not address SEWB context or family-centred preferences and underuse local services. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.rationale: Engagement with the Aboriginal community-controlled health service and SEWB worker centres cultural context, family, and continuity of care. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

explanation.summary: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure modestly and can unmask underlying structural cardiac disease or arrhythmia. Pre-treatment screening involves cardiovascular history, family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 years, examination, blood pressure and pulse, and ECG if any red flags. Cardiology referral with echocardiogram is indicated for first-degree family history of sudden cardiac death, syncope, or examination abnormality. Atomoxetine and guanfacine also affect cardiovascular parameters and are not exempt.
key_points: Family history SCD under 40 in first-degree relative: cardiology review
Syncope and structural exam findings need workup
Both stimulants and non-stimulants affect cardiovascular parameters
Continue BP and pulse monitoring throughout treatment
explanation.pearls: Methylphenidate typically raises resting heart rate by 5 to 10 bpm and systolic blood pressure by 2 to 5 mmHg; absolute cardiovascular event rates are low in healthy adults but family history of SCD under 40 mandates pre-treatment workup.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: First-degree family history of sudden cardiac death warrants cardiology workup before stimulant initiation. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)
Stimulants can unmask arrhythmia or structural disease; family history of SCD requires workup first. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)
Atomoxetine also affects blood pressure and pulse and is not exempt from cardiac workup with this family history. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)
Holter alone does not screen for structural disease; cardiology assessment with ECG and echocardiogram is preferred. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)
CBT alone is insufficient for most adult ADHD; pharmacotherapy is the first-line intervention after cardiac workup. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)

explanation.summary: Refugee health assessment requires trauma-informed care, accredited interpreters, and validated screening tools. The Refugee Health Screener RHS-15 is the recommended initial screening tool for distress, anxiety, depression, and PTSD symptoms in primary care. Onward referral to specialist services such as the state Survivors of Torture and Trauma services (STARTTS, FASST, ASeTTS) is indicated for positive screens or complex presentations. Pharmacotherapy is added after engagement with specialist trauma services where possible.
key_points: Use RHS-15 with accredited interpreter as initial screen
Refer positive screens to specialist torture and trauma services
Engage trauma-informed care principles
Pharmacotherapy follows specialist input where possible
explanation.pearls: The RHS-15 takes about 10 to 15 minutes, is available in over 15 languages, and uses a positive screen cut-off of 12 or above which flags about 80 percent of refugees with significant mental health needs.

options.rationale: Generic PHQ-9 has limited validity in refugee populations and a six-week passive review delays specialist input. (Source: FASSTT; RACGP)
Inpatient admission is disproportionate in a man without acute risk and may retraumatise a detention survivor. (Source: FASSTT)
Empiric pharmacotherapy without trauma-informed assessment misses culture and engagement priorities. (Source: FASSTT)
Avoiding mental health topics misses an opportunity to engage and signpost specialist trauma services. (Source: FASSTT)
The Refugee Health Screener RHS-15 with an accredited interpreter is the recommended initial screening and gates onward STARTTS referral. (Source: FASSTT; RACGP)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR, hypotension, and seizures. Treatment of QRS over 100 ms or R wave in aVR over 3 mm is intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus repeated until QRS narrows. Hypertonic saline is an alternative. Lidocaine is reserved for refractory ventricular arrhythmia. Activated charcoal is contraindicated with unprotected airway. Intralipid is a salvage option in cardiac arrest.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or R in aVR over 3 mm = sodium channel blockade
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus
Flumazenil contraindicated due to seizure risk
Secure airway before any oral charcoal
explanation.pearls: A terminal R wave in aVR greater than 3 mm predicts arrhythmia in TCA overdose with sensitivity around 80 percent; QRS over 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia and indicates aggressive sodium bicarbonate dosing.

options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose as it lowers seizure threshold further. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre; Therapeutic Guidelines)
This rhythm is sinus with sodium channel blockade, not a re-entrant SVT; adenosine has no role here. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)
QRS over 100 ms with R wave in aVR over 3 mm indicates sodium channel blockade and is the threshold for IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)
Glucagon is for beta-blocker overdose; she is tachycardic with sodium channel blockade requiring bicarbonate. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)
Charcoal is contraindicated with reduced GCS and unprotected airway; secure airway and correct sodium channel blockade first. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is characterised by one or more non-bizarre delusions for at least one month with otherwise preserved function, no prominent hallucinations or thought disorder, and no significant negative symptoms. Persecutory type is the most common subtype in late life. Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis usually includes hallucinations or thought disorder. Cognitive testing and imaging help exclude dementia. Treatment is challenging because insight is typically nil; second-generation antipsychotics at low dose are first-line with strong attention to therapeutic alliance.
key_points: Non-bizarre fixed delusion with preserved function
No prominent hallucinations or thought disorder
Persecutory subtype most common in late life
Second-generation antipsychotic at low dose first-line
