source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is the answer when catatonia fails an adequate benzodiazepine trial or the patient is deteriorating, not after a clear response (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Observation is appropriate only once signs have stayed absent off treatment; here the signs have already returned (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Hypotension in tricyclic poisoning has two mechanisms that need separating. Sodium channel blockade impairs myocardial conduction and contractility and is treated with sodium bicarbonate and sodium loading, which is what narrowed the QRS here. Peripheral alpha adrenoceptor blockade causes vasodilatation, which persists after alkalinisation and responds to a direct-acting vasopressor titrated to a mean arterial pressure that restores urine output. Inotropes, indirect agents and rescue therapies address problems this patient does not have. In context: tricyclic antidepressants remain among the most lethal agents in Australian deliberate self-poisoning. Management is airway control, sodium bicarbonate for a QRS above 100 ms or hypotension, benzodiazepines for seizures, a vasopressor for refractory shock, and early Poisons Information Centre advice on 13 11 26.

sources.label: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: The shock here is vasodilatory, from alpha blockade, once sodium channel blockade has been treated. A direct alpha agonist is the vasopressor of choice in Australian toxicology sources for tricyclic-induced hypotension that persists after fluid and alkalinisation.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: Dobutamine is an inotrope for cardiogenic shock with a poor cardiac index and adequate systemic vascular resistance, such as decompensated heart failure. Its vasodilator effect would worsen a blood pressure that is already low from alpha blockade.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: Dopamine acts partly by releasing stored noradrenaline, which tricyclics deplete and whose reuptake they block, so the response is unreliable. It is no longer recommended for undifferentiated shock in any case.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: More fluid is the right move when the patient is genuinely volume deplete, for example after prolonged vomiting or a long lie. He has already had an adequate bolus and further loading risks pulmonary oedema without correcting the vasodilatation.

Lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for cardiac arrest or peri-arrest from a lipophilic poison, classically local anaesthetic toxicity, when standard measures have failed. It is not used for hypotension that has not yet been treated with a vasopressor.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

explanation.summary: Separating a stimulant-induced psychosis from a primary psychotic illness is a longitudinal judgement, because the cross-sectional picture is identical and persecutory delusions, hostility and hallucinations occur in both. The features that point to the substance are onset in close temporal relation to use, resolution within days to weeks of abstinence, and a normal mental state during a verified drug-free interval such as a custodial period. Acute treatment does not differ much, since a short course of an antipsychotic with a benzodiazepine settles the episode either way, but the long-term plan does. In context: methamphetamine use disorder is common in Australian presentations of first-episode psychosis, and roughly a quarter of people with a stimulant-induced psychosis later meet criteria for a primary psychotic illness, so the label is provisional and the patient needs ongoing review, withdrawal and relapse-prevention support rather than indefinite antipsychotic therapy by default.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Psychosis beginning during or soon after intoxication, resolving within weeks of abstinence, and absent during prolonged verified drug-free periods, is attributable to the substance.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: This needs major mood episodes for most of the illness plus two weeks of psychosis without one. He has neither a mood episode nor psychosis when abstinent.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder describes psychosis lasting a day to a month with full return to baseline, often after a marked stressor, and it is diagnosed only when a substance is not responsible.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: This applies when psychotic symptoms persist through sustained abstinence or predate the drug use. It is the diagnosis to revisit if he becomes psychotic while clearly drug free.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires at least a month of non-bizarre delusions with preserved functioning and without a substance explanation, typically in an older patient.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

explanation.summary: Lithium chronic interstitial nephropathy presents as gradual eGFR decline over years. Routine monitoring is 3-monthly lithium and 6-monthly renal, thyroid, and calcium tests. Decline of around 25 percent from baseline or eGFR under 60 prompts confirmation of rate and nephrology referral to weigh continuation, dose reduction with closer level monitoring, or switching. Abrupt cessation risks relapse and is not done without a parallel plan.
key_points: Routine lithium monitoring: 3-monthly level, 6-monthly renal/thyroid/calcium
25 percent eGFR drop or eGFR under 60 triggers escalation
Confirm trajectory before changing therapy
Nephrology involvement guides continuation vs switch
explanation.pearls: Lithium nephropathy thresholds: confirm trajectory, refer nephrology when eGFR falls 25 percent from baseline or below 60 mL/min, do not stop lithium abruptly because relapse risk is high.

options.rationale: A persistent eGFR decline of around 25 percent from baseline over 6 years signals chronic lithium nephrotoxicity and warrants escalation rather than waiting for a worse eGFR. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

A trajectory of progressive decline with eGFR drop of 25 percent over years signals lithium-induced chronic interstitial nephropathy; confirming the rate and involving nephrology for risk-benefit re-evaluation is the recommended pathway. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

Abrupt lithium cessation increases relapse risk markedly; switching is a deliberate decision after nephrology input and consideration of alternatives and tapering. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

Adding ARB risks lithium toxicity through reduced renal perfusion and sodium handling and does not arrest lithium nephropathy; nephrology assessment first guides safe management. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

Halving dose risks loss of mood control and subtherapeutic levels without nephrology input; arbitrary dose reduction is not the appropriate response to a declining eGFR trend. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

explanation.summary: Smoking in pregnancy is managed with structured behavioural support first: brief advice at booking, referral to Quitline, and early review. Nicotine replacement is offered when behavioural support alone has not worked, with intermittent forms (gum, lozenge, inhaler, mouth spray) preferred over a patch, and any patch removed overnight, because pregnancy accelerates nicotine clearance but total fetal exposure is the concern. Varenicline and bupropion are not recommended in pregnancy on current Australian advice. In context: smoking in pregnancy raises the risk of fetal growth restriction, placental abruption, preterm birth, stillbirth and sudden unexpected death in infancy, and cessation before 15 weeks recovers most of the birthweight deficit, which is why the booking visit is the highest-value point to intervene.
key_points: Behavioural support with Quitline referral is first-line in pregnancy
Nicotine replacement is second-line; intermittent forms preferred, patch removed overnight
Varenicline and bupropion are not recommended in pregnancy
Household smoking and postpartum relapse are addressed at the same visits
explanation.pearls: Quitting before 15 weeks gestation returns birthweight close to that of non-smokers, so the booking visit carries more preventive value than any later antenatal contact.

options.rationale: Structured behavioural support is first-line in pregnancy and the only intervention with clear benefit and no fetal exposure; pharmacotherapy is considered if she continues to smoke despite it. (Source: Pregnancy Care Guidelines: Tobacco smoking)

Varenicline is the most effective agent outside pregnancy, where it is first-line for a dependent smoker. Safety data in pregnancy are insufficient and it is not recommended. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)
Bupropion is a second-line option for a non-pregnant smoker without seizure risk or an eating disorder. It is not recommended in pregnancy. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)

Replacement is offered when behavioural support alone fails, and then intermittent forms are preferred; a patch is removed overnight to limit total fetal nicotine exposure. (Source: Pregnancy Care Guidelines: Tobacco smoking)

Reduction is a reasonable interim goal only for a woman who refuses a quit attempt. Cutting down does not remove the risks of growth restriction, abruption and stillbirth. (Source: RANZCOG: Substance use in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is best treated with structured psychological therapy delivered over at least 12 months: dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy, schema therapy, or transference-focused psychotherapy. Medication is adjunctive for co-morbid depression, anxiety, or psychotic-like symptoms but not first-line monotherapy. Brief admissions for safety are acceptable; long admissions are counterproductive. Crisis planning, written safety plans, and consistent case management are foundational.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy at least 12 months is first-line
DBT, MBT, schema, or TFP are evidence-based
Medications adjunctive only
Avoid prolonged inpatient stays
explanation.pearls: NHMRC BPD guideline: structured psychotherapy (DBT/MBT/schema/TFP) for at least 12 months is the first-line; long admissions worsen outcomes through dependency.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient admission for BPD reinforces dependency and undermines self-regulation skills; community-based structured psychotherapy is the first-line. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: There is no medication approved as first-line monotherapy for BPD; medications are used adjunctively for specific co-morbidities. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Brief CBT is insufficient for BPD; structured longer-term therapies such as DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, or schema therapy have evidence for sustained improvement. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: The NHMRC BPD guideline recommends structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy, or transference-focused psychotherapy) for at least 12 months as the first-line treatment, with crisis planning and case management. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Discharge without structured therapy misses the evidence-based intervention; SSRIs are not specifically effective for BPD as monotherapy. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring requires baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids, blood pressure, and ECG. Reassessment at 6 and 12 weeks then 3-monthly to 1 year is recommended for second-generation agents, with annual review thereafter if stable. Deterioration prompts lifestyle intervention, consideration of switching to less metabolically active agents (such as aripiprazole), and adjuncts such as metformin where appropriate. Continued treatment is essential in first-episode psychosis.
key_points: Baseline + 6, 12 week, 3-monthly to 1 year, then annual
Aripiprazole less weight/glucose adverse than olanzapine
Metformin adjunct can mitigate weight gain
Lifestyle intervention always added
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine carries highest metabolic burden of second-generation antipsychotics; switching to aripiprazole when deterioration occurs improves the metabolic trajectory while maintaining psychosis treatment.

options.rationale: Multiple metabolic parameters have moved adversely (weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids, BP), reflecting evolving metabolic syndrome; intervention rather than annual review is needed. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

Metformin can mitigate antipsychotic weight gain but is added alongside diet, exercise, and consideration of antipsychotic switch where appropriate, not as the sole intervention. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

Abrupt cessation with cross-taper to ziprasidone, which has QTc concerns and is not currently PBS-listed in Australia, is not appropriate as the immediate response. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

First-episode psychosis benefits from at least 12 to 24 months of maintenance treatment to reduce relapse; abandonment of antipsychotic therapy after metabolic concerns alone is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

RANZCP recommends combining lifestyle intervention with consideration of switching to a less weight-and-glucose-adverse antipsychotic such as aripiprazole when metabolic deterioration develops; reassessment within 12 weeks confirms response. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is associated with around 10 percent neural tube defects, cleft palate, hypospadias, and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental impairment in exposed offspring. TGA guidance restricts valproate prescription in women of childbearing potential to those for whom no alternative is appropriate, mandates highly effective contraception (LARC or sterilisation), and requires annual review with risk acknowledgement. Cross-taper to lamotrigine or low-dose lithium are preferred when planning pregnancy, with perinatal psychiatry support.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity: ~10 percent major malformation, 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandatory in women of childbearing potential
Switch to lamotrigine or low-dose lithium before conception
Perinatal psychiatry referral for planning
explanation.pearls: Valproate in pregnancy: 10 percent major malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental harm; TGA mandates highly effective contraception and transition to lamotrigine before planned conception.

options.rationale: Valproate causes neural tube defects in around 10 percent and cognitive impairment in around 30 to 40 percent of exposed offspring; folate supplementation does not mitigate these risks. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)
Teratogenicity is dose-related but no dose is considered safe in early pregnancy; reducing dose risks relapse and does not eliminate teratogenicity. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (around 3 percent neural tube defects, hand abnormalities, and cardiac defects) and is not the preferred substitute in women planning pregnancy. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

Australian TGA pregnancy-prevention guidance for valproate requires highly effective contraception in women of childbearing potential, transition to a safer mood stabiliser such as lamotrigine before conception, and specialist perinatal psychiatric input. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

Untreated bipolar disorder during planned conception risks severe relapse with associated maternal and fetal harm; substitution rather than monotherapy cessation is required. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

explanation.summary: SSRI discontinuation syndrome appears within 1 to 7 days of stopping or markedly reducing an SSRI/SNRI and is most common with paroxetine and venlafaxine (short half-lives). Features (FINISH mnemonic) include flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbance (electric-shock paraesthesia), and hyperarousal. Distinguish from depressive recurrence by rapid onset, prominent physical/sensory features, preserved mood reactivity, and resolution within 24 to 48 hours of reinstating the SSRI. Management is restart and slow taper, with fluoxetine bridging reserved for resistant cases.
key_points: Onset 1-7 days post stop; resolves within 1-3 weeks if untreated.
Paroxetine and venlafaxine highest risk.
FINISH: flu, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory, hyperarousal.
Restart + slow taper; fluoxetine bridge only if persistent.
explanation.pearls: Taper paroxetine by 5 mg every 1 to 2 weeks (or slower) and watch for re-emergence at each step; agomelatine and bupropion have low discontinuation rates and may be preferable in patients with poor taper tolerance.

options.rationale: Fluoxetine bridging is reserved for severe persistent discontinuation symptoms despite reintroduction of the original SSRI; first step is to resume the original drug and taper. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

Symptomatic treatment with antiemetics does not address the underlying serotonergic withdrawal and adds prochlorperazine-related extrapyramidal risk; addressing the cause is preferable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

Symptoms are functionally limiting and last 1 to 3 weeks if untreated with paroxetine (highest-risk SSRI for discontinuation due to short half-life); resumption and slow taper is recommended over watchful waiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

Mood remains in remission with reactive affect, preserved enjoyment, sleep, appetite, and no suicidality; symptom timing and physical features (paraesthesia, electric shocks) point to discontinuation syndrome rather than depressive recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

Onset within days of cessation with classic FINISH features (flu-like, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory paraesthesia, hyperarousal) plus preserved mood and reactivity strongly favours discontinuation syndrome; resumption resolves symptoms within 24 to 48 hours then slow taper prevents recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

explanation.summary: For self-harm crises in BPD, Australian NHMRC guidelines emphasise active coordination with the existing structured psychotherapy team (DBT, MBT, schema), use of the patient's individualised safety plan, family/carer involvement when agreed, and avoiding both lengthy inpatient admission (which can reinforce maladaptive behaviour) and reflexive involuntary detention. Brief admission is reserved for risk that cannot be managed in community. No psychotropic medication has been shown to treat the core features of BPD; pharmacotherapy is reserved for clearly diagnosed comorbid disorders and reviewed regularly. Rapid follow-up within 24 to 72 hours is critical.
key_points: Avoid prolonged admission for BPD self-harm.
Coordinate with existing DBT/MBT/schema team.
Activate individualised safety plan + carer involvement.
No drug treats BPD; treat clear comorbidities only.
explanation.pearls: Means restriction (small quantities of analgesics, locked supply with carer) reduces lethality of impulsive overdoses; document the safety plan jointly and share it with the GP and DBT team before discharge.

sources.label: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for BPD

options.rationale: NHMRC guidelines recommend avoiding lengthy psychiatric admission for BPD self-harm and instead coordinating with the existing structured treatment (DBT) team, activating an agreed safety plan, ensuring rapid follow-up and engaging family/carer support; this preserves therapeutic momentum and avoids reinforcing maladaptive coping. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: There is no PBS-recognised medication that treats BPD itself; quetiapine has unproven benefit, sedates, contributes to metabolic side effects, and a 7-day supply hands a vulnerable patient potential overdose means. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic recurrent low-lethality self-harm in BPD is not therapeutic, breaches least-restrictive principles, and may damage the established therapeutic relationship; criteria for compulsion are not met. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Brief admission for BPD self-harm is associated with worsening behaviour, regression, and dependency; Australian guidelines advise the shortest possible admission only when there is acute risk that cannot be managed in the community. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Discharge without contacting the existing care team fragments care and misses the opportunity to align with her individualised crisis and safety plan; this is the commonest preventable adverse outcome after ED presentation in BPD. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: ANZAED and RANZCP criteria for medical inpatient admission in anorexia include BMI under 14 (or under 15 in some thresholds), HR under 40, postural drop above 20 mmHg or postural HR rise above 20, hypothermia under 35.5 C, hypoglycaemia under 3.0, hypokalaemia under 3.0, hypophosphataemia, QTc above 460 ms, syncope, severe dehydration, or organ failure. Admission allows cardiac monitoring, supervised refeeding (start at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with daily phosphate and electrolyte checks), and management of refeeding syndrome. Family-based or CBT-E therapy follows once medically stable.
key_points: Medical admit: BMI<14, HR<40, postural drop, QTc>460.
Hypophosphataemia and hypokalaemia are red flags.
Refeed at 20-30 kcal/kg/day, monitor phosphate daily.
Family-based or CBT-E once stable.
explanation.pearls: Phosphate falls within 24 to 72 hours of refeeding starting; supplement prophylactically with oral or IV phosphate when baseline is at or below 0.7 mmol/L, and consider thiamine 100 mg before any carbohydrate-containing fluids.

options.rationale: Day programs suit medically stable patients with BMI typically above 14 to 15; current vital signs and biochemistry require inpatient cardiac monitoring and supervised refeeding. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

Multiple ANZAED medical admission criteria are met (BMI 13.8, HR 38, postural BP drop, hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, QTc 478, hypothermia 35.4); inpatient medical admission for cautious refeeding with cardiac monitoring is required to prevent arrhythmia and refeeding syndrome. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

Olanzapine has weak evidence in anorexia and does not address the acute medical instability; medical stabilisation is the priority and pharmacotherapy is adjunctive at best. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

She meets multiple ANZAED medical admission criteria (BMI under 14, bradycardia under 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg, hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, hypothermia, QTc above 460); outpatient management is unsafe at this acuity. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

She has capacity, insight and is engaged; voluntary admission should be attempted first. Mental Health Act use is reserved for refusal of life-saving treatment when capacity is lost. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ECT is first-line in severe depression with high suicide risk, food/fluid refusal, severe psychomotor retardation or stupor, psychotic features, catatonia, treatment-resistance, or in pregnancy when medication risk is unacceptable. It has 70 to 90 percent response rate with onset within 1 to 2 weeks (faster than pharmacotherapy). In Australia it is delivered under general anaesthesia and muscle relaxant, typically 2 to 3 times weekly for 6 to 12 sessions, with maintenance ECT as appropriate. Major risks are anaesthetic, transient anterograde and retrograde memory disturbance (which usually resolves), and headache.
key_points: Indications: severe depression, food refusal, catatonia, suicidality, resistance.
Onset 1-2 weeks; 70-90 percent response.
2-3 sessions/week, 6-12 acute, maintenance considered.
Memory loss usually transient anterograde.
explanation.pearls: Bilateral ECT is faster acting but with more cognitive side effects than right unilateral; in elderly patients with severe psychotic depression bilateral is often preferred for life-threatening illness.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: rTMS has good evidence for moderate treatment-resistant depression but slower onset and is not recommended for severe psychotic depression with imminent food refusal where ECT is first-line. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

Two adequate antidepressant trials with augmentation have failed and the man is at imminent risk from dehydration and starvation; further pharmacotherapy alone is not safe at this acuity. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

Esketamine has TGA approval for treatment-resistant depression but is not indicated in patients with imminent risk needing rapid stabilisation, and is contraindicated when patients cannot safely follow post-dose monitoring requirements. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

Life-threatening severe depression with food refusal, psychomotor retardation, treatment resistance, and psychotic features has level-1 evidence for ECT in Australian guidelines with rapid onset of action (1 to 2 weeks); intravenous fluids bridge dehydration. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

MAOI switch requires a 1 to 2 week washout (longer for fluoxetine) and would not act in time to address food refusal and dehydration; ECT is the indicated rapid treatment in this acuity. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Risperidone, amisulpride, and paliperidone reliably cause hyperprolactinaemia by D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway. Symptomatic patients (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, bone loss, gynaecomastia) should be switched to a prolactin-sparing agent: aripiprazole (best evidence), olanzapine, quetiapine, or clozapine. Aripiprazole is added or switched (cross-titration over 2 to 4 weeks) and effectively normalises prolactin within weeks. Cabergoline is generally avoided in schizophrenia because of relapse risk. Bone density assessment is indicated if amenorrhoea has lasted over 6 months.
key_points: Prolactin-raising: risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride.
Prolactin-sparing: aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine.
Switch or add aripiprazole 10-15 mg as standard intervention.
Cabergoline avoided - psychosis relapse risk.
explanation.pearls: Document baseline prolactin before starting risperidone or paliperidone and at 3 months; ask routinely about menstrual cycle, sexual function and galactorrhoea, which patients often do not volunteer.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.rationale: Risperidone-related prolactin elevation is dose-related but reductions often do not normalise prolactin without losing efficacy; aripiprazole switch achieves both goals. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.rationale: Amisulpride raises prolactin more than risperidone and would worsen amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and bone loss; it is the wrong switch in this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.rationale: Dopamine agonist add-on in patients with schizophrenia is generally avoided because it risks worsening psychotic symptoms by stimulating mesolimbic dopamine; switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic is the recommended first step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.rationale: Aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist) reliably lowers prolactin and is the standard switch in antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia with adverse effects; cross-titration over 2 to 4 weeks minimises relapse risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.rationale: MRI pituitary is normal and prolactin elevation is consistent with risperidone effect; invasive biopsy is not indicated and the cause is iatrogenic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as failure to respond to two adequate trials (4 to 6 weeks at therapeutic dose with confirmed adherence) of different antipsychotics, at least one of which is not clozapine. Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with superior efficacy in this group and is recommended as the third antipsychotic. Monitoring is mandatory: weekly FBC for 18 weeks then monthly indefinitely for agranulocytosis; baseline and serial ECG plus troponin in the first 4 weeks for myocarditis; weight, glucose, and lipids for metabolic syndrome.
key_points: Definition: two adequate trials at therapeutic dose with adherence.
Clozapine third antipsychotic - unique efficacy.
Weekly FBC 18 weeks then monthly for agranulocytosis.
ECG + troponin first 4 weeks for myocarditis.
explanation.pearls: Stop clozapine for neutrophils below 1.5 x10^9/L (red zone); rechallenge requires haematology review and is generally only for life-threatening psychosis without alternative. Avoid co-prescribing other agents that lower neutrophils (e.g. carbamazepine).

options.rationale: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate antipsychotic trials is the standard indication for clozapine; mandatory monitoring includes weekly FBC for 18 weeks, then monthly, with cardiac and metabolic baselines because of agranulocytosis and myocarditis risk. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

Lithium augmentation of antipsychotics has limited efficacy in primary schizophrenia (better evidence in schizoaffective with mood features); clozapine remains the indicated treatment after two failed trials. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

rTMS for hallucinations has limited and inconsistent evidence; clozapine remains first-line for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate antipsychotic trials. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

He meets Australian criteria for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (two adequate trials of different antipsychotics) and clozapine is the recommended next step with strongest evidence; high-dose olanzapine augmentation has limited evidence. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

Adherence has been confirmed during the 6 months of risperidone LAI, so non-adherence is not the cause; he meets clozapine criteria now and further antipsychotic trials delay benefit. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

explanation.summary: Clinicians routinely defer smoking cessation in people being treated for alcohol or other drug dependence, on the intuition that removing a second substance will destabilise recovery. The evidence points the other way: concurrent tobacco treatment does not worsen alcohol outcomes and is associated with better abstinence from both, and people in treatment for alcohol dependence are more likely to die of tobacco-related disease than of alcohol. Bupropion requires care where abrupt alcohol withdrawal is a risk, but he is two weeks abstinent and stable, so varenicline or combination nicotine replacement with behavioural support are both appropriate. In context: tobacco dependence is the most lethal and most under-treated comorbidity in addiction medicine, and a patient already engaged in treatment is the easiest one to help.
key_points: Concurrent smoking cessation does not jeopardise alcohol abstinence
People in alcohol treatment die more often of tobacco-related than alcohol-related disease
Use the existing treatment engagement rather than deferring to an arbitrary milestone
Bupropion is avoided where abrupt alcohol withdrawal is possible
explanation.pearls: Treating one substance at a time is a common error; tobacco is treated alongside, not after, the presenting dependence.

options.rationale: Treating tobacco dependence concurrently does not compromise alcohol abstinence and is associated with better outcomes for both; the motivated moment inside an existing treatment episode is the one to use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Sequencing would be justified if concurrent cessation destabilised recovery, which the evidence does not show. Deferral usually means the attempt never happens. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

Counselling without pharmacotherapy is the choice for a light smoker or a patient in whom all agents are contraindicated. He is highly dependent and pharmacotherapy roughly doubles his chance. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

Gradual reduction is an interim plan for someone unwilling to set a quit date. He has asked to stop, and reduction alone rarely reaches abstinence in heavy dependence. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)
Residential withdrawal is for unsafe home detoxification or repeated failed community withdrawal. He is already two weeks abstinent on community treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation halves cardiovascular mortality regardless of psychiatric comorbidity. First-line pharmacotherapy is varenicline; combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is the alternative. Varenicline was previously flagged for neuropsychiatric adverse effects but the EAGLES trial showed safety in stable severe mental illness. Bupropion is third-line and avoided with clozapine because of compound seizure risk. Cigarette smoke induces CYP1A2, the enzyme that metabolises clozapine and olanzapine, so plasma levels rise on cessation; dose reduction is often needed and toxicity may occur. Behavioural support adds independent benefit and Quitline support should be offered routinely.
key_points: Varenicline or combination NRT is first-line.
EAGLES trial: varenicline safe in stable severe mental illness.
Avoid bupropion with clozapine due to seizure risk.
Monitor clozapine and olanzapine levels after quitting.
Add behavioural support and Quitline referral.
explanation.pearls: After quitting smoking, expect clozapine plasma concentration to rise by around 50% over 1 to 2 weeks; pre-empt with a 25% dose reduction in heavy smokers and recheck a trough level at 2 weeks.

options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and combined with clozapine substantially increases seizure risk; this combination is generally avoided. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

Varenicline is first-line, safe in stable schizophrenia, and clozapine levels rise on quitting (cytochrome P450 1A2 induction by cigarette smoke is lost) so monitoring is needed. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)
Combination NRT is effective but he has previously failed monotherapy NRT; clozapine levels still rise on quitting and require monitoring. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)
Hypnotherapy and acupuncture have weak evidence; smokers with serious mental illness benefit equally from first-line pharmacotherapy. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)
Stable clozapine should not be switched; varenicline can be used with clozapine but levels must still be monitored. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treated primarily with structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy, transference-focused therapy). Brief involuntary or voluntary admissions for chronic self-harm do not improve outcomes and may worsen them by reinforcing crisis behaviour and disrupting community treatment. Inpatient care is reserved for acute psychiatric emergencies, severe comorbid depression with imminent suicide risk, or where outpatient resources are not available. Pharmacotherapy is symptom-targeted (eg short courses of antipsychotic for psychotic-like symptoms) and not first-line; benzodiazepines are best avoided because of disinhibition and dependence. Engaging existing community supports and family is central.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy is the primary treatment.
Avoid brief inpatient admissions for chronic self-harm.
No first-line pharmacotherapy for BPD itself.
Avoid benzodiazepines.
Engage existing community supports and family.
explanation.pearls: Use chain analysis collaboratively at every contact - mapping prompting event, vulnerabilities, links and consequences - to convert each crisis into a DBT skill-building opportunity rather than an isolated incident.

options.rationale: Brief admissions for self-harm in BPD without acute risk worsen outcomes by reinforcing crisis behaviour and disrupting community DBT; community management is preferred. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)
Benzodiazepines are not recommended in BPD; they cause disinhibition, dependence and worsen long-term outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

Community-based management with structured follow-up and engagement of existing DBT supports is the evidence-based approach for BPD self-harm without acute suicidal intent. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)
Mental Health Act admission requires acute mental illness with imminent risk; chronic self-harm in BPD without acute risk does not meet criteria. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)
Polypharmacy is not recommended in BPD; medications target specific comorbid symptoms only, and self-harm itself is treated with psychotherapy. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 criteria: five or more symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, several present before age 12, present in 2 or more settings, causing functional impairment, and not better explained by another condition. Assessment uses clinical interview with validated tools (DIVA-5, ASRS) and collateral history. Comorbidities are common - anxiety, depression, substance use, sleep disorders, ASD - and require parallel management. Stimulants (methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine, dexamfetamine) are first-line treatment; non-stimulant atomoxetine or guanfacine are alternatives. Specialist credentialling rules vary by state but all currently require psychiatrist or paediatrician initiation in Australia.
key_points: DSM-5 needs childhood onset and 2+ settings.
Use validated rating scales and collateral history.
Screen for common comorbidities.
Stimulants are first-line; non-stimulants second.
Specialist diagnosis required for first prescription.
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine has lower abuse potential than immediate-release dexamfetamine because it requires red cell hydrolysis to produce active drug, giving a smoother onset and longer duration.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Stimulant prescription requires specialist diagnosis and an authority script; trial first is not appropriate in primary care. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Routine neuroimaging and sleep study are not standard ADHD work-up; selected screening tests may be appropriate but not all of these. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: ADHD persists into adulthood in 50 to 70% of childhood cases; refusing assessment is not appropriate when symptoms are present since childhood. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Formal diagnosis by an appropriately credentialed specialist using DSM-5 criteria and collateral history is required before stimulant prescription. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Atomoxetine in adults still requires specialist diagnosis; first prescription is by a specialist with GP shared care thereafter. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Catatonia tolerates benzodiazepine doses that would sedate other patients, and the dose is titrated against the motor signs. As the catatonia resolves that tolerance falls, so a dose that was well tolerated on day one can oversedate on day four. Excess sedation is managed by holding doses and observing, with oxygen and airway attention as needed, then resuming at a lower dose. Flumazenil is avoided outside life threatening respiratory failure because it precipitates seizures and an immediate return of catatonia.
key_points: Sedative tolerance in catatonia falls as the syndrome resolves
Manage oversedation by holding doses, not by reversal
Flumazenil risks withdrawal seizures and immediate relapse of catatonia
Resume at a lower dose once the respiratory rate recovers
explanation.pearls: Improving motor signs alongside new drowsiness usually means the patient no longer needs the dose that was needed at diagnosis. In context: benzodiazepine treatment of catatonia is a titration against signs, reviewed daily, not a fixed prescription (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Rising sedation with respiratory depression calls for the dose to be held and the patient observed with supplemental oxygen while the drug is cleared (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Reversal is reserved for life threatening respiratory failure, since it precipitates withdrawal seizures and returns the catatonia within minutes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).
Continuing unchanged is reasonable when sedation is mild and the respiratory rate is normal, which is not the case here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
Electroconvulsive therapy follows an adequate benzodiazepine trial that has failed, not a trial that is working but is oversedating (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Midazolam suits brief procedural sedation; its shorter action makes it a poor choice for sustained treatment of catatonia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: PTSD is diagnosed when characteristic symptoms (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, arousal) follow exposure to a traumatic event and persist beyond 1 month with functional impairment. First-line treatment is trauma-focused psychological therapy delivered by a trained clinician: trauma-focused CBT and EMDR both have strong evidence. Pharmacotherapy with sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine is second-line or adjunct when therapy is unavailable, declined, or insufficient. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they impair fear extinction. Prazosin is added for trauma nightmares. Antipsychotic augmentation is for severe treatment-resistant cases. Single-session debriefing is no longer recommended.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR are first-line.
Sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine if pharmacotherapy needed.
Avoid benzodiazepines.
Add prazosin for trauma-related nightmares.
Single-session debriefing does not prevent PTSD.
explanation.pearls: Prazosin reduces noradrenergic activity through alpha-1 blockade and is started at 1 mg at night titrated to 5 to 15 mg; first-dose hypotension is the main precaution especially in older adults.

options.rationale: Trauma-focused psychological therapy is first-line for PTSD; pharmacotherapy is second-line or used in parallel when psychotherapy is unavailable. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
TF-CBT or EMDR are first-line for PTSD with strongest evidence; both are equally effective. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes by impairing fear extinction learning and risk dependence; they are contraindicated. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Single-session debriefing does not prevent PTSD and may worsen outcomes; structured trauma-focused therapy is required. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
PTSD without psychosis, suicidality or inability to function is managed in the community; admission is not indicated. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance management follows a stepped approach: verbal de-escalation first, then offered oral medication, then intramuscular monotherapy, then IM combination if needed. Olanzapine wafer 5 to 10 mg is a fast-acting oral option that matches the patient's previous response. IM options are droperidol 10 mg or olanzapine 10 mg; combination IM droperidol plus midazolam is reserved for severe disturbance with respiratory monitoring. Avoid IM olanzapine within 1 hour of IM benzodiazepine because of respiratory depression. Continuous monitoring of airway, breathing and circulation is mandatory after any IM sedation. Document Mental Health Act status and review medication regularly.
key_points: Verbal de-escalation always first.
Offer oral medication before IM where possible.
Droperidol or olanzapine IM are monotherapy options.
Avoid IM olanzapine with IM benzodiazepine within 1 hour.
Continuous airway, breathing and circulation monitoring after IM.
explanation.pearls: Droperidol carries a black box QT warning but at typical sedation doses (5 to 10 mg IM) the absolute torsades risk is very low and ECG screening is reserved for risk factors or repeated dosing.

options.rationale: Long-acting zuclopenthixol acetate is not appropriate for acute behavioural disturbance because its 48 to 72 hour effect cannot be titrated. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

Oral medication should be offered first when feasible; combination IM droperidol plus midazolam carries respiratory depression risk and is reserved for failure of monotherapy. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)
Ketamine sedation is reserved for severe refractory cases requiring physical restraint with anaesthetic backup; not first-line. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

High-dose haloperidol with promethazine carries QT prolongation and over-sedation risk; modern Australian practice favours droperidol or olanzapine first. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)
Oral medication is preferred over IM where the patient can accept it; olanzapine wafer is rapid-onset and matches his past response. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal afferent arteriolar dilation, lowering glomerular filtration and lithium clearance. Plasma lithium levels can rise 30 to 60% over 7 to 10 days of NSAID co-administration. Paracetamol with topical NSAIDs is a safer analgesic strategy. If an oral NSAID is unavoidable, the lithium dose is reduced empirically by 25 to 50% and a level checked within 5 to 7 days, alongside close monitoring of renal function and clinical signs of toxicity.
key_points: Oral NSAIDs raise lithium levels by 30 to 60% within 7 to 10 days.
Paracetamol with topical NSAIDs avoids the interaction.
If oral NSAIDs are unavoidable, reduce lithium dose and check level within a week.
explanation.pearls: Co-prescription of an oral NSAID with lithium raises lithium levels by up to 60% within 7 days; if unavoidable, drop the lithium dose by a quarter and check the level at day 5.

options.rationale: COX-2 selective NSAIDs interact with lithium similarly to non-selective NSAIDs and offer no safe-co-prescription advantage in this context. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)
Co-prescribing an oral NSAID with lithium is generally avoided; checking the level afterwards manages the consequence rather than preventing it. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)
Oral NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance and can raise lithium levels by 30 to 60%, precipitating toxicity; paracetamol and topical NSAIDs avoid this interaction. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)
Opioids for mechanical low back pain risk dependence and falls and are not first-line; non-opioid options that do not interact with lithium are preferred. (Source: AMH; eTG: Pain)
Stopping lithium risks relapse of bipolar disorder; abrupt withdrawal also increases the risk of rebound mania within weeks. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: RANZCP guidance for first-episode psychosis emphasises early treatment, lower starting doses, shared decision-making and avoidance of olanzapine where metabolic concerns are present. Aripiprazole and risperidone are reasonable first-line options. Baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids, prolactin and ECG should be measured before starting and reviewed at 3 and 12 months. Long-acting injectables should be discussed early as an option after stabilisation to support adherence.
key_points: Aripiprazole and risperidone are first-line for first-episode psychosis.
Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden; discuss this explicitly.
Baseline metabolic, cardiac and prolactin screening precedes antipsychotic start.
explanation.pearls: First-episode psychosis starts with low-dose aripiprazole or risperidone, baseline weight, fasting glucose, lipids and ECG, with metabolic review at 3 and 12 months.

options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics; using it first-line is not supported. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Aripiprazole has a lower metabolic burden than olanzapine while maintaining efficacy in first-episode psychosis and aligns with the patient's stated concern. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders; eTG: Psychotropic)

Olanzapine is effective but carries the greatest weight-gain risk of the second-generation agents; given this patient's stated concerns it is not the best first choice. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

First-generation antipsychotics have higher rates of EPS and tardive dyskinesia and are not preferred first-line for medication-naive young men with first-episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

Benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychotic symptoms; antipsychotic therapy should not be delayed once first-episode psychosis is diagnosed. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is most common in the first 4 weeks of treatment. Surveillance includes baseline and weekly troponin, CRP and clinical review during titration. A troponin rise above twice the upper limit, a CRP above 100 mg/L, fever, tachycardia disproportionate to dose or any unexplained constitutional symptoms triggers immediate clozapine cessation, cardiology referral and echocardiography. Rechallenge has been described under highly specialised circumstances but is not routine.
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis peaks in the first 4 weeks of titration.
Cease clozapine immediately when troponin rises or constitutional symptoms appear.
Echocardiography and cardiology referral guide diagnosis and prognosis.
explanation.pearls: During clozapine titration any troponin above twice the upper limit, CRP above 100 mg/L or unexplained tachycardia in the first 4 weeks means stop the drug today and call cardiology.

options.rationale: Steroid therapy does not allow continued clozapine exposure in established myocarditis and there is no evidence base for routine corticosteroid use here. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)
Dose reduction does not protect against ongoing myocarditis; continued exposure risks fulminant cardiomyopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)
Continuing the offending drug in suspected clozapine myocarditis is dangerous and contradicts the recommended cessation pathway. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)

Within the first 4 weeks of clozapine titration any constitutional symptoms with troponin rise, CRP rise or tachycardia mandate immediate clozapine cessation; rechallenge requires specialist cardiology and psychiatry input. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine; AMH)
Cardiac workup must continue regardless of antipsychotic switch; ignoring the troponin and CRP rise misses cardiomyopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects approximately 1 in 1000 births and clusters in women with bipolar disorder or a family history. Onset is typically within the first 2 weeks postpartum with rapid escalation of insomnia, mood lability, psychosis and risk to mother and baby. Management is psychiatric emergency: admission to a mother-baby unit, antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser where indicated, and ECT for severe or refractory presentations. Olanzapine is preferred for breastfeeding-compatible rapid antimanic effect.
key_points: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency with rapid escalation.
Admit to a mother-baby unit when available; start oral antipsychotic immediately.
Olanzapine is the preferred initial breastfeeding-compatible antipsychotic.
explanation.pearls: Day 3 to 14 postpartum onset of insomnia, mood elevation and delusions is postpartum psychosis until proven otherwise - admit today and start olanzapine 5 to 10 mg at night.

options.rationale: General adult wards separate mother and baby unnecessarily; benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychosis or mania. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health)
Outpatient management of postpartum psychosis is unsafe; lithium also has lower breastfeeding compatibility than olanzapine and is rarely first acute choice. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health)

Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency requiring inpatient care; olanzapine is compatible with breastfeeding, has rapid antimanic effect and is the preferred first-line acute treatment in this setting. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health; RANZCP: Perinatal)
Deferring treatment for 48 hours in postpartum psychosis exposes both mother and baby to substantial harm including infanticide and maternal suicide risk. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health)

ECT is highly effective in postpartum psychosis but is reserved for severe non-response, catatonia or refusal of oral therapy; oral antipsychotic is the standard first step. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal)

explanation.summary: Major depression with psychotic features in older adults carries a high mortality from suicide and physical decline. Adequate antidepressant trial is at least 6 to 8 weeks at therapeutic dose. After two such failures, particularly with malnutrition or active suicide risk, ECT is the preferred next step with response rates of 70 to 90% within 6 to 12 sessions. Capacity should be assessed and informed consent obtained; involuntary treatment under the relevant Mental Health Act may apply when capacity is lost.
key_points: Two adequate antidepressant trials precede ECT in non-emergent cases.
Psychotic depression with malnutrition or suicide risk justifies earlier ECT.
Capacity assessment and informed consent precede ECT where possible.
explanation.pearls: Older adult with psychotic depression refusing food after 2 antidepressant failures should be offered ECT within days; expected response rate is 70 to 90% in 6 to 12 sessions.

options.rationale: A third sequential antidepressant trial delays definitive treatment in a malnourished psychotically depressed older patient; ECT has superior response rate and speed. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Antipsychotic augmentation is reasonable for non-psychotic treatment-resistant depression, but slow onset and inadequate efficacy in nihilistic delusions with malnutrition make ECT preferable here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

Psychotic depression in older adults responds rapidly to ECT and is the preferred next step when two adequate antidepressant trials have failed and there is malnutrition or risk to life. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders; eTG: Psychotropic)
Lithium augmentation in an older adult with reduced GFR and dehydration risk is high-risk and slow-acting, not the optimal next step here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)
TMS lacks adequate evidence in psychotic depression and is generally avoided in this subgroup; inpatient ECT is preferred. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a transdiagnostic syndrome of mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, mutism and stupor. The Bush-Francis scale screens and grades severity. First-line treatment is a lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg with response monitored; titration up to 8 to 24 mg daily may be needed. ECT is indicated when benzodiazepines fail, when malignant catatonia evolves with autonomic instability and elevated CK, or when life-threatening complications such as dehydration emerge. Antipsychotics may precipitate or worsen catatonia and are avoided until resolution.
key_points: Bush-Francis screening confirms catatonia; lorazepam challenge is first-line.
ECT is the next step when benzodiazepine fails or malignant catatonia evolves.
Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia.
explanation.pearls: When a lorazepam challenge gives only transient benefit and CK rises with autonomic instability, malignant catatonia is evolving and ECT should start within 24 hours.

options.rationale: NMDA antagonists are an unproven third-line option after benzodiazepines and ECT have failed; they should not displace ECT in this presentation. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)

Lorazepam non-response within 48 to 72 hours alongside complications mandates escalation to ECT rather than further dose increases; prolonged immobility risks rhabdomyolysis and DVT. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)
Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and may precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are generally avoided until catatonia has resolved. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)

Catatonia not responding to a lorazepam challenge requires prompt ECT, particularly when there is dehydration, immobility complications and creatine kinase elevation suggesting evolving malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP: ECT; eTG: Psychotropic)
Watchful waiting in a dehydrated immobile patient with rising CK risks progression to malignant catatonia with multi-organ failure. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)

explanation.summary: Australian antipsychotic monitoring guidance recommends baseline assessment of weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose, lipids, ECG and prolactin and review at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then yearly. Risperidone causes early weight gain and dyslipidaemia in younger patients. The 12-week review is the critical decision point: if metabolic shift is evident, intensify lifestyle measures, consider metformin, and discuss switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic such as aripiprazole if change persists. Smoking cessation should also be addressed because of independent cardiovascular and CYP1A2 effects.
key_points: Repeat metabolic panel at 6 and 12 weeks post-initiation.
Yearly metabolic review thereafter is the standard.
Intensify lifestyle measures and consider metformin early.
Switching to lower-risk agent is appropriate if changes persist.
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 mg twice daily has good evidence for attenuating antipsychotic-induced weight gain in patients with at least 5 kg gain in 3 months; start it alongside structured lifestyle support rather than after a metabolic syndrome has developed.

options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic to detect early metabolic shift; 12 months is the next routine interval after that. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)
Young men are at meaningful metabolic risk on antipsychotics and a full panel is recommended at the 12-week review, not selective monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

RANZCP and Australian guidelines recommend full metabolic monitoring at 12 weeks plus lifestyle counselling, given the early-onset weight gain seen in this patient. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)
Switching antipsychotics should be considered after weight gain is confirmed and lifestyle measures trialled; routine switch at 12 weeks is not recommended. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)
OGTT and cortisol are not part of routine antipsychotic monitoring; standard fasting glucose and lipid screening is the recommended baseline at 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Australian perinatal psychiatry guidance favours continuing effective antidepressants in pregnancy because relapse risk often outweighs the small absolute risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome. Sertraline is one of the SSRIs with the most reassuring breastfeeding data. Neonates exposed in the third trimester should be observed for 24 to 48 hours for jitteriness, feeding difficulties and respiratory symptoms. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn is a rare and largely transient association. A maternal mental health plan and EPDS monitoring postpartum are routine.
key_points: Continue effective antidepressants in stable pregnant women.
Watch for neonatal adaptation in the first 24 to 48 hours.
Sertraline and paroxetine have lower breast milk concentrations.
Add EPDS at 6 weeks and 3 months postpartum to detect relapse.
explanation.pearls: Neonatal adaptation syndrome occurs in around 30 percent of SSRI-exposed infants, peaks at 24 to 48 hours and resolves within a week without specific treatment; rooming-in plus paediatric observation is sufficient in most term babies.

options.rationale: Stopping antidepressants in late pregnancy carries a substantial relapse risk in postpartum depression and is not recommended in stable, well patients. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)

Australian practice is to continue effective antidepressants through pregnancy and breastfeeding, with paediatric review for neonatal adaptation syndrome in the first 24 to 48 hours after birth. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)
Tapering before delivery to reduce neonatal symptoms increases maternal relapse risk and is not recommended in well stable patients on a maintenance SSRI. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)
Fluoxetine has a long half-life and may extend exposure rather than reduce neonatal symptoms; switching well-tolerated treatment in late pregnancy is not recommended. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)
Switching from effective pharmacotherapy to psychological therapy alone late in pregnancy risks relapse; both modalities can be combined when clinically indicated. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment with fetal exposure. Australian pregnancy prevention program guidance requires highly effective contraception such as long-acting reversible contraception, annual reauthorisation, and documented patient acknowledgement of risks. In women planning pregnancy, switch to a safer mood stabiliser such as lithium or lamotrigine before conception. Folic acid 5 mg daily is added if conception is planned despite valproate.
key_points: Use LARC for highly effective contraception on valproate.
Document the pregnancy prevention plan and review annually.
Switch to safer agents before planned conception.
Prescribe 5 mg folic acid daily if conception is planned.
explanation.pearls: The risk of neural tube defects with valproate exposure is highest in the first 28 days; brief pre-conception switching may not eliminate risk if the embryo is already implanted, so LARC is preferable to depending on a planned switch alone.

options.rationale: Valproate has a 10 percent major congenital malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental impairment risk; highly effective contraception is required throughout treatment. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

Tapering a stabilising mood stabiliser without secured alternative cover risks severe relapse with prior psychiatric hospitalisation; secure contraception is the immediate priority. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

Switching mood stabilisers in a stable patient introduces relapse risk; the immediate need is highly effective contraception while continuing the stabilising agent. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

Combined oral contraception alone meets effectiveness criteria but the pregnancy prevention program requires annual review and documented risk acknowledgement, not contraception alone. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

Australian and TGA-aligned pregnancy prevention program requires highly effective contraception such as a LARC plus documented annual risk acknowledgement when valproate is used in women of reproductive potential. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics sit awkwardly beside catatonia. Dopamine blockade can induce catatonia, can deepen it once present, and raises the risk of malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which share hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability and a rising creatine kinase. When catatonia emerges in a patient taking an antipsychotic, the safe move is to withhold the drug, treat the catatonia with a benzodiazepine, and revisit antipsychotic cover once the motor syndrome has settled. Continuing or escalating the antipsychotic is the common error.
key_points: Antipsychotics can both cause and worsen catatonia
Withhold the dopamine blocker while catatonia is treated
Watch temperature, pulse, blood pressure and creatine kinase for malignant progression
Reintroduce antipsychotic cover only after the motor syndrome settles
explanation.pearls: A normal creatine kinase and temperature do not make the antipsychotic safe to continue; they only say that malignant catatonia has not yet developed. In context: catatonia in a patient on an antipsychotic is a medication decision as much as a psychiatric one (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Dopamine blockade can precipitate and worsen catatonia and risks progression to a malignant form, so the antipsychotic is withheld while catatonia is treated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Raising the dose is the answer when persisting positive symptoms occur without motor signs and the current dose has been tolerated (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: A high potency agent would be considered for acute behavioural disturbance in a patient without catatonia; here it increases the risk further (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Anticholinergic cover is the answer for acute dystonia or drug induced parkinsonism, which produce rigidity and tremor rather than posturing and negativism (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
Dantrolene is reserved for neuroleptic malignant syndrome with hyperthermia, autonomic instability and a markedly raised creatine kinase (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade, anticholinergic toxicity, alpha-adrenergic blockade and seizures. A QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmia; a terminal R in aVR above 3 mm is a sensitive marker. Sodium bicarbonate boluses of 1 to 2 mmol/kg narrow the QRS and reverse hypotension. Aim for arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55 and sodium 145 to 155 mmol/L. Lipid emulsion is rescue therapy for collapse not responding to bicarbonate, with toxicology input.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms drives bicarbonate therapy decision.
Aim for pH 7.50 to 7.55 and sodium 145 to 155 mmol/L.
Avoid class Ia, Ic and III antiarrhythmics.
Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory collapse.
explanation.pearls: Seizures cause profound metabolic acidosis that worsens TCA cardiotoxicity within minutes; treat with benzodiazepines first-line and avoid phenytoin which is also a sodium channel blocker and may precipitate ventricular tachycardia.

options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms with terminal R wave in aVR signifies sodium channel blockade in TCA toxicity; sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus reverses the conduction abnormality. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)
Lipid emulsion is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to bicarbonate in lipophilic drug toxicity; sodium bicarbonate is first-line for TCA QRS widening. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in TCA overdose; it can precipitate seizures in mixed ingestions. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)
Magnesium is an adjunct for torsades de pointes and refractory dysrhythmia, not the primary therapy for TCA-induced sodium channel blockade. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)
Class 1a antiarrhythmics are sodium channel blockers themselves and will worsen TCA cardiotoxicity; they are contraindicated. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome from MAOI plus tramadol is a clinical diagnosis using Hunter criteria: spontaneous or inducible clonus, ocular clonus, agitation, hyperreflexia, hypertension and hyperthermia. NMS instead features lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and slow onset after antipsychotic dose escalation. Treatment is removal of serotonergic agents, intravenous fluid, cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, and cyproheptadine if symptoms persist. Severe hyperthermia above 41 °C warrants intubation, paralysis and active cooling in ICU.
key_points: Clonus and hyperreflexia favour serotonin syndrome over NMS.
Benzodiazepines plus cyproheptadine are specific therapy.
Avoid antipsychotics in serotonin syndrome.
Intubate and paralyse if T above 41 °C with rigidity.
explanation.pearls: Cyproheptadine loading is 12 mg orally, then 2 mg every 2 hours up to 32 mg in 24 hours; if the patient cannot swallow, crush and give via nasogastric tube because there is no parenteral preparation in Australia.

options.rationale: Adrenaline and steroids have no role and may worsen hypertension and hyperthermia; benzodiazepines plus cyproheptadine are first line. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

Bromocriptine and dantrolene are reserved for neuroleptic malignant syndrome which features lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia; this presentation is serotonin syndrome. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

Antipsychotics worsen autonomic instability and can precipitate NMS; agitation in serotonin syndrome is treated with benzodiazepines and removal of serotonergic agents. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)
Mirtazapine has 5HT2A blocking properties but should never be restarted with phenelzine; both serotonergic drugs must be ceased. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

The Hunter criteria pattern of inducible clonus, ocular clonus and hyperreflexia fit serotonin syndrome; benzodiazepines and the 5HT2A antagonist cyproheptadine are the specific Australian-recommended therapy. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Varenicline produces higher continuous abstinence rates than bupropion or single-agent NRT in tobacco dependence. RACGP guidance recommends varenicline first-line for highly dependent smokers without recent suicidal ideation, severe mood disorder or pregnancy. Initiation is staged over the first week with a quit date in week 2 to maximise tolerability. Combination NRT is reserved as second-line and bupropion as third-line; behavioural support adds to all options.
key_points: Varenicline produces the highest continuous abstinence rates.
Start at 0.5 mg daily and titrate over a week.
Quit date is set in week 2 of treatment.
Combination NRT is second-line; bupropion is third-line.
explanation.pearls: Varenicline can intensify the effects of alcohol with reports of disinhibition and amnesia; counsel patients to avoid alcohol particularly during the first few weeks and re-question carefully at follow-up because behaviour change can be subtle.

options.rationale: Combination NRT plus bupropion lacks superior outcomes over single agent and increases the chance of adverse effects without clear benefit. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)
Combination NRT is acceptable but varenicline has higher quit rates and is preferred first-line in patients without contraindication. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)
Combining noradrenergic agents increases seizure and serotonergic risk and is not first-line; nortriptyline is rarely used now. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)
Hypnotherapy has no robust evidence of benefit in tobacco dependence and delays the chance of a pharmacologically supported quit. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

Varenicline is first-line pharmacotherapy in Australian guidance for highly dependent smokers without significant psychiatric instability; titration over the first week reduces nausea. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires DSM-5 criteria including pervasive symptoms in two or more settings, functional impairment and evidence of childhood symptoms before age 12. Diagnostic assessment must currently be made by a psychiatrist or paediatrician, who may also initiate stimulant therapy. Collateral information from family, employers or old school reports strengthens the diagnostic process. Comorbid mood, anxiety and substance disorders should be screened for and managed concurrently.
key_points: DSM-5 requires childhood symptoms before age 12.
Specialist diagnosis is mandatory before stimulant initiation.
Collateral evidence supports the diagnostic process.
Screen and treat comorbid mood, anxiety and substance disorders.
explanation.pearls: Women and girls are systematically under-diagnosed because inattentive presentations attract less referral than hyperactive ones; a normal childhood school record does not exclude ADHD in a woman presenting with adult functional decline.

options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis and stimulant initiation in Australia requires a psychiatrist or paediatrician with collateral evidence of pre-12-year symptoms; this case has both childhood documentation and current functional impairment. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

Stimulant initiation in adult ADHD in Australia is restricted to authorised specialists (psychiatrist or paediatrician); GP initiation is not permitted without prior specialist diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)
TFTs are already normal in this case; thyroid disease is excluded as an organic mimic and further screening alone delays definitive diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)
Occupational therapy alone cannot establish the diagnosis or initiate appropriate pharmacotherapy if indicated; psychiatric assessment is the formal pathway. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)
Therapeutic trials are not the diagnostic pathway; stimulants must follow a formal specialist diagnosis under Australian regulation. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: NHMRC guidance positions structured psychotherapy as the core treatment for borderline personality disorder, with dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy and schema therapy all evidence-supported. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive and short-term, used for clearly defined comorbid disorders rather than core BPD symptoms. Crisis care plans, validation, and continuity of care reduce hospital use and self-harm. Carer involvement supports recovery when consented.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy is first-line for BPD.
DBT, MBT and schema therapy all have evidence.
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive and time-limited.
Crisis plans and continuity reduce hospital use.
explanation.pearls: Brief admissions for BPD often worsen long-term outcomes by reinforcing self-harm cycles and disrupting therapy; a 'partial hospitalisation' day program or planned crisis respite is usually better than ad hoc inpatient stays.

options.rationale: Antidepressant escalation is unlikely to address the core symptoms of BPD; structured psychotherapy is the recommended first-line intervention. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)

Australian NHMRC guidance places structured psychotherapy first-line for borderline personality disorder; dialectical behaviour therapy is the most studied program with effect on self-harm and emotion regulation. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)
