Antipsychotics are not first-line for BPD; their use is restricted to short-term crisis management or specific symptom domains under specialist guidance. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)
Lithium is reserved for bipolar mood stabilisation; it has no role in BPD and adds toxicity and monitoring burden. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)
ECT has no place in BPD treatment; it is reserved for severe affective and psychotic illness unresponsive to other measures. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Risperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin substantially through D2 antagonism in the tuberoinfundibular pathway. Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, reduced libido, gynaecomastia, low bone density) warrants action. Aripiprazole, a partial D2 agonist, is the preferred switch in stable patients because it lowers prolactin and preserves antipsychotic cover. Cross-titration over 2 to 4 weeks reduces relapse risk. Cabergoline alone risks worsening psychosis.
key_points: Risperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin most.
Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing through partial D2 agonism.
Cross-titrate to minimise relapse risk during switch.
Avoid cabergoline alone in psychotic illness.
explanation.pearls: Chronic untreated hyperprolactinaemia from antipsychotics can cause osteoporosis in young women; check bone density if levels stay above 1000 mIU/L for more than 6 months, particularly in women under 30 with no other osteoporosis risk.

options.rationale: Adding cabergoline risks worsening psychosis through dopamine agonism and is not preferred when antipsychotic substitution is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)
Reducing risperidone below the therapeutic threshold risks relapse of psychosis; dose reduction is only partially effective at lowering prolactin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)
Antipsychotic cessation in well-controlled schizophrenia carries high relapse and rehospitalisation risk; substitution is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing through partial D2 agonism and is the preferred switch agent for prolactin-related side effects in stable patients with cross-titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)
Masking symptoms with an oestrogen-containing pill does not address chronically elevated prolactin or its long-term consequences on bone density. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Australian admission criteria for severe anorexia nervosa include any of HR under 40, BP under 80/50, postural drop above 20 mmHg, K under 3.0, phosphate under 0.5, BMI under 14, rapid weight loss or significant ECG changes. Refeeding syndrome risk peaks in the first week of nutritional restoration as intracellular electrolyte shift drives hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia. Thiamine 100 mg daily and gradual calorie escalation reduce this risk. Family-based therapy remains the outpatient gold standard once medically stable.
key_points: HR under 40 or BP under 80/50 meets admission criteria.
K under 3.0 or phosphate under 0.5 mandates admission.
Refeeding syndrome peaks in the first week of restoration.
Family-based therapy follows medical stabilisation.
explanation.pearls: Always check phosphate, magnesium and potassium daily for the first week of refeeding; an asymptomatic phosphate of 0.4 on day 3 is the classic harbinger of cardiac arrest in refeeding syndrome and must trigger immediate replacement and pause in calorie advancement.

options.rationale: Family-based therapy is the gold standard outpatient model but cannot manage severe bradycardia, postural hypotension and electrolyte derangement; medical admission is required first. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)
Olanzapine has only modest evidence in anorexia and does not address medical instability; medical admission and refeeding take precedence. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)

Bradycardia under 40, postural hypotension, BMI under 14 and hypokalaemia or hypophosphataemia each independently meet admission criteria; supervised refeeding with phosphate and thiamine cover prevents refeeding syndrome. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)
Dietetic input is essential but inadequate alone when medical instability is established; supervised refeeding requires a hospital environment. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)
Outpatient management is unsafe when admission criteria are met; medical complications including arrhythmia and death are well described in this group. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The complications that kill in catatonia are mostly mechanical. Days of immobility with poor oral intake produce venous thromboembolism, pressure injury, aspiration, contracture and rhabdomyolysis. Thromboprophylaxis with a prophylactic dose of low molecular weight heparin, together with mechanical measures and attention to hydration, nutrition, pressure areas and mouth care, is part of the treatment plan from the day catatonia is diagnosed rather than an afterthought once the psychiatric treatment is settled.
key_points: Immobility in catatonia carries a real venous thromboembolism risk
Prophylactic low molecular weight heparin plus mechanical measures is standard
Mechanical measures alone are for patients in whom anticoagulation is contraindicated
Hydration, pressure area and mouth care belong in the same plan
explanation.pearls: A mental health unit bed does not change the risk assessment; the same prophylaxis standard applies as on a medical ward. In context: the general medical care of the immobile catatonic patient carries as much of the mortality as the psychiatric treatment does (Source: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard).

sources.label: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Sustained immobility is a recognised thromboembolism risk, and prophylactic low molecular weight heparin with mechanical measures is standard for immobile inpatients (Source: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard).
source_refs: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Aspirin is the answer for cardiovascular secondary prevention; it is not adequate thromboprophylaxis for an immobile medical inpatient (Source: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard).
source_refs: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Mechanical measures alone are the answer when anticoagulation is contraindicated, for example by active bleeding or severe thrombocytopenia (Source: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard).
source_refs: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Serial imaging investigates suspected thrombosis in a symptomatic patient; it prevents nothing (Source: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard).
source_refs: ACSQHC Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Warfarin is the answer for long term treatment of established thromboembolism or atrial fibrillation, not for short term inpatient prophylaxis (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is defined by one or more non-bizarre fixed false beliefs for at least 1 month without prominent hallucinations, thought disorder or negative symptoms, and with otherwise preserved functioning. Treatment combines antipsychotic medication with engagement-focused psychotherapy. Response rates to antipsychotics are lower than in schizophrenia but partial improvement supports ongoing care. Involuntary treatment is reserved for cases that meet the relevant Mental Health Act threshold.
key_points: Non-bizarre delusion for at least 1 month defines the disorder.
Antipsychotic is first-line; aripiprazole is well tolerated.
Response is partial; engagement strategies matter.
Involuntary care requires risk or grave disability.
explanation.pearls: The persecutory subtype most often presents to general practice through a third party such as a partner or police; refusal of treatment does not equate to grave disability, and forced admission of well-functioning patients risks harming the long-term therapeutic relationship.

options.rationale: Involuntary admission requires risk to self or others or grave disability; isolated non-bizarre delusion with preserved function does not meet the legal threshold. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)
There is no depressive syndrome here; sertraline alone will not treat persistent delusions and may delay appropriate antipsychotic therapy. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

CBT for psychosis is a useful adjunct but is not first-line monotherapy for delusional disorder; antipsychotic therapy is the recommended core intervention. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)
ECT is not indicated as first-line for delusional disorder; antipsychotic trial should be undertaken before any ECT consideration. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

An antipsychotic with strong tolerability is reasonable first-line; aripiprazole produces fewer metabolic and prolactin side effects than older agents and supports engagement in long-term community care. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia but carries a 0.4 to 0.9% risk of agranulocytosis. The Australian central monitoring system (ClopineCentral, ClozaCare) mandates weekly full blood examinations for the first 18 weeks, fortnightly to 12 months, and monthly thereafter. Dispensing is contingent on a result-positive flag within the monitoring system. Myocarditis screening with troponin and C-reactive protein is performed during the first 4 weeks because of a separate cardiac risk.
key_points: Agranulocytosis risk peaks between weeks 6 and 18 of clozapine treatment
Australian monitoring: weekly to week 18, fortnightly to 12 months, monthly thereafter
Red traffic light is neutrophils under 1.5 x10^9/L and requires clozapine cessation
Cardiac monitoring with troponin and CRP screens for myocarditis in the first month
Constipation can progress to ileus, which is a leading cause of clozapine-related death
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced constipation is dose-related and managed with osmotic laxatives such as macrogol from initiation; stimulant laxatives are added if symptoms persist.

options.rationale: Risk of clozapine-induced neutropenia falls after the first 18 weeks; weekly testing for the entire treatment duration is unnecessary and not part of the Australian monitoring schedule. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

Australian clozapine monitoring requires weekly FBE for the first 18 weeks of treatment, fortnightly to 12 months and then monthly while clozapine continues; this matches the time-course of agranulocytosis risk. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

Monthly monitoring is not introduced until after 12 months of treatment in Australia; the agranulocytosis risk peaks between weeks 6 and 18, so monthly testing at 8 weeks is unsafe. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

Routine FBE monitoring is mandatory under the Australian clozapine monitoring scheme; symptom-only monitoring misses early neutropenia and is not permitted. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

Cardiac surveillance with troponin and C-reactive protein is recommended in the first month for myocarditis screening, not weekly thereafter, and is separate from the haematological monitoring schedule. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

explanation.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder is diagnosed by persistent intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions and hyperarousal symptoms following trauma. Australian guidelines from Phoenix Australia recommend trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy or eye movement desensitisation reprocessing as first-line treatment for adults. Pharmacotherapy with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or venlafaxine is considered when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined, or insufficient. Benzodiazepines and stand-alone supportive counselling are explicitly not recommended.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first-line psychological therapies for adult PTSD
Sertraline, paroxetine and venlafaxine are first-line pharmacotherapies if medication is required
Benzodiazepines are not recommended because they impair fear extinction
Atypical antipsychotics are used as augmentation in treatment-resistant PTSD only
Comorbid depression and substance use are treated concurrently to avoid undertreatment
explanation.pearls: PTSD with complex presentations involving prolonged interpersonal trauma may meet criteria for complex PTSD in ICD-11 and benefits from phased therapy with stabilisation before trauma-focused processing.

options.rationale: Trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy and eye movement desensitisation reprocessing are first-line in Australian PTSD guidelines for adults; psychological therapy is preferred over pharmacotherapy as the initial intervention. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Benzodiazepines do not improve PTSD outcomes, may worsen the trauma response and risk dependence; they are not recommended as monotherapy or first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Atypical antipsychotics are used as augmentation in treatment-resistant PTSD, not as a first-line monotherapy; first-line is psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

Symptoms persisting beyond one month with significant distress meet PTSD criteria and warrant active first-line therapy; watchful waiting alone is not appropriate at six months. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

Generic supportive counselling is not trauma-focused and shows inferior outcomes compared with trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy; pharmacotherapy alone is also not first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the most effective long-term treatment for bipolar I disorder and is the only mood stabiliser with a clear anti-suicidal effect. Long-term toxicity affects the thyroid (hypothyroidism in around 20%), parathyroid (hypercalcaemia in around 10%) and kidney (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and slowly progressive chronic kidney disease). The Australian monitoring schedule pairs 6-monthly lithium with electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function, plus annual eGFR. Any dose, illness, diuretic or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory change triggers an interim level.
key_points: Target range is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance and 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for acute mania
Monitoring: 6-monthly lithium, urea, electrolytes, calcium and thyroid; annual eGFR
Hypothyroidism occurs in around 20% and hypercalcaemia in around 10% on long-term lithium
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is the most common renal adverse effect
Drug interactions: non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, ACE inhibitors and thiazides raise levels
explanation.pearls: A 50% rise in lithium level with the introduction of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory is common; advise patients to use paracetamol preferentially and to alert their prescriber before any new medication.

options.rationale: Three-monthly monitoring is the initial schedule but not required indefinitely; once levels are stable, monitoring extends to six-monthly intervals. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
Routine surveillance must continue lifelong because of cumulative renal, thyroid and parathyroid toxicity; stopping monitoring is not safe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Six-monthly serum lithium, electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function with annual eGFR is the Australian long-term monitoring schedule for stable patients on lithium; additional testing is triggered by dose, illness or interacting medication changes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Long-term lithium does not inevitably cause clinically significant chronic kidney disease in most patients; switching to lamotrigine in a euthymic patient with normal renal function is not indicated. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

Annual lithium alone misses thyroid, parathyroid and renal complications; renal and thyroid screening at least 6-monthly remains the Australian standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Opioid agonist therapy with buprenorphine or methadone reduces all-cause mortality by around 50% in people with opioid use disorder. Sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred initially because of its partial agonist ceiling effect, lower respiratory depression risk and intrinsic abuse deterrent through naloxone. Long-acting depot buprenorphine (weekly or monthly subcutaneous formulations) is particularly useful for unstable housing or poor adherence. Methadone is reserved for patients with high tolerance, failed buprenorphine response or specific clinical contexts.
key_points: Buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred initially because of its ceiling effect and lower overdose risk
Induction requires objective opioid withdrawal (COWS at least 12) to avoid precipitated withdrawal
Depot buprenorphine improves adherence in unstable housing and reduces takeaway diversion risk
Methadone induction starts at 20 to 30 mg with cautious uptitration over weeks
Naltrexone requires 7 to 10 days of opioid abstinence before initiation
explanation.pearls: Naloxone is offered to every patient at induction and to their household contacts; intranasal naloxone is now subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for take-home use in Australia.

options.rationale: Methadone induction starts at 20 to 30 mg with cautious titration over weeks because of risk of accumulation and overdose; starting at 80 mg risks fatal respiratory depression. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

Naltrexone requires sustained opioid abstinence for 7 to 10 days before initiation to avoid precipitated withdrawal; it is not appropriate for a person currently using heroin daily. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)
Detoxification without agonist therapy has high relapse and overdose rates; benzodiazepines plus opioids carry overdose risk. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

Opioid agonist therapy is first-line for opioid use disorder and reduces mortality by around 50%; deferring it for psychological therapy alone is not best practice. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

Sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone is the preferred initial agonist for most patients in Australia because of its safety ceiling and overdose protection; long-acting depot buprenorphine improves adherence in unstable housing. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome arises within hours of a new serotonergic agent and is diagnosed by the Hunter criteria, which emphasise clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diaphoresis and autonomic instability. Tramadol is a common precipitant in patients already on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and should be flagged in medication review. Treatment is supportive: cease the agent, give benzodiazepines, cool and hydrate. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome by contrast develops over days, presents with lead-pipe rigidity and bradykinesia, and follows dopamine antagonist exposure.
key_points: Hunter criteria: spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis
Serotonin syndrome develops within hours; NMS develops over 1 to 3 days
Treatment is cessation, benzodiazepines, active cooling and supportive care
Cyproheptadine 12 mg orally is considered in refractory cases
Tramadol, fentanyl, pethidine, linezolid and St John's wort are common co-precipitants
explanation.pearls: MAO inhibitors plus serotonergic agents can cause life-threatening serotonin syndrome that persists for weeks; a 14-day washout is required before switching from a MAO inhibitor to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

options.rationale: Hunter criteria with clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation and autonomic instability after addition of tramadol to sertraline confirm serotonin syndrome; cessation, benzodiazepines and supportive care are first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Bromocriptine and dantrolene are reserved for neuroleptic malignant syndrome with lead-pipe rigidity and dopamine antagonist exposure; the clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome, not NMS. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, which causes dry skin and absent bowel sounds rather than diaphoresis and clonus; it does not address serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Adding antipsychotics or increasing serotonergic agents in suspected serotonin syndrome will worsen the syndrome and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome from haloperidol. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Lithium is not the primary serotonergic agent here, and continuing tramadol and sertraline will perpetuate the syndrome; offending agents must be ceased immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Acute mania with psychotic features is preferentially treated with combination therapy of a mood stabiliser plus a second-generation antipsychotic. Combination treatment achieves a higher response rate than either agent alone. Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole and asenapine have evidence in acute mania; choice is guided by metabolic profile, sedation, prior response and patient preference. Antidepressants are avoided in acute mania because they can worsen the episode and induce rapid cycling.
key_points: Combination of a mood stabiliser and antipsychotic outperforms either alone in acute mania
Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole and asenapine are first-line antipsychotic options
Antidepressants are contraindicated in acute mania because they worsen the episode
Lamotrigine is for bipolar maintenance and depressive episodes, not acute mania
Metabolic monitoring at baseline and 12 weekly is required with second-generation antipsychotics
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole at 15 to 30 mg has the lowest metabolic burden among the second-generation antipsychotics used in mania; it is preferred when long-term cardiometabolic risk is a concern.

options.rationale: Lithium monotherapy is insufficient for severe mania with psychotic features and acute behavioural disturbance; combination with an antipsychotic is required. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)
Switching mood stabilisers in someone with a previously good lithium response is inappropriate; combination treatment with an antipsychotic is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

Adding a second-generation antipsychotic such as olanzapine to lithium is first-line for severe mania with psychotic features in Australia; combination therapy outperforms either agent alone. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)
Antidepressants are contraindicated in acute mania because they risk worsening the manic episode and inducing rapid cycling. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

Lamotrigine has efficacy in bipolar maintenance and depressive episodes, not in acute mania; its slow titration over 6 weeks is unsuitable for acute control. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian RANZCP guidance recommends fluoxetine as the first-line antidepressant in adolescents because it has the strongest randomised controlled trial evidence in this age group, in particular the TADS trial. Combination therapy with cognitive behavioural therapy is more effective than either modality alone. Weekly face-to-face review is recommended for the first 4 weeks because of a small absolute increase in suicidality in the early weeks of treatment. A written safety plan and engagement of family or carers are integral to safe prescribing in this age group.
key_points: Fluoxetine is first-line antidepressant in adolescents
Combine pharmacotherapy with CBT for best outcomes
Weekly face-to-face review for first 4 weeks to monitor suicidality
Engage family and document a written safety plan
Other SSRIs and venlafaxine are second line because of evidence gaps and side effects
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily is the target dose in adolescents with response typically assessed at 4 to 6 weeks before considering increase or switch.

options.rationale: Sertraline is not the first-line antidepressant for adolescents in Australia because evidence for efficacy in this age group is strongest for fluoxetine, which is the recommended initial choice. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
Mirtazapine is not recommended first line in adolescents; the strongest randomised evidence in this age group supports fluoxetine, which is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Failure of an adequate trial of psychological therapy in moderate adolescent depression is an indication to add pharmacotherapy; delay risks ongoing functional impairment. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
Venlafaxine is not first line in adolescents because of higher rates of suicidality and discontinuation syndrome compared with fluoxetine. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Fluoxetine is the first-line antidepressant for adolescent depression in Australia because it has the strongest evidence in this age group; weekly review covers the early increase in suicidality risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Lithium remains a first-line mood stabiliser for bipolar I relapse prevention. Baseline workup before initiation includes renal function (U&E and creatinine), thyroid function, calcium, ECG, weight and a pregnancy test in women of reproductive potential because lithium is teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly). Ongoing monitoring includes serum lithium level 5 to 7 days after each dose change, then every 3 months, and 6-monthly U&E plus thyroid plus calcium with annual eGFR thereafter. The narrow therapeutic window (0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance) requires patient education about dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
key_points: Baseline: U&E, TFT, calcium, ECG, weight, pregnancy test
Ongoing: 3-monthly level, 6-monthly U&E plus TFT plus calcium
Therapeutic range 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L maintenance, 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L in older adults
Avoid in early pregnancy because of Ebstein anomaly
Counsel on dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides as toxicity precipitants
explanation.pearls: Lithium levels should be taken 12 hours post-dose (trough), with target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance and 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L in adults over 65 years.

options.rationale: FBE, LFTs and prolactin are not the core baseline panel for lithium; the relevant tests are urea and electrolytes, thyroid function, calcium, ECG, weight and a pregnancy test. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Lithium baseline panel covers renal function, thyroid function, calcium, ECG and pregnancy status because of long-term renal, thyroid, parathyroid, cardiac and teratogenic risks. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Renal function alone misses thyroid and parathyroid screening required because of hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism risks, and pregnancy must be excluded because of Ebstein anomaly risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
Echocardiography and stress testing are not part of routine lithium initiation; a baseline 12-lead ECG suffices in patients without cardiac history. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
Neuroimaging and EEG are not part of routine lithium initiation; baseline neurological screening is clinical only and no imaging is required. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is predicted by daily intake, duration, previous withdrawal complications and concurrent illness. Patients with previous withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, intake above 150 g daily, significant comorbidity or unstable home environment warrant inpatient detoxification with symptom-triggered diazepam (loaded 20 mg every 2 hours by CIWA-Ar score) and parenteral thiamine cover. Thiamine 300 mg intramuscular or intravenous daily for at least 3 days precedes any glucose-containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Long-acting benzodiazepines are preferred for smoother withdrawal except in significant hepatic impairment where lorazepam or oxazepam are used.
key_points: Previous withdrawal seizures mandate inpatient detoxification with benzodiazepine cover
Diazepam 20 mg loading every 2 hours symptom-triggered is the Australian standard
Parenteral thiamine before any glucose-containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Lorazepam or oxazepam in significant hepatic impairment because they avoid hepatic oxidation
CIWA-Ar score guides ongoing dosing
explanation.pearls: Parenteral thiamine 300 mg intramuscular daily for at least 3 days is given before any intravenous glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in chronic alcohol use.

options.rationale: A history of two previous withdrawal seizures makes seizure recurrence likely without benzodiazepine cover; thiamine alone is insufficient for prophylaxis. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

Previous withdrawal seizures and high daily intake mandate inpatient detox with diazepam symptom-triggered dosing plus parenteral thiamine cover for Wernicke prevention. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

Lorazepam at this dose is unlikely to control withdrawal in heavy drinkers with previous seizures, and outpatient management is unsafe in this risk profile. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

Carbamazepine is occasionally used in mild withdrawal but is not first line in Australia and is inadequate alone for heavy drinkers with a seizure history. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

Outpatient fixed-schedule benzodiazepine in a patient with previous withdrawal seizures and heavy intake is unsafe, and thiamine cover is required regardless of nutritional appearance. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine antagonists. Diagnosis rests on recent exposure plus the tetrad of hyperthermia, generalised rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental state, with creatine kinase typically above 1000 U/L. Management is immediate cessation of the offending agent, supportive care (cooling, intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction, myoglobinuric renal protection), intensive care admission and pharmacological options of dantrolene, bromocriptine or amantadine. Distinguish from serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, recent serotonergic exposure) and malignant catatonia.
key_points: Immediate cessation of the offending dopamine antagonist is the first priority
Supportive care: cooling, intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction
Renal protection for rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria
Dantrolene or bromocriptine for severe cases in intensive care
Differentiate from serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia) and catatonia
explanation.pearls: Rechallenge with a different antipsychotic is possible after at least 2 weeks of full recovery, ideally with a low-potency atypical agent and slow titration.

options.rationale: Continuing the offending dopamine antagonist worsens neuroleptic malignant syndrome and risks death; immediate cessation is required. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

Hyperthermia, autonomic instability and CK over 1000 with recent dopamine antagonist exposure point to NMS rather than isolated catatonia; haloperidol must be ceased and supportive care escalated. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

NMS requires immediate cessation of the offending agent, aggressive supportive care including cooling and fluid resuscitation, and consideration of dantrolene or bromocriptine; renal protection addresses myoglobinuric injury. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

Switching to another antipsychotic continues dopamine blockade and worsens NMS; cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome, which has clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)
Procyclidine treats acute dystonia and parkinsonian extrapyramidal side effects, not NMS; continuing haloperidol perpetuates the syndrome. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

explanation.summary: Australian NHMRC guidelines establish structured psychological therapies, in particular dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based therapy, as the core treatment for borderline personality disorder. Hospital admission is generally avoided for chronic recurrent self-harm because it can reinforce maladaptive patterns and rarely changes long-term trajectory. Acute presentations focus on physical wound care, brief safety planning, communication with the existing treating team and timely outpatient follow-up. Pharmacotherapy has at most an adjunct role for comorbid conditions and short-term crisis use.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy is the core treatment for borderline personality disorder
Routine hospital admission for recurrent self-harm is not therapeutic
Acute care focus is wound management, brief safety planning, team communication, follow-up
Medications have at most adjunct roles for comorbid conditions
Benzodiazepines should generally be avoided because of dependence and disinhibition risk
explanation.pearls: Brief admission may be considered when there is a clear acute risk above baseline or comorbid major depression, but should be planned, time-limited and discharge focused.

options.rationale: Hospital admission for chronic recurrent self-harm in borderline personality disorder is generally not therapeutic and can be iatrogenic; outpatient psychological therapy is the evidence-based core treatment. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

Routine benzodiazepines have no role in chronic borderline personality disorder and risk dependence and disinhibition; communication with the existing treating team is essential. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

Best-practice care for borderline personality disorder presenting after non-lethal self-harm involves wound management, brief safety planning, communication with the treating team and timely outpatient follow-up rather than admission. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

Pharmacotherapy has no first-line role for the core features of borderline personality disorder, and bypassing the existing treating team fragments care. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)
ECT has no role in the treatment of borderline personality disorder; it is reserved for severe treatment-resistant depression or catatonia. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, cause weight gain, dyslipidaemia and dysglycaemia. RANZCP recommends weight, waist, BP, fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months and then 6-monthly. Lifestyle intervention is first-line; metformin can be added when insulin resistance is established or weight gain progresses despite lifestyle. Switching antipsychotics is considered when metabolic harm exceeds psychiatric benefit.
key_points: Olanzapine has high metabolic risk; clozapine highest
Monitor weight, BP, fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then 6-monthly
Lifestyle intervention is first-line for weight gain and dyslipidaemia
Metformin can be added when insulin resistance is established or weight gain progresses
Switching antipsychotic is considered when metabolic harm outweighs psychiatric benefit
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole and ziprasidone have the lowest weight gain profile among second-generation antipsychotics and are favoured in first-episode psychosis when metabolic syndrome risk is high or already present.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend 3-month then 6-monthly metabolic monitoring for second-generation antipsychotics with intervention via lifestyle and medication review when weight, glucose or lipid changes appear. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Metformin is considered after lifestyle measures fail or when significant insulin resistance is present; pre-emptive use in mild weight gain without dysglycaemia is not first-line. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Switching antipsychotic in stable first-episode response carries relapse risk and is reserved for significant intolerance; risperidone has different but not negligible metabolic and prolactin effects. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Stress echocardiography is not indicated in an asymptomatic 23-year-old; cardiovascular risk reduction in early psychosis hinges on lifestyle and medication selection, not advanced imaging. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Stopping the antipsychotic in a first-episode patient with response risks relapse; benzodiazepines do not treat psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder and first-episode schizophrenia overlap significantly and are not reliably distinguishable at first presentation. Around half of cannabis-induced psychoses transition to a primary psychotic disorder within 3 years, so management mirrors first-episode psychosis with antipsychotic treatment, AOD intervention and structured follow-up. High-potency cannabis use confers the greatest risk. Voluntary admission is preferred when engagement allows.
key_points: Cannabis-induced and primary psychotic disorders overlap clinically at first presentation
Around 50% of cannabis-induced psychoses transition to primary psychotic disorder within 3 years
Treat with antipsychotic plus abstinence support and structured follow-up
High-potency cannabis use confers the greatest risk
Voluntary admission is preferred when the patient is engaging and safe
explanation.pearls: Daily use of high-potency cannabis (over 10% THC content) is associated with a nearly 5-fold increased risk of psychotic disorder compared with non-users; risk is highest under 18 years of age.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychotic symptoms; same-day discharge from ED without an antipsychotic plan or specialist follow-up misses the early-intervention window. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Active psychotic symptoms are unsafe to manage at home and warrant antipsychotic treatment; abstinence alone often does not resolve symptoms quickly. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Compulsory detention is reserved for refusal of treatment with risk; he is calm and agreeable. Haloperidol intramuscular every 6 hours is overaggressive and risks extrapyramidal side effects. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: SSRIs do not treat psychosis and can worsen symptoms; antipsychotic is required. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: First-presentation psychosis in the context of heavy cannabis use needs antipsychotic treatment, abstinence support, and structured follow-up because around half of cannabis-induced psychoses transition to a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome of stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and echophenomena, frequently associated with mood disorders, psychotic illness and medical conditions. The lorazepam challenge with 1 to 2 mg IM or IV provides rapid diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic effect; responders continue scheduled lorazepam. Non-responders or those with malignant features (autonomic instability, hyperthermia) need urgent ECT. Antipsychotics are avoided until catatonia resolves.
key_points: Catatonia features include stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and echophenomena
Lorazepam challenge is the diagnostic and therapeutic standard
Scheduled lorazepam continues for responders; ECT for non-response or malignant features
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves due to malignant catatonia risk
Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale aids diagnosis and severity tracking
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, severe rigidity) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome are increasingly viewed as variants of the same neurochemical spectrum; ECT is effective for both and should not be delayed in critically ill patients.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and worsen the syndrome; they are avoided in suspected catatonia until benzodiazepines are first trialled. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

The lorazepam challenge is the standard diagnostic and therapeutic test for catatonia; a marked reduction in catatonic features within 30 minutes confirms the diagnosis and supports continued benzodiazepine treatment, with ECT for non-response. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

Lithium augmentation is not the treatment for catatonia and the level is already therapeutic; a benzodiazepine challenge addresses the immediate problem. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

Valproate is not first-line for catatonia and combined valproate-lithium does not address the syndrome; benzodiazepines plus ECT are the evidence-based path. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

NG feeding may be needed but does not treat catatonia; deferring psychotropic intervention prolongs the syndrome and risks complications such as pulmonary embolism and contractures. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

explanation.summary: Valproate causes major congenital malformations in around 10% of exposed pregnancies and neurodevelopmental impairment in 30 to 40%, particularly autism spectrum and reduced IQ. The TGA pregnancy prevention program requires annual specialist review, documented contraception and a signed acknowledgement for women of reproductive potential. Pregnancy planning requires transition to safer agents such as lamotrigine under specialist supervision before conception. Folate does not mitigate teratogenicity.
key_points: Valproate causes around 10% major malformations and 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental impairment
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates annual review and documented contraception
Transition to safer agents such as lamotrigine occurs before conception, not during pregnancy
Folate does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity
Lamotrigine has the lowest teratogenic risk of the mood stabilisers (around 2% major malformation)
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance increases by up to 250% during pregnancy due to glucuronidation induction; doses typically need to rise from second trimester and return to baseline within 2 weeks postpartum to avoid toxicity.

sources.label: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

options.rationale: Carbamazepine has higher major malformation rates (around 5%) than lamotrigine (around 2%) and is not the preferred switch for pregnancy planning in bipolar disorder. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Folate does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity or neurodevelopmental risk; continuation in pregnancy planning is contraindicated outside extraordinary circumstances. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

options.rationale: Valproate carries 10% major congenital malformation risk and a 30 to 40% risk of neurodevelopmental impairment; women of reproductive potential planning pregnancy require transition to safer agents under specialist supervision with continued contraception. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

options.rationale: Abrupt valproate cessation in bipolar I without bridging risks severe relapse; transition under specialist guidance to a maintenance-effective alternative is required. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Neural tube defect risk is highest in the first trimester so continuing valproate during that window is exactly the wrong sequence; safer agents must be in place before conception. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade (wide QRS, terminal R in aVR), QT prolongation, hypotension, anticholinergic delirium, seizures and arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg is the antidote, narrowing QRS by sodium loading and alkalosis-driven protein binding. Airway protection precedes any procedure on a falling GCS. Class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics, physostigmine and flumazenil are contraindicated.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or terminal R in aVR over 3 mm signals significant TCA cardiotoxicity
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg is the antidote targeting QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55
Intubate before lavage or charcoal if GCS is falling
Avoid class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics, physostigmine and flumazenil
ICU admission until ECG is normal off bicarbonate for at least 6 hours
explanation.pearls: Intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg of 20% solution is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse from lipophilic drug toxicity including amitriptyline, and may be considered when bicarbonate and standard resuscitation are insufficient.

sources.label: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine Toxicology Reference

options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms with terminal R in aVR over 3 mm signals significant TCA cardiotoxicity; sodium bicarbonate narrows QRS by sodium loading and pH-driven protein binding shift, intubation protects the airway with deteriorating GCS, and ICU is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine Toxicology Reference

options.rationale: Charcoal at 90 minutes after overdose has limited benefit and is contraindicated with a falling GCS without airway protection; QRS widening already mandates bicarbonate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose with TCA because it can precipitate seizures by lowering the seizure threshold against the proconvulsant TCA effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose due to the risk of asystole; reversal of anticholinergic features does not address the sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

Class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated in TCA toxicity; treatment is sodium bicarbonate and supportive care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Acute severe behavioural disturbance in Australia uses parenteral rapid tranquillisation when de-escalation fails. Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg is first-line in adults with cardiac monitoring and oximetry; the Druid 1 and Druid 2 trial program supports efficacy and acceptable QTc safety. Olanzapine intramuscular 10 mg is an alternative. Ketamine is reserved for refractory cases. Mechanical restraint and post-tranquillisation observation are mandatory components.
key_points: IM droperidol 10 mg is the Australian first-line for adult acute behavioural disturbance
Cardiac monitoring and oximetry are mandatory during and after rapid tranquillisation
Olanzapine IM 10 mg is an alternative first-line in adults
Ketamine is reserved for refractory cases with anaesthetic backup
De-escalation precedes pharmacological intervention; restraint is the last resort
explanation.pearls: Combined intramuscular olanzapine and benzodiazepines within 60 minutes of each other are associated with hypotension and respiratory depression; if recent IM lorazepam or midazolam has been given, droperidol is preferred over olanzapine.

sources.label: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.rationale: Promethazine combinations are no longer preferred in Australian guidance due to lower efficacy than droperidol; cardiac monitoring is required for all parenteral antipsychotic use in this setting. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy at 10 mg carries higher airway and oversedation risks than droperidol at this dose in adult acute behavioural disturbance; combination or antipsychotic monotherapy is preferred. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.rationale: He has refused oral medication; oral routes are not appropriate in active behavioural disturbance requiring tranquillisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Australian rapid tranquillisation guidance recommends intramuscular droperidol 10 mg as first-line for adult acute behavioural disturbance with cardiac monitoring; large RCT data (DORM trial) support efficacy and safety. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.rationale: Ketamine is a salvage option for failure of standard rapid tranquillisation, not first-line; its use mandates anaesthetic backup and is not the initial step. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

explanation.summary: ADHD and stimulant use disorder co-occur frequently and each worsens the other if untreated. Australian guidance prioritises non-stimulant pharmacotherapy (atomoxetine, less commonly bupropion) in adults with active or recent stimulant use disorder, with structured addiction medicine engagement throughout. Stimulant trial may be revisited after demonstrated stability, using long-acting formulations and tight prescriber controls. Driving capacity, cardiovascular screening and contraceptive counselling are part of standard ADHD initiation.
key_points: Atomoxetine is first-line for adult ADHD with comorbid stimulant use disorder
Indefinite deferral of pharmacotherapy worsens outcomes
Long-acting stimulants are preferred over immediate-release if later required
Baseline cardiovascular and driving screening is essential
Concurrent addiction medicine engagement is mandatory
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine titration typically takes 4 to 6 weeks for full clinical effect, unlike stimulants which act within hours; this slow onset is a useful counselling point because patients often expect rapid stimulant-like response and disengage if not prepared.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Guanfacine ER is approved in Australia for children and adolescents but is not first-line for adult ADHD; atomoxetine is the standard adult non-stimulant. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Immediate-release stimulants carry the highest diversion and misuse risk and are not first-line in active or recent stimulant use disorder. Long-acting formulations are preferred if a stimulant trial is later required. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Although long-acting stimulants have lower diversion risk than immediate-release, Australian guidance recommends a period of demonstrated stability and non-stimulant trial first in comorbid stimulant use disorder. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Indefinite deferral worsens ADHD symptom burden and risks return to methamphetamine self-medication; non-stimulant trial can proceed safely with addiction medicine engagement. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Australian ADHD guidelines recommend non-stimulant first-line treatment in adults with comorbid stimulant use disorder due to diversion and relapse risk; atomoxetine is the standard non-stimulant choice. Reassessment after substance-use stabilisation guides any later stimulant decision. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Medical admission criteria for anorexia nervosa include BMI under 14, bradycardia under 40, postural drop, hypothermia, electrolyte derangement, QTc over 450 and recent syncope. Inpatient care prioritises cautious refeeding to avoid refeeding syndrome, starting at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring. Phosphate, potassium and magnesium are replaced before and during feeding, with prophylactic thiamine. Use of the Mental Health Act is reserved for refusal of life-saving treatment.
key_points: Admit if BMI under 14, HR under 40, postural drop, QTc over 450 or electrolyte derangement
Refeed at 5-10 kcal/kg/day, escalate slowly with daily electrolytes
Replace phosphate, potassium, magnesium before and during feeds
Thiamine 200 mg daily prophylaxis
Mental Health Act for refusal of life-saving treatment only
explanation.pearls: Phosphate is the single most reliable early biochemical marker of refeeding syndrome; a drop below 0.6 mmol/L in the first week of refeeding warrants dose reduction, supplementation and senior review.

sources.label: MARSIPAN UK adapted Australian medical care of severe anorexia

options.rationale: BMI 13.5 with bradycardia, hypotension, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and QTc prolongation all meet inpatient admission criteria for anorexia nervosa. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)
Starting feeds at 30 kcal/kg/day in a high-risk patient risks refeeding syndrome; initial feeds are 5-10 kcal/kg/day with cautious escalation. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)

Inpatient management of severe anorexia with multiple medical criteria includes thiamine, electrolyte correction before feeding and cautious refeeding starting at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with daily phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose monitoring. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)
source_refs: MARSIPAN UK adapted Australian medical care of severe anorexia

options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is not first-line; oral or nasogastric refeeding is preferred. Use of the Mental Health Act is reserved for refusal of life-saving treatment without insight. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)
Acute medical instability requires immediate medical admission rather than outpatient bridging while awaiting a private bed. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines for PTSD recommend trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first-line treatment. SSRIs (sertraline or paroxetine) are second-line or used as adjuncts when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable or ineffective. Prazosin can target nightmares in refractory cases. Atypical antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for partial response after first- and second-line measures. Mindfulness and supportive counselling alone are not sufficient.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first-line in PTSD
Sertraline and paroxetine are second-line SSRIs
Prazosin can target nightmares in refractory cases
Atypical antipsychotic augmentation is third-line
Supportive counselling alone is inadequate for core PTSD symptoms
explanation.pearls: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) is non-inferior to trauma-focused CBT and may be preferred when patients find prolonged narrative exposure too distressing; benzodiazepines are not recommended in PTSD because they worsen recovery.

options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not first-line in PTSD and supportive counselling alone is inferior to trauma-focused therapy for core PTSD symptoms. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Atypical antipsychotic augmentation is third-line in PTSD and carries metabolic risk; first-line escalation is trauma-focused psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)
Prazosin is an option for refractory nightmares but does not substitute for first-line trauma-focused psychological therapy in PTSD. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

Australian PTSD guidelines place trauma-focused CBT and EMDR as first-line therapy; supportive counselling is insufficient and pharmacotherapy is second-line or adjunctive. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)
MBSR is not first-line for PTSD and SSRI discontinuation in partial responders is not warranted; trauma-focused therapy is the next step. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Delirium tremens is a medical emergency with mortality up to 15% if untreated. Management requires high-dependency or intensive care monitoring, intravenous benzodiazepine titration (diazepam or midazolam), parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and electrolyte correction. Antipsychotics are avoided as primary therapy because they lower the seizure threshold. Intubation and propofol are reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: DT requires HDU or ICU monitoring
IV benzodiazepine titration is first-line
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg TDS before glucose
Correct magnesium, potassium, phosphate
Avoid first-generation antipsychotics as primary therapy
explanation.pearls: Score severity of withdrawal with CIWA-Ar but use the score to titrate benzodiazepine dose rather than to triage location; any seizure, autonomic instability or hallucinations escalate the patient to high-dependency or intensive care regardless of the numeric score.

options.rationale: Established delirium tremens with seizure and autonomic instability requires intravenous benzodiazepine titration in a high-dependency setting, not oral symptom-triggered dosing on a general ward. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Use Disorders)

First-generation antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are inappropriate as primary therapy in delirium tremens; benzodiazepines remain the cornerstone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Phenytoin is not effective for alcohol withdrawal seizures and does not treat the underlying autonomic instability; benzodiazepine titration is first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
Intubation and propofol are reserved for refractory delirium tremens after high-dose benzodiazepine titration has failed; titration is the first step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Established delirium tremens with seizure mandates HDU care, IV benzodiazepine titration, parenteral thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy and electrolyte correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires a structured assessment, evidence of symptoms before age 12, functional impairment across two or more settings, and exclusion of mimics. Stimulant medication is first-line treatment and requires a stimulant authority held by a psychiatrist or paediatrician. Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive obligates notification of the driver licensing authority when ADHD has safety-relevant features or pharmacotherapy is being commenced. CBT and skills coaching are adjunctive.
key_points: DSM-5 onset before age 12 with cross-setting impairment
Stimulants are first-line; authority required to prescribe
Atomoxetine is second-line when stimulants contraindicated
Austroads driver licensing notification for safety-relevant ADHD
CBT and coaching are adjunctive
explanation.pearls: Baseline ECG is recommended before stimulant initiation in patients with family history of sudden cardiac death, structural heart disease, syncope, palpitations or pre-existing hypertension; stimulant cardiovascular safety in healthy adults is otherwise good.

options.rationale: Stimulant initiation requires a stimulant authority (psychiatrist or paediatrician) in Australia and Austroads requires patient notification of the driver licensing authority for treated ADHD with safety-relevant features. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)
General practitioners cannot independently initiate stimulant therapy for adult ADHD in Australia; this requires a stimulant authority. (Source: PBS Stimulants for ADHD authority)
Stimulants are first-line for adult ADHD in Australia; atomoxetine is second-line when stimulants are contraindicated or not tolerated. (Source: RACGP: Adult ADHD)
CBT is adjunctive in moderate-severe adult ADHD; pharmacotherapy is the primary intervention with greatest effect size. (Source: RACGP: Adult ADHD)
DSM-5 lowered the age-of-onset criterion to before age 12 and the diagnosis can be confirmed in adulthood with appropriate collateral. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is distinguished from bipolar I with psychotic features by the presence of 2 or more weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a major mood episode. Mood episodes must be present for the majority of the total illness duration. Schizophrenia is distinguished by mood symptoms being brief relative to active and residual phases. Treatment of schizoaffective bipolar type uses a combination of antipsychotic and mood stabiliser. The diagnosis influences both pharmacotherapy and prognosis.
key_points: Schizoaffective: 2+ weeks of psychosis without mood episode plus mood episodes for majority of illness
Bipolar with psychotic features: psychosis only during mood episodes
Schizophrenia: mood symptoms brief relative to active and residual
Brief psychotic disorder: less than 1 month duration
Schizoaffective bipolar type: antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser
explanation.pearls: Lithium and lamotrigine are both reasonable mood-stabilising adjuncts in schizoaffective bipolar type; lithium has greater anti-manic and anti-suicide effect while lamotrigine targets depressive episodes with lower upfront monitoring burden.

options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires two or more weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a major mood episode, with mood episodes present for the majority of total illness duration. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Psychotic symptoms persisted for 5 weeks during normal mood, which is incompatible with bipolar I psychotic features (where psychosis occurs only during mood episodes). (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Schizophrenia requires significant mood symptoms to be brief relative to active and residual phases; sustained mania for 3 weeks excludes schizophrenia. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Urine drug screen is negative and the persistence of psychotic symptoms during normal mood does not fit substance-induced psychosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Brief psychotic disorder is by definition less than 1 month duration; this presentation has lasted 8 weeks. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: First-line antidepressant in geriatric depression is an SSRI, with sertraline typically preferred due to its favourable interaction profile with apixaban relative to other SSRIs, low anticholinergic burden and stability in moderate renal impairment. Citalopram is dose-restricted in older adults due to QTc prolongation. Tricyclics are avoided. Mirtazapine, venlafaxine and duloxetine are second-line. Monitoring of sodium at 2 and 4 weeks detects SSRI-induced hyponatraemia.
key_points: Sertraline is preferred first-line SSRI in older adults
Citalopram limited to 20 mg in over-65s due to QTc
Avoid tricyclics in older adults (Beers list)
Mirtazapine and SNRIs are second-line
Monitor sodium at 2 and 4 weeks for SSRI hyponatraemia
explanation.pearls: SSRIs increase upper gastrointestinal bleeding risk by approximately 2-fold; in older adults on concurrent anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy consider co-prescription of a proton pump inhibitor and document the risk-benefit discussion.

sources.label: TGA citalopram QT prolongation safety advisory

options.rationale: Tricyclics are avoided in older adults because of anticholinergic, cardiac and falls risk; they appear on the Beers list and STOPP/START criteria as potentially inappropriate. (Source: AGS Beers Criteria)

Sertraline is a first-line SSRI in older adults: no significant interaction with apixaban for bleeding (lower compared with paroxetine and fluoxetine), low anticholinergic burden, dose adjustment not required for moderate CKD. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Mirtazapine is a reasonable second-line in older adults but is not preferred over sertraline as first-line; first-line remains SSRI per Australian guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
Citalopram is restricted to 20 mg in adults over 65 due to dose-dependent QTc prolongation; her baseline QTc is already 460 ms. (Source: TGA citalopram QT prolongation safety advisory)
source_refs: TGA citalopram QT prolongation safety advisory

options.rationale: SNRIs are reserved for second-line in older adults due to blood pressure effects and a higher discontinuation profile; SSRI is preferred first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Clozapine carries a 1 to 2% lifetime risk of agranulocytosis and 3% of neutropenia. The Australian monitoring system uses traffic-light thresholds (specific thresholds may vary by manufacturer but a common scheme is): green WBC at least 3.5 and ANC at least 2.0, amber WBC 3.0 to 3.5 or ANC 1.5 to 2.0 (continue with weekly FBC) or WBC 2.0 to 3.0 or ANC 1.0 to 1.5 (continue with twice-weekly FBC, look for infection), red WBC under 2.0 or ANC under 1.0 (stop clozapine immediately, admit, haematology referral, sepsis workup, consider G-CSF). After 18 weeks monitoring drops to monthly, but any abnormal result reverts to weekly or more frequent.
key_points: Clozapine agranulocytosis risk 1-2% lifetime; highest in first 6 months
Green: WBC at least 3.5 AND ANC at least 2.0
Amber WBC 2.0-3.0 or ANC 1.0-1.5: continue, twice-weekly FBC
Red WBC under 2.0 or ANC under 1.0: STOP, admit, haematology, sepsis workup
After 18 weeks: monthly FBC, but abnormal reverts to weekly+
explanation.pearls: The lifetime clozapine rechallenge after stopping for haematological reasons is generally only permitted via the manufacturer's special-access scheme and after haematology and psychiatric MDT review; do not casually restart clozapine after a red result.

options.rationale: ANC of 1.1 x10^9/L is an amber result requiring twice-weekly monitoring and immediate review; clinical assumption of viral cause does not exempt from protocol. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

Reducing dose without proper protocol does not address agranulocytosis risk; the Australian clozapine monitoring system uses specific action thresholds, not arbitrary dose halving. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)
This is the appropriate action for a red result (ANC under 1.0 x10^9/L) or for clinical sepsis; the current result is amber and not yet red. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

Switching antipsychotic on a single amber FBC bypasses the recommended monitoring escalation; abrupt cessation of clozapine also risks rebound psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

ANC 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L (or WBC 2.0 to 3.0) is an amber result: continue clozapine, monitor twice weekly, review for infection and notify the clozapine coordinator. Stop only if ANC under 1.0 or there are clinical features of sepsis. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium therapy requires monitoring for therapeutic level (narrow therapeutic index 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L), nephrotoxicity (chronic interstitial nephritis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), hypothyroidism (around 10 to 20% over years), and hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia. The recommended monitoring for stable maintenance therapy is 6-monthly lithium level, UEC, TFTs and corrected calcium. Initiation or dose change triggers more frequent monitoring (5 to 7 days after dose change). Drug interactions to flag are NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides (all raise lithium), and dehydration (volume contraction raises lithium). Levels are measured 12 hours post-dose (trough).
key_points: Stable maintenance lithium: 6-monthly level, UEC, TFTs, corrected calcium
Therapeutic range: 0.6-0.8 maintenance, 0.8-1.0 acute
Level taken 12 hours post-dose (trough)
Watch interactions: NSAIDs, ACEI/ARBs, thiazides all raise lithium
Long-term risks: CKD, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, nephrogenic DI
explanation.pearls: If a patient on chronic lithium presents with polyuria and polydipsia, do not assume diabetes mellitus; a urine osmolality below serum osmolality despite hyperosmolar plasma confirms nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and may persist after lithium cessation.

options.rationale: RANZCP and AMH guidance is 6-monthly lithium level plus 6-monthly UEC, TFTs and corrected calcium in stable maintenance lithium beyond the first year. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))
Monthly lithium and UEC is unnecessarily frequent for a stable patient and not recommended; this schedule applies to initiation or dose change. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))
Annual monitoring intervals are too long; 6-monthly is the recommended minimum for stable maintenance. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))
Three-monthly lithium and UEC is more frequent than required for stable patients and not consistent with Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))
Routine TFTs, UEC and corrected calcium are required, not only if symptomatic, because hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism can be insidious. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose presents with anticholinergic features, CNS depression, cardiovascular toxicity (sodium channel blockade) and seizures. ECG markers of significant toxicity include QRS over 100 ms (sensitivity ~80%), R wave in aVR over 3 mm, terminal R/S ratio in aVR over 0.7, and rightward axis. Sodium bicarbonate boluses (1 to 2 mmol/kg, often 100 mmol in adults) are indicated for QRS over 100 ms, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia or seizures. Target pH 7.45 to 7.55. Intubation and hyperventilation aid alkalinisation. IV lipid emulsion and ECMO are last-line. Activated charcoal only if airway secured and within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion.
key_points: TCA toxicity ECG: QRS over 100 ms, R in aVR over 3 mm
Sodium bicarbonate: 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, target pH 7.45-7.55
Intubate for GCS under 9 or for hyperventilation to aid alkalinisation
Avoid: flumazenil, beta-blockers, class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics, physostigmine
Refractory: lipid emulsion, ECMO support
explanation.pearls: Apparent benzodiazepine-responsive seizures in TCA overdose still trigger urgent sodium bicarbonate because the underlying mechanism is sodium channel blockade; once a TCA seizes the patient is at imminent risk of cardiac arrest from the same channel block.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists Toxicology Network

options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms with hypotension and an R wave in aVR over 3 mm meets criteria for immediate sodium bicarbonate; activated charcoal alone is inadequate given the cardiac toxicity. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)

QRS over 100 ms, R in aVR over 3 mm, hypotension and CNS depression in TCA overdose are indications for sodium bicarbonate boluses titrated to QRS narrowing and pH 7.45-7.55, plus intubation for airway and crystalloid resuscitation. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)
Beta-blockade in TCA overdose worsens hypotension; tachycardia is compensatory for vasodilation and direct cardiac toxicity. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed or unknown overdoses (precipitates seizures); rapid alkalinisation is the indicated treatment, not a hazard. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)
Sodium bicarbonate is indicated at QRS over 100 ms, not over 160 ms; magnesium alone does not address sodium channel blockade. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a treatable syndrome with motor, behavioural and autonomic features. Recognition relies on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale or DSM criteria (at least 3 of mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia, mannerisms, stereotypy, grimacing, agitation, mutism). The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or sublingual) achieves partial or complete response in about 50% within 10 minutes; this both confirms the diagnosis and is the start of treatment. Scheduled lorazepam 2 mg three times daily is continued. ECT is highly effective and is recommended if there is no response in 48-72 hours, for malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia), or for life-threatening features. Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves due to NMS risk.
key_points: Diagnosis: 3+ of mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia (DSM)
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV challenge: 50% partial response within 10 minutes
Scheduled lorazepam 2 mg TDS as ongoing first-line
ECT if no response in 48-72 hours or for malignant catatonia
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves (NMS risk)
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis) clinically overlaps with NMS and serotonin syndrome; in either picture, withhold antipsychotics, give benzodiazepines, and consider urgent ECT if there is no rapid improvement.

sources.label: Sienaert et al. A clinical review of catatonia

options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and may precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepines (lorazepam challenge) are first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Nutritional support is appropriate but should not delay catatonia-specific treatment; the catatonia itself is reversible with lorazepam in most cases and treating it will restore oral intake. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Autoimmune encephalitis is a consideration but lorazepam challenge is the recommended next step and gives both diagnostic and therapeutic information rapidly. NMDAR antibodies, EEG and LP are part of workup. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Lorazepam challenge is the standard initial step for suspected catatonia; partial improvement supports the diagnosis and informs ongoing scheduled lorazepam. ECT is indicated if no response in 48-72 hours or for malignant catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
Withholding pharmacotherapy delays both diagnosis and treatment; lorazepam challenge is recommended on the day of presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires symptoms onset before age 12 (DSM-5), persistence into adulthood, functional impairment in two or more settings, and not better explained by another condition. The AADPA guideline (2022) is the current Australian standard. Diagnosis is by specialist (psychiatrist) using structured interview such as DIVA-5 plus screening tools (ASRS-v1.1). Stimulant initiation requires Schedule 8 authority; ongoing prescribing can be shared-care with GPs in some states. Atomoxetine, guanfacine and bupropion are non-stimulant options. Austroads requires disclosure when symptoms (with or without treatment) might affect safe driving; most well-controlled adults can hold an unconditional licence.
key_points: DSM-5 ADHD: childhood onset (under 12), persistent, impairing, 2+ settings
Specialist diagnosis with DIVA-5 or ASRS-v1.1
Stimulants are Schedule 8: authority psychiatrist (or paeds) initiates
Non-stimulants: atomoxetine, guanfacine, bupropion
Austroads: disclose if symptoms affect driving; conditional licence possible
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD presentations in women are commonly missed because hyperactivity manifests as internal restlessness and inattention dominates; longstanding sense of underperformance, chronic disorganisation and burnout out of proportion to load is a soft red flag to screen formally rather than label as anxiety.

sources.label: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.rationale: GPs cannot initiate stimulants in adult ADHD in most Australian states; an authority psychiatrist (or in some states paediatrician) must confirm the diagnosis and initiate stimulant therapy under Schedule 8 authority. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.rationale: She describes longstanding childhood-onset symptoms documented by teachers, not adult-onset, and meets symptom thresholds; CBT alone without considering ADHD misses the diagnosis. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)
