options.rationale: Atomoxetine still requires diagnostic confirmation before initiation; AADPA recommends formal diagnosis through a specialist with structured assessment, not GP commencement on screening features. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.rationale: Routine EEG, MRI and polysomnography are not indicated unless specific clinical features suggest these diagnoses; this delays appropriate ADHD pathway. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.rationale: AADPA recommends specialist diagnostic confirmation with validated tools (DIVA-5, ASRS), comorbidity assessment, and driver-licensing implications under Austroads should be discussed where symptoms could affect driving. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))

explanation.summary: Combined behavioural support (Quitline) plus pharmacotherapy is the most effective approach. Varenicline (TGA-approved, 12-week course, quit date at day 8-14) has the highest 6-month abstinence rates per EAGLES and Cochrane network meta-analyses. Combination NRT (patch plus oral) is similar in efficacy. Bupropion is effective but contraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorders and severe hepatic impairment. EAGLES confirmed varenicline and bupropion neuropsychiatric and cardiovascular safety in patients with and without mental health conditions. Post-MI is a high-leverage teachable moment; cessation halves 5-year mortality. Pregnant women are typically offered NRT (oral forms preferred), and adolescents NRT only.
key_points: First-line: varenicline OR combination NRT (patch + oral)
Bupropion: contraindicated in seizures, EDs, severe hepatic disease
EAGLES (2016): varenicline cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric safety confirmed
Behavioural support: Quitline 13 78 48 adds substantially to pharmacotherapy
Pregnancy: NRT (oral preferred); adolescents NRT only
explanation.pearls: Schedule the quit date 8 to 14 days after starting varenicline so the patient is steroid-stated on the medication; ramping the dose first reduces nausea, which is the main reason for early discontinuation.

sources.label: EAGLES trial: Anthenelli et al. Lancet 2016

options.rationale: Single-form NRT is less effective than combination NRT or varenicline; given high dependence (Fagerstrom 8) a more effective regimen should be offered. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)
Varenicline is safe and effective in stable post-MI patients beyond 2 weeks; deferral until 6 months loses a key teachable moment. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

Varenicline has the highest evidence for sustained 6-month abstinence; the EAGLES trial confirmed cardiac and neuropsychiatric safety. Standard 12-week course with quit date at day 8-14 plus Quitline. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

Bupropion is effective but slightly less so than varenicline; it is contraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorders and severe hepatic impairment. Varenicline has stronger evidence post-MI. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

Combination NRT is a reasonable second choice but is less effective than varenicline and behavioural support (Quitline) significantly increases abstinence; not offering it is suboptimal. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

explanation.summary: Australian ED protocols (NSW Health, Victorian DHHS) for acute severe behavioural disturbance prioritise de-escalation first. If failed, first-line parenteral options include droperidol 10 mg IM (repeat at 15 min, max 20 mg), olanzapine IM 10 mg or midazolam IM 5 to 10 mg, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring. Avoid combinations of benzodiazepines and antipsychotics where possible due to additive respiratory depression. Ketamine 4 to 5 mg/kg IM is a third-line option with airway-capable clinician present. Document indication, dose, monitoring and review interval. Apply restraint principles consistent with the local Mental Health Act.
key_points: De-escalation first (15 min); chemical restraint if failed
First-line IM: droperidol 10 mg (repeat at 15 min) OR olanzapine 10 mg OR midazolam 5-10 mg
Continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring required post-dose
Avoid routine combination of benzodiazepine + antipsychotic
Ketamine 4-5 mg/kg IM is tertiary option with airway support
explanation.pearls: Document the failure of de-escalation, the specific indication, the consent or legal authority (e.g. Mental Health Act ITO), the dose, route and time, and the planned review at 15 minutes; the audit trail matters as much as the choice of agent in subsequent medico-legal review.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: NSW Health rapid tranquillisation guidance for acute severe behavioural disturbance in adults endorses droperidol 10 mg IM as a first-line option, with repeat at 15 minutes and standard monitoring. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: Haloperidol-promethazine combination is no longer first-line in Australian ED rapid tranquillisation; droperidol IM (or olanzapine IM, midazolam IM in some protocols) is preferred. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: Midazolam IM monotherapy is an option in protocols but mandates continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring (respiratory depression risk); intermittent vitals are inadequate. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: Ketamine is a tertiary option (failed other agents) and is given by experienced clinicians with airway capability; not first-line in standard ED protocols. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: Oral medication assumes cooperation that has clearly already failed; parenteral chemical restraint is required for documented refractory severe behavioural disturbance. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)

explanation.summary: BPD is best managed by evidence-based structured psychotherapy programs delivered over at least 12 months: dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT, Linehan), mentalisation-based therapy (MBT, Bateman & Fonagy), schema-focused therapy (SFT, Young) or transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP, Kernberg). NHMRC guidelines recommend these as first-line over pharmacotherapy. Medications are used for specific comorbid disorders (depression, anxiety) or symptom targets (impulsivity), not for BPD as a whole; polypharmacy should be rationalised. Long-stay admissions are generally avoided; brief crisis admission only for acute risk that cannot be safely managed in community. Crisis plans and safety plans are core community components.
key_points: First-line: structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, SFT, TFP) 12+ months
Pharmacotherapy: comorbidity-targeted only; rationalise polypharmacy
Long-stay admission avoided; brief crisis admission for acute risk only
Safety plans and crisis lines as part of community care
Family/carer support is recommended
explanation.pearls: Stress prescribing in BPD (adding more drugs after crises) tends to accumulate sedating polypharmacy that worsens function and falls risk without changing self-harm rates; structured deprescribing in stable phases is as important as introducing therapy.

sources.label: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first-line for BPD; structured psychotherapy is the recommended treatment. Polypharmacy without specific indication should be avoided. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: NHMRC and RANZCP recommend evidence-based structured psychotherapies (DBT, MBT, SFT, transference-focused psychotherapy) as first-line for BPD with active rationalisation of pharmacotherapy. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: Long-stay psychiatric admission for BPD is generally counterproductive and not recommended; brief crisis admission only for acute risk. ECT is not indicated. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: Recurrent self-harm and previous admissions indicate need for specialist structured psychotherapy, not discharge. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.rationale: Naltrexone and topiramate are not recommended as first-line for BPD; psychotherapy is first-line. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

explanation.summary: AN causes hypothalamic amenorrhoea with low oestradiol, low gonadotropins and low IGF-1, plus relative hypercortisolaemia, all of which impair bone turnover. The most effective intervention for BMD is weight restoration; this should always be the primary target. Adjunct measures include optimisation of vitamin D and calcium, treatment of comorbid hypothyroidism or hyperprolactinaemia. Physiological transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progesterone has evidence for improving BMD in adolescents/young adults with persistent amenorrhoea despite weight restoration. COCP does not improve BMD. Bisphosphonates and denosumab are not first-line in premenopausal women with AN due to long-term safety in pregnancy and rebound concerns respectively. DEXA is repeated 1-2 yearly.
key_points: Primary intervention: weight restoration (highest impact on BMD)
Adjuncts: vitamin D, calcium, treat comorbid endocrinopathy
Persistent low BMD: transdermal oestradiol + cyclical progesterone (not COCP)
Avoid bisphosphonates and denosumab as first-line in premenopausal AN
DEXA every 12-24 months while underweight
explanation.pearls: Adolescents with AN can lose peak bone mass at the very age that determines lifetime fracture risk; aggressive weight restoration in the early years is the only intervention with long-term BMD benefit and the brief window before age 25 is when the gains are made.

sources.label: ANZAED clinical practice guideline for eating disorders

options.rationale: COCP has not been shown to improve BMD in AN-related hypogonadism and may give false reassurance of normalised menstruation; transdermal physiological oestrogen replacement has better evidence in adolescents. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

Bisphosphonates are not first-line in young women with AN due to long bone half-life and uncertainty around fetal exposure if she later conceives; weight restoration with adjunct physiological oestrogen replacement is preferred. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)
Teriparatide is reserved for severe established osteoporosis with fragility fracture and is not first-line in young women with AN-related low BMD. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

Weight restoration is the most effective intervention for BMD in AN; nutritional sufficiency, vitamin D and calcium optimisation, and physiological transdermal oestrogen replacement when BMD is persistently low or fractures occur are recommended adjuncts. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)
Denosumab is not first-line in premenopausal AN and has issues with rebound vertebral fracture risk if discontinued; not the recommended choice. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder (DSM-5 conversion disorder) is a positive diagnosis made on demonstrating internal inconsistency or incongruence with recognised neurological disease using rule-in signs (Hoover's sign, hip abductor sign, tremor entrainment, video-EEG of typical seizure with normal ictal EEG). It is not a diagnosis of exclusion; relabelling "medically unexplained" symptoms as FND requires positive clinical signs. Distinguishing features from factitious disorder (conscious symptom production to assume sick role) and malingering (conscious production for external incentive) rest on intentionality and motivation. Treatment is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, psychology (CBT or psychodynamic), patient education about the diagnosis and self-management strategies. Prognosis improves with early diagnosis and engaged treatment.
key_points: FND: positive rule-in signs (Hoover's, distractibility, normal ictal EEG)
Factitious: conscious symptom production for internal sick-role gain
Malingering: conscious production for external incentive (money, drugs, legal)
FND treatment: physiotherapy + psychology + patient education
Early diagnosis and engagement improve prognosis
explanation.pearls: Hoover's sign (involuntary extension of the affected leg when the contralateral leg is flexed against resistance) has very high specificity for functional weakness; demonstrate it to the patient and show that the muscle works, which is the start of treatment, not just diagnosis.

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance
Stone J. Functional neurological disorders. Practical Neurology 2016

options.rationale: Malingering requires intentional symptom production for external incentive (financial, legal, drug-seeking); there is no such incentive here. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires conscious symptom production with the internal motivation of assuming the sick role; this patient is distressed and wants to return to work, which is incongruous. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

options.rationale: FND is diagnosed by positive rule-in signs (Hoover's, distractibility, video-EEG of typical event with normal EEG) without conscious symptom production; the patient is genuinely distressed. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

options.rationale: Anxiety with somatic symptoms does not produce non-anatomical motor weakness with positive Hoover sign or non-epileptic seizures; FND is a separate, more specific diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

options.rationale: MS does not produce non-anatomical weakness with Hoover's sign or non-epileptic seizures with normal video-EEG; the rule-in signs identify FND positively. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is associated with major congenital malformation in around 10% of in-utero exposed pregnancies and neurodevelopmental delay in 30 to 40%. The TGA pregnancy prevention program (since 2023) requires that valproate is not used in women of reproductive age unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, the woman is using highly effective contraception, and risks are discussed annually using a risk acknowledgement form. For bipolar disorder in women of reproductive age, lamotrigine (depression-predominant), olanzapine or quetiapine are typical alternatives. Lithium is also teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly, ~0.1% absolute risk) but has lower overall teratogenicity than valproate. Lamotrigine titration is slow (25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg over weeks).
key_points: Valproate teratogenic risk: 10% major malformation, 30-40% neurodevelopmental delay
TGA PPP: only use if other Rx ineffective AND effective contraception AND annual risk form
Alternatives in reproductive-age women: lamotrigine, olanzapine, quetiapine, lithium
Lamotrigine titration: slow over 6+ weeks to avoid SJS
LARC options if avoiding CHC: copper IUD, LNG-IUS, depot implant
explanation.pearls: The risk acknowledgement form must be signed annually and at each new prescription, not just at initiation; failure to document at each renewal is the most common compliance failure flagged in TGA audits of valproate prescribing.

sources.label: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.rationale: Continuing valproate without reliable contraception in a woman of reproductive age does not meet the TGA pregnancy prevention program requirements; alternative mood stabilisers or contraception planning is required. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, craniofacial); it is not a safer alternative for pregnancy planning. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.rationale: Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly over at least 6 weeks to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome; rapid titration is unsafe and abrupt valproate cessation risks relapse. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.rationale: Pregnancy prevention program requires highly effective contraception; this patient does not use any reliable contraception, so enrolment alone is insufficient. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.rationale: TGA pregnancy prevention program requires risk discussion, transition to non-teratogenic alternative (lamotrigine, olanzapine etc) and effective contraception. LARC (copper IUD or LNG-IUS) is appropriate given her wish to avoid CHC. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder DSM-5 criteria require: (A) uninterrupted illness with major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with active phase psychotic symptoms, (B) delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of major mood episode during the lifetime of the illness, (C) mood episodes present for majority of total active and residual illness, and (D) not attributable to substance or medical condition. Schizoaffective bipolar type includes manic episodes; depressive type only depressive. Treatment combines antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser or antidepressant as appropriate. Distinguishing from bipolar with psychotic features hinges on criterion B (mood-independent psychosis), and from schizophrenia hinges on criterion C (substantial mood component).
key_points: Schizoaffective DSM-5: mood + psychosis concurrent, plus 2+ weeks pure psychosis lifetime
Mood episodes must be majority of total illness time (active + residual)
Type: bipolar type (mania) vs depressive type
Bipolar I with psychosis: psychosis only during mood episodes
Schizophrenia: mood symptoms brief over total course
explanation.pearls: Documenting the exact temporal relationship between mood and psychotic symptoms over years is essential; without longitudinal records, distinguishing schizoaffective from bipolar with psychotic features is often impossible in cross-section.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires (i) concurrent mood episode with psychosis at some time, (ii) at least 2 weeks of psychosis in the absence of major mood episode during lifetime illness, (iii) mood episodes are present majority of total illness time; his pattern fits. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis only during mood episodes; the documented 4 weeks of pure psychosis without mood symptoms excludes pure bipolar with psychotic features. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires mood symptoms to be present only briefly during total illness; this patient has substantial mood episodes (mania and depression) constituting a major part of his course. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: MDD with psychotic features does not account for the prior manic episode in 2017; the diagnosis must encompass the entire illness course. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: No substance use is documented on urine screen and history is not consistent; the diagnosis must be primary. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: First-episode schizophrenia is treated with a second-generation antipsychotic at the lowest effective dose, allowed at least 4 to 6 weeks to assess full response. Olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole and amisulpride are common first-line choices; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness after two failed trials. Baseline workup includes ECG (QTc), FBC, UEC, LFTs, fasting lipids, glucose, prolactin and weight/waist. RANZCP monitoring is weekly weight for 6 weeks, lipids and glucose at baseline, 3 months and 12 months, prolactin if symptomatic. Smoking cessation, exercise, dietitian and metabolic syndrome prevention are integral. CBT for psychosis, family therapy and supported employment are added.
key_points: SGA at lowest effective dose; allow 4-6 weeks for full effect
Baseline: ECG (QTc), FBC, UEC, LFTs, lipids, glucose, prolactin, weight
Monitor weight weekly to 6 weeks then 3-monthly
Lipids and glucose at baseline, 3 months, 12 months
Clozapine after two failed trials
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine has the largest weight gain and metabolic effect of common SGAs; aripiprazole is most weight-neutral but more activating. Prolactin elevation is greatest with risperidone and amisulpride.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic recommend continuing the initial effective antipsychotic with structured metabolic monitoring (weight monthly for 3 months then 3-monthly, lipids and glucose at baseline, 3 months and 12 months) for all first-episode patients on second-generation agents. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: FGAs cause more EPS and tardive dyskinesia and similar long-term metabolic concerns; switching after a partial response in 2 weeks is premature. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: Valproate is not first-line augmentation for first-episode schizophrenia and adds teratogenicity, weight gain and hepatotoxicity risks without clear benefit at 2 weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: CBT for psychosis is an adjunct to antipsychotic medication, not a substitute; discontinuation risks rapid relapse in first-episode schizophrenia. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.rationale: LAI is appropriate in selected first-episode patients with adherence concerns, but is given alongside specialist multidisciplinary follow up, not discharge without it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis using the Hunter Criteria: serotonergic agent plus one of spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus, tremor and hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 and either ocular or inducible clonus. Lower-limb-predominant clonus and hyperreflexia distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (lead-pipe rigidity). Management is cessation of all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepine sedation, active cooling, IV hydration, and cyproheptadine 12 mg PO load then 2 mg every 2 hours for moderate to severe cases (max 32 mg/day). ICU and paralysis with intubation are required for hyperthermia over 41.1 degrees C.
key_points: Hunter Criteria: serotonergic agent + characteristic neuromuscular signs
Clue: clonus and hyperreflexia greater in lower limbs
Cease all serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, linezolid, MAOIs)
Benzodiazepines first-line for agitation and autonomic features
Cyproheptadine 12 mg PO load, 2 mg q2h for moderate to severe
explanation.pearls: Common SSRI plus tramadol is a high-yield combination at GP-prescribing interfaces; education at the SSRI prescription stage helps the patient flag risk if subsequently offered tramadol.

options.rationale: Magnesium and beta-blockers are not first-line; cessation of serotonergic agents and benzodiazepines are the foundation of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

Tramadol is a known serotonergic agent and combination with high-dose SSRI causes serotonin syndrome; treating symptoms without ceasing the precipitants risks progression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

NMS is associated with antipsychotic dopamine antagonism, with lead-pipe rigidity not the lower-limb-predominant clonus, hyperreflexia and dilated pupils of serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

Serotonin syndrome management is cessation of all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepine sedation for agitation, active cooling, IV hydration; cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as a 5-HT2A antagonist is added for moderate to severe cases per Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

Physostigmine is the antidote for anticholinergic toxicity, not serotonin syndrome; the dilated pupils, sweating and hyperactive bowels here are pro-serotonergic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

explanation.summary: Acute alcohol withdrawal management uses symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing guided by the CIWA-Ar score (or equivalent AWS scale). Diazepam 10 to 20 mg orally every 1 to 2 hours is given until CIWA-Ar falls below 8 to 10. Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IM or IV daily for at least 3 days then 100 mg orally three times daily prevents Wernicke encephalopathy. Glucose-containing fluids must be preceded by thiamine. Magnesium and folate are replaced if low. Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are avoided unless severe agitation persists despite adequate benzodiazepine. Severe AWS, history of delirium tremens or seizures or significant medical comorbidity warrant ICU consideration.
key_points: CIWA-Ar score 8-10 triggers benzodiazepine dosing
Diazepam 10-20 mg PO q1-2h symptom-triggered
Thiamine 300 mg parenteral daily for at least 3 days before glucose
Avoid antipsychotics (lower seizure threshold)
ICU if severe, prior DT or seizures, comorbidity
explanation.pearls: Phenobarbital is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory withdrawal under specialist supervision; propofol intubation is used in delirium tremens not controlled by maximal benzodiazepines.

sources.label: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems (NHMRC)

options.rationale: RACP and Therapeutic Guidelines Addiction recommend symptom-triggered diazepam (or chlordiazepoxide) loading guided by CIWA-Ar at or above 8 to 10, with parenteral thiamine 300 mg IM/IV daily for at least 3 days before oral, and monitoring for AWS complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and do not prevent the GABA-mediated complications of withdrawal; benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)
Glucose before thiamine in a chronic alcohol user precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine before any glucose is the order. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

Baclofen and acamprosate are relapse-prevention agents started after acute withdrawal is complete, not during it; benzodiazepines are needed for acute management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)
Alcohol tapering is not endorsed in Australian inpatient detox protocols; benzodiazepine cover is the standard substitute. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Untreated moderate to severe depression in pregnancy is itself associated with preterm birth, low birthweight and poor mother-infant attachment; treatment is therefore indicated when the depression is more than mild. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding due to its low placental transfer, low milk-to-plasma ratio and extensive safety data. Citalopram and escitalopram are acceptable alternatives, especially with documented prior response. Paroxetine is avoided in the first trimester due to a small increase in cardiac malformations. SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are used when SSRIs fail. Lithium and antipsychotics may be required for bipolar relapse or psychotic depression. Perinatal mental health teams provide stepped care including CBT, IPT and shared decision making.
key_points: Untreated moderate-severe MDD in pregnancy is harmful: treat
Sertraline is the preferred first-line SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Avoid paroxetine first trimester (small cardiac malformation increase)
SNRIs as second line if SSRI fails
Perinatal mental health team + psychological therapy alongside drug
explanation.pearls: Neonatal poor adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, feeding difficulty, transient respiratory distress) occurs in 10 to 30 percent of SSRI-exposed neonates and is self-limiting over 1 to 2 weeks - not a reason to stop the SSRI in the third trimester.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Paroxetine has been associated with a small absolute increase in cardiac malformations (RR around 1.5) and is not first-line in Australian perinatal guidelines. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: SSRIs (except paroxetine, with some cardiac concerns) do not significantly increase major malformation risk; deferring treatment of relapsed moderate-severe MDD with SI is unsafe. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Citalopram is acceptable but sertraline has more pregnancy and breastfeeding data and is generally preferred for new initiation in pregnancy; previous response is a reasonable argument to restart citalopram, but RANZCP and Australian Prescriber lean to sertraline as first-line in perinatal initiation. The more correct answer is sertraline as the safer first-line choice when starting fresh in pregnancy after a gap. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding due to extensive data and the lowest milk-to-plasma ratio of SSRIs; treating moderate-severe MDD with relapse and passive SI in pregnancy is mandated rather than expectant. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Venlafaxine is used in pregnancy when SSRIs fail but is not first-line; SSRI (sertraline) is preferred as first-line. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects 1 to 2 per 1000 deliveries and presents in the first 2 weeks postpartum with rapid onset of insomnia, perplexity, fluctuating mood, delusions (often centred on the baby) and confusion. Family or personal history of bipolar disorder increases risk 10 to 25 fold. It is a psychiatric emergency due to elevated risk of suicide and infanticide. Management is urgent admission to a mother-baby unit (or general psychiatric unit if MBU not available), second-generation antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) with consideration of lithium for prophylaxis. ECT is highly effective for refractory or catatonic presentations. Pregnancy planning with mood stabiliser prophylaxis from delivery onwards reduces recurrence in subsequent pregnancies.
key_points: Psychiatric emergency due to suicide and infanticide risk
Urgent MBU admission (or general unit if unavailable)
Antipsychotic + consider lithium for prophylaxis
ECT for refractory or catatonic illness
Recurrence risk in next pregnancy 30 to 50 percent without prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Lithium initiated within the first 48 hours postpartum in women with bipolar history reduces postpartum psychosis recurrence from around 50 percent to under 15 percent and is given despite breastfeeding considerations with neonatal monitoring.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines
COPE Australia: Perinatal mental health guideline

options.rationale: Normal TFTs exclude postpartum thyroiditis as the cause; even if thyroiditis coexisted, antipsychotic management of psychosis is still required. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Symptoms of perplexity, fluctuating mood and delusions days after delivery are characteristic of postpartum psychosis, not psychotic depression; home management is unsafe due to infanticide and suicide risk. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Baby blues is mild mood lability without psychotic features or perplexity and resolves by day 10; this is psychosis and demands urgent specialist care. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency due to risk of suicide and infanticide; urgent MBU admission, antipsychotic initiation and lithium prophylaxis (especially in those with bipolar diathesis) is the RANZCP standard. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Home supervision is inadequate for postpartum psychosis given the rapid and unpredictable risk trajectory; inpatient MBU admission is needed. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is characterised by fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and spontaneous parkinsonism. Antipsychotic medications (especially first-generation and high-D2-occupancy SGAs like risperidone) can precipitate severe extrapyramidal reactions and NMS-like presentations in 30 to 50 percent of patients with DLB. First-line treatment of cognitive and hallucinatory symptoms is a cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine or donepezil), with quetiapine as the safest antipsychotic if pharmacotherapy of psychosis is essential. Levodopa for motor symptoms is used cautiously because it can exacerbate hallucinations. Multidisciplinary care addresses falls risk, autonomic dysfunction and carer support.
key_points: DLB: fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + REM sleep behaviour disorder
Severe antipsychotic sensitivity in 30-50% (NMS-like reactions)
First-line for cognitive/psychotic features: cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine)
If antipsychotic essential: low-dose quetiapine
L-dopa cautiously for motor symptoms
explanation.pearls: DaT-SPECT (dopamine transporter scan) showing reduced striatal uptake supports DLB and PD over Alzheimer disease; it is the imaging biomarker used to distinguish DLB from AD with parkinsonian features.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies
Dementia Australia: Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.rationale: Increasing the antipsychotic worsens the antipsychotic-sensitivity reaction; rigidity is part of NMS-like physiology not just behavioural agitation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.rationale: Severe antipsychotic sensitivity reaction with NMS-like features in a man with parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations is classical for DLB; haloperidol must be ceased and cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine) is the disease-targeted treatment per RANZCP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.rationale: All dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotics can cause severe sensitivity reactions in DLB; risperidone is not safer here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.rationale: L-dopa would worsen psychosis, and continuing haloperidol perpetuates the antipsychotic-sensitivity NMS-like reaction; cessation of haloperidol is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.rationale: Cessation of the precipitating antipsychotic is the foundation of NMS treatment; dantrolene and bromocriptine are second-line in severe cases but never used while continuing the antipsychotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD in Australia is a stimulant (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine), titrated to effect with monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, weight and sleep. Atomoxetine is second-line and reserved for stimulant intolerance, contraindications, or significant misuse risk. Psychological therapy is combined with pharmacotherapy, not used to delay it when impairment is significant. Authority and prescriber registration requirements apply by jurisdiction. Pre-treatment ECG is indicated when cardiovascular risk factors or family history are present.
key_points: First-line: stimulant (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) titrated to effect
Second-line: atomoxetine (noradrenergic non-stimulant), preferred if substance use disorder or diversion risk
Monitor: BP, HR, weight, sleep, appetite, mood, diversion risk; ECG if cardiac history
Combine pharmacotherapy with psychoeducation and ADHD-adapted CBT for best outcomes
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD stimulants are Schedule 8 with state-specific authority requirements; in NSW and several other states only psychiatrists or paediatricians can initiate, with GP shared care possible once stable - know your state's pathway before promising to start.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Bupropion is not first-line for adult ADHD in Australian guidance; stimulants and atomoxetine have stronger evidence and clear regulatory positioning. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line; reserved for patients who do not tolerate or respond to stimulants, who have a substance use disorder, or where stimulant diversion is a major concern. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) are first-line for adult ADHD in Australian guidance; immediate-release methylphenidate with cardiovascular and weight monitoring is a standard initial choice. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Psychological therapy is recommended in combination with pharmacotherapy rather than as a delay strategy when the diagnosis is clear and functional impairment is substantial. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Clonidine is not a first-line agent for adult ADHD; alpha-2 agonists are used in paediatric ADHD, often as adjuncts, and rarely as monotherapy in adults. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: BPD self-harm in the absence of acute imminent risk is best managed by a structured discharge that maintains continuity with the patient's existing therapy. Brief admission is reserved for an acute change in risk profile, severe comorbid depression or psychosis, or when no community supports exist. BPD-specific psychotherapies (DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy) carry the strongest evidence; pharmacotherapy is targeted at specific comorbid syndromes rather than the personality disorder itself. Safety planning, handover to the treating team and clear next contact are the disposition essentials.
key_points: Chronic suicidality without acute change usually does not warrant admission in BPD
Continuity with existing therapist and structured safety plan are highest-value interventions
Pharmacotherapy targets specific comorbidities only; no medication is first-line for BPD itself
DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy and TFP are the evidence-based BPD-specific psychotherapies
explanation.pearls: When in doubt about admit vs discharge in BPD, ask: has the risk changed acutely from baseline? If chronic suicidality is at the patient's baseline and a coherent therapy plan exists, discharge with a safety plan and same-day handover is almost always safer than admission.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD
RANZCP: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of BPD

options.rationale: Clozapine has no role in BPD self-harm management; even short admissions can reinforce unhelpful patterns when chronic suicidality is the presentation rather than an acute crisis. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Discharge without a structured safety plan and handover to her existing treating team fails to leverage the strongest predictor of safety in BPD: continuity of therapeutic relationships. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: Inpatient admission for chronic suicidality in BPD without an acute imminent risk often worsens long-term outcomes; routine pharmacotherapy is not first-line and BPD-specific psychotherapy carries the evidence. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: She has chronic suicidality with no acute imminent risk, an existing therapeutic relationship and engaged DBT plan; structured handover and discharge with a clear safety plan is the evidence-based response. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.rationale: ECT is not indicated for BPD self-harm without a clear concurrent severe depressive episode meeting criteria; this would be over-treatment and not aligned with BPD-specific guidance. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies presents with the core features of fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and spontaneous parkinsonism. Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine first, donepezil second) have the strongest evidence for both cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB is severe and includes NMS-like reactions; antipsychotics are largely avoided and, if absolutely required, quetiapine at very low dose is preferred. Levodopa worsens psychosis; benzodiazepines worsen cognition and falls. Address modifiable triggers (pain, infection, environment) before any pharmacology.
key_points: DLB core features: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, parkinsonism
First-line cognitive Rx: rivastigmine; donepezil second
Antipsychotics largely avoided due to severe neuroleptic sensitivity; quetiapine very low dose if essential
Benzodiazepines and levodopa worsen DLB outcomes; address modifiable triggers first
explanation.pearls: If a person with new-onset dementia has well-formed visual hallucinations, REM behaviour disorder and falls, suspect DLB and never reach for haloperidol or risperidone first - the neuroleptic sensitivity reaction can be fatal.

options.rationale: Rivastigmine has the best evidence for cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms in DLB; neuroleptic sensitivity is severe in DLB and includes risk of NMS-like reactions, so antipsychotics are largely avoided and modifiable triggers addressed first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

Memantine has weaker evidence in DLB than cholinesterase inhibitors and benzodiazepines worsen falls, cognition and confusion in older people, particularly in DLB. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

Non-pharmacological interventions are important but the rapid functional decline and characteristic symptom cluster warrant prompt rivastigmine initiation rather than deferral. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

Levodopa can worsen psychosis in DLB and risperidone carries neuroleptic sensitivity risk; cholinesterase inhibitor first and antipsychotics avoided are the standard package. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

Haloperidol can precipitate severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions including NMS-like syndromes in DLB and is specifically discouraged; rivastigmine has the strongest evidence base. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia nervosa with BMI under 13, marked bradycardia, postural hypotension and electrolyte derangement is medically high risk for refeeding syndrome. Initial nutritional rehabilitation starts at approximately 20 kcal/kg/day (5 to 10 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases), with empirical replacement of phosphate, magnesium, potassium and thiamine before significant feeding, frequent biochemistry, continuous cardiac monitoring, and a multidisciplinary plan. Wernicke prophylaxis precedes any carbohydrate load. Feeding is uptitrated as biochemistry tolerates over 5 to 7 days.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome risk factors: BMI under 16, weight loss above 15% in 3 to 6 months, low baseline phosphate/Mg/K
Start at approximately 20 kcal/kg/day; even lower (5-10 kcal/kg/day) in extreme malnutrition
Prophylactic thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 5 to 7 days before or with carbohydrate load
Replace phosphate, magnesium, potassium pre-emptively; monitor biochemistry 12-hourly initially
explanation.pearls: Thiamine before glucose is non-negotiable in severely malnourished patients - giving carbohydrate first risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy that can leave permanent amnestic deficits even after good nutritional recovery.

sources.label: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders
RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Delay risks rapid deterioration; medical stabilisation and prophylactic electrolyte replacement must begin immediately at the current facility, and involuntary admission is decided on capacity grounds rather than as a transfer device. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Starting above 30 kcal/kg/day in a severely underweight patient with established hypophosphataemia exceeds the safe initial caloric load; prophylactic electrolyte replacement should precede feeding. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Aggressive initial feeding precipitates refeeding syndrome with potentially fatal hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmias and Wernicke encephalopathy; current Australian guidance favours cautious initial caloric load with prophylactic replacement. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.rationale: MARSIPAN and Australian eating-disorders guidance recommend low-rate initial feeding (around 20 kcal/kg/day) with empirical electrolyte and thiamine replacement, frequent biochemistry, and continuous cardiac monitoring in patients with established hypophosphataemia and a prolonged QTc. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.rationale: Intravenous dextrose without prior thiamine and electrolyte replacement can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy and rebound hypophosphataemia; thiamine must precede or accompany any glucose load. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes a sodium-channel-blocker cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR, ventricular arrhythmias) plus anticholinergic and alpha-blocking effects. QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmias and is the trigger for sodium bicarbonate boluses targeted to narrow the QRS to under 100 ms and a serum pH 7.45 to 7.55. Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Flumazenil, physostigmine, and class I/III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Supportive care includes airway protection, fluid resuscitation and seizure management with benzodiazepines.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or R wave aVR over 3 mm: high risk of seizures and ventricular arrhythmias
First-line antidote: sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg boluses, target QRS under 100 ms and pH 7.45 to 7.55
Avoid flumazenil, physostigmine, class I/III antiarrhythmics; benzodiazepines for seizures
Lipid emulsion as rescue therapy for cardiovascular collapse refractory to standard measures
explanation.pearls: Look at aVR on the 12-lead: a terminal R wave above 3 mm with rightward terminal axis is the TCA-toxicity signature and predicts arrhythmias - it is the cleanest single trigger for early sodium bicarbonate.

sources.label: Australian Poisons Information Centre: TCA overdose

options.rationale: QRS prolongation above 100 ms in TCA overdose predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmias; sodium bicarbonate is the first-line antidote, with the dual mechanism of alkalinisation and increased extracellular sodium to overcome sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate asystole through bradyarrhythmia in the setting of TCA-induced conduction abnormalities. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

Intravenous lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse, not first-line; sodium bicarbonate should be tried first and titrated to QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

Class III antiarrhythmics worsen TCA cardiotoxicity by prolonging QT and depressing conduction; sodium bicarbonate is the indicated antidote and most antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses and in TCA toxicity because it can precipitate seizures; airway management is the priority and chemical reversal is not appropriate here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic of the mood stabilisers, with 10% major malformation rate (notably neural tube defects), and 30 to 40% adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes (lower IQ, autism spectrum disorders). Australian regulators have implemented pregnancy prevention programs requiring documented contraception in women of childbearing potential. For pre-conception planning in bipolar I, lithium is the preferred maintenance agent (with anomaly scan and serial monitoring), with lamotrigine the alternative for predominantly depressive presentations. Cross-titration to lithium with overlap, baseline renal and thyroid function, high-dose preconception folate, and counselling about Ebstein anomaly (lithium first-trimester risk is modest at around 1 in 1000) are key.
key_points: Valproate: 10% major malformation rate, 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental impact; pregnancy prevention program required
Lithium: preferred maintenance in bipolar I planning pregnancy; Ebstein anomaly risk around 1 in 1000
Lamotrigine: alternative for predominantly depressive bipolar; safer than valproate but less effective for mania prevention
High-dose folate 5 mg daily preconceptionally for women on any anti-seizure medication
explanation.pearls: Folic acid does not rescue valproate teratogenicity - the combination is misleadingly reassuring and the patient still carries a 10% major malformation risk; switching to lithium pre-conception is the right ask, not adding folate.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement
TGA: Valproate use and pregnancy prevention

options.rationale: Folic acid does not fully mitigate valproate teratogenicity; valproate use in pregnancy carries unacceptable risk in women planning conception when alternative effective agents exist. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Risk reduction with valproate is not proportionate to dose reduction at clinically effective doses, and any continued valproate in pregnancy carries unacceptable teratogenicity when alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Valproate carries a 10% major malformation rate (especially neural tube defects) and a 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental impact; pre-conception switch to lithium (preferred maintenance in childbearing women with bipolar I) with cross-titration and high-dose folate is recommended Australian practice. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Topiramate is itself teratogenic (oral clefts, low birth weight), is not licensed as a mood stabiliser in Australia, and is not first-line in bipolar maintenance. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Discontinuation of mood stabiliser in bipolar I carries high relapse risk, particularly in pregnancy and the postpartum period; treatment is changed to a safer agent rather than stopped. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder presents with paranoia, perceptual disturbances and disorganised behaviour in the context of cannabis use, classically with high-potency THC products and adolescent or young-adult onset. Acute management combines short admission for safety and observation, antipsychotic treatment (commonly olanzapine or risperidone), substance use intervention with motivational interviewing, and assertive early intervention follow-up. A substantial proportion (around 20 to 40%) of cannabis-induced psychoses progress to a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder over the following decade, particularly with ongoing cannabis use, so longitudinal follow-up is essential.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychosis: paranoia and perceptual disturbances with cannabis use, especially high-potency THC
Acute management: short voluntary admission, antipsychotic (olanzapine or risperidone), cessation intervention
Risk of progression to primary psychotic illness: 20 to 40% over the next decade
Assertive early intervention follow-up improves long-term function and reduces relapse
explanation.pearls: Even when psychosis is clearly substance-induced, the appropriate disposition is short admission with antipsychotic and early intervention follow-up - not direct discharge - because the cumulative risk of progression to schizophrenia warrants longitudinal engagement.

sources.label: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.rationale: Active psychotic symptoms with paranoia and recent dangerous behaviour preclude direct discharge to a housemate without specialist follow-up; benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychotic symptoms. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.rationale: Involuntary admission is reserved for patients lacking capacity or with risk profiles unsafe for voluntary care; he is engaging with assessment, and mood stabiliser addition is not indicated in substance-induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.rationale: Direct discharge without specialist follow-up risks decompensation and undertreatment; assertive early intervention in psychosis with specialist follow-up improves long-term outcomes. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics; first-episode cannabis-induced psychosis should not be treated with clozapine. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.rationale: Acute cannabis-induced psychosis with significant symptoms warrants short admission, an antipsychotic to treat acute symptoms (olanzapine is a reasonable choice), cessation counselling, and structured follow-up given the elevated risk of progression to a primary psychotic illness. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

explanation.summary: GHB withdrawal in heavy daily users can begin within 4 to 6 hours of last dose, escalates rapidly over 24 to 72 hours, and produces an alcohol-withdrawal-like syndrome that is characteristically benzodiazepine-resistant with delirium, autonomic instability and seizures. Management is inpatient with high-dose benzodiazepine loading guided by sedation and seizure response, GABAergic adjuncts (baclofen or, in some centres, pharmaceutical sodium oxybate where available), and ICU-level monitoring for airway and ventilation. Antipsychotics worsen the delirium and lower seizure threshold. Mortality without appropriate inpatient management is significant.
key_points: GHB withdrawal in heavy daily users: onset 4 to 6 hours, peak 24 to 72 hours, prolonged course
Classically benzodiazepine-resistant; high-dose loading with baclofen adjunct often required
ICU monitoring for airway, autonomic instability and prolonged sedation requirements
Avoid antipsychotics: lower seizure threshold, worsen delirium; magnesium and thiamine are supportive only
explanation.pearls: If 60 mg of diazepam over 2 hours has barely touched the agitation in a daily GHB user, do not just keep stepping benzodiazepines - add baclofen and call ICU early, because the syndrome can progress to refractory delirium and respiratory arrest within hours.

sources.label: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and worsen delirium in GHB withdrawal; the syndrome is recognised clinically and sedation with high-dose benzodiazepines plus baclofen is the appropriate next step. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.rationale: Severe GHB withdrawal is benzodiazepine-resistant and progresses rapidly to seizures, delirium and autonomic instability; high-dose benzodiazepines with GABAergic adjuncts (baclofen) and ICU admission for airway management are the recognised escalation pathway. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.rationale: Alpha-2 agonists alone do not control GHB withdrawal-related seizures and delirium; the central problem is GABA-B underactivity and benzodiazepine-resistant agitation, requiring high-dose benzodiazepines and GABAergic adjuncts. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.rationale: Magnesium and thiamine are supportive only; severe GHB withdrawal requires high-dose benzodiazepines, GABAergic adjuncts and ICU-level monitoring rather than magnesium and thiamine as the primary intervention. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.rationale: Severe GHB withdrawal with seizures and delirium has a mortality risk and is not safe for community withdrawal; it requires inpatient and often intensive care management with airway support available. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single-form pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation, and combination NRT (patch plus a short-acting oral form) is as effective as varenicline; both are more effective than single-form NRT. Cochrane 2023 found no clear difference between varenicline and combination NRT (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.20). The EAGLES trial found no significant increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events with varenicline, including in people with treated psychiatric illness. Varenicline is titrated to 1 mg twice daily, started 1 to 2 weeks before the quit date and continued for 12 weeks, with a further 12 weeks considered to reduce relapse.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent; combination NRT has similar efficacy
Single-form NRT is less effective than either
Bupropion needs caution with SSRIs; nortriptyline is second-line
A failed course of patch alone points to varenicline or combination NRT, not a repeat of the patch
explanation.pearls: Monitor for abnormal dreams, nausea, and any new suicidal ideation; warn that nicotine plasma levels may shift causing transient mood changes.

sources.label: Cochrane 2023: Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation

options.rationale: RACGP: varenicline is the most effective single-form pharmacotherapy, and the EAGLES trial found no significant increase in moderate-to-severe neuropsychiatric adverse events. Start 1 to 2 weeks before the quit date and encourage completion of 12 weeks. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation: Pharmacotherapy)

Bupropion is less effective than varenicline or combination NRT, and RACGP advises caution with SSRIs (lower seizure threshold, CYP2D6 inhibition raising SSRI levels). (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation: Pharmacotherapy)

He has already relapsed on patch alone, and RACGP states that single-form NRT is less effective than either combination NRT or varenicline. Combination NRT (patch plus a short-acting form) is as effective as varenicline and would be a reasonable alternative. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation: Pharmacotherapy; Cochrane 2023: Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation)
source_refs: Cochrane 2023: Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation

options.rationale: RACGP lists nortriptyline as second-line because of adverse effects (dry mouth, constipation, nausea, sedation) and arrhythmia risk; sertraline can also raise nortriptyline levels. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation: Pharmacotherapy)

Brief advice without pharmacotherapy has lower quit rates than advice with pharmacotherapy, and he is a heavy smoker with clear motivation; Quitline referral belongs alongside medication, not instead of it. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation: Pharmacotherapy)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium use can cause progressive interstitial nephropathy, primary hyperparathyroidism and hypothyroidism, all of which are present here. In a woman planning pregnancy with multi-organ lithium effects and stable mood, cross-titration to an alternative mood stabiliser with multidisciplinary input (psychiatry, nephrology, endocrinology, obstetrics) is appropriate rather than continuing unchanged or abrupt cessation. Lithium should never be stopped abruptly outside of life-threatening toxicity due to high relapse risk.
key_points: Lithium long-term effects: nephropathy, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism, NDI
Never stop lithium abruptly; cross-titrate over weeks
Valproate contraindicated in women of childbearing age unless pregnancy-prevention program in place
explanation.pearls: Annual monitoring: eGFR, electrolytes, calcium, PTH, TSH; lithium level 12 hours post-dose every 3-6 months; weight, BP, ECG as clinically indicated.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Progressive renal decline plus emerging hyperparathyroidism and subclinical hypothyroidism warrants a change in approach rather than another 12 months of unchanged therapy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Lithium-related progressive renal decline, hyperparathyroidism and subclinical hypothyroidism in a woman planning pregnancy warrant gradual cross-titration with specialist input rather than abrupt discontinuation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Dose reduction alone does not reliably reverse lithium nephropathy and risks subtherapeutic levels and relapse; it does not address parathyroid pathology. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Amiloride may be considered for established nephrogenic DI but does not address the broader pattern of multi-organ lithium toxicity here, especially with pregnancy planned. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Abrupt lithium discontinuation markedly increases relapse risk, and valproate is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy due to major teratogenicity. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Australian first-line parenteral therapy for acute severe behavioural disturbance is IM droperidol 10 mg (or IM olanzapine 10 mg as alternative); both have superior evidence to haloperidol-based regimens. The dose can be repeated at 15-minute intervals if needed. Continuous observation for sedation, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation is essential. IM is preferred over IV when restraint is required because IV cannulation in an agitated patient is unsafe.
key_points: First-line IM: droperidol 10 mg or olanzapine 10 mg
Avoid combining IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine (excess sedation/respiratory depression)
Continuous observation: airway, breathing, circulation, sedation score
explanation.pearls: Droperidol has a black box warning for QT prolongation but Australian ED trials (e.g., DORM study) have shown it is safe at 10 mg IM with appropriate monitoring.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance
Calver et al DORM Study Annals Emerg Med

options.rationale: Droperidol 10 mg IM is Australian first-line for acute severe behavioural disturbance with a faster onset, fewer EPS than haloperidol, and a strong evidence base from emergency department trials. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Haloperidol plus lorazepam is older practice and is associated with higher EPS, dystonia, and more cumulative sedation than droperidol monotherapy in Australian protocols. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: IM diazepam is erratically absorbed and not recommended for acute behavioural disturbance; lorazepam IM is the preferred benzodiazepine if one is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: IV access in a violently agitated patient before sedation is high risk for staff and patient; IM is preferred until safe sedation is achieved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Zuclopenthixol acetate is not first-line for acute behavioural disturbance and is reserved for established psychosis when shorter-acting agents have failed and longer effect is genuinely desired. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

explanation.summary: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) is diagnosed by positive clinical signs of inconsistency and incongruence with neurological disease, such as Hoover sign for functional leg weakness or tremor entrainment for functional tremor. It is not a diagnosis of exclusion. Symptoms are genuinely experienced and not deliberately produced. Management is via clear non-stigmatising explanation, physiotherapy, and psychological therapy.
key_points: FND: diagnosed by positive signs (Hoover, entrainment), not exclusion
Malingering requires external incentive; factitious requires deliberate production
Treatment: explanation, physiotherapy, CBT, treat comorbid mood/anxiety
explanation.pearls: Communicating the diagnosis as a 'software not hardware' problem of the nervous system improves engagement and outcome; avoid 'all in your head' framing.

sources.label: Stone et al BMJ Functional Symptoms

options.rationale: Malingering requires an external incentive (compensation, legal, drug-seeking) which is absent here; the patient is genuinely distressed and not seeking external benefit. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

Factitious disorder requires deliberate production of symptoms, which is excluded here by history; functional symptoms in FND are involuntary and genuinely experienced. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

FND is now diagnosed by positive clinical signs (e.g., Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness) rather than by exclusion alone, and structural investigations are typically normal. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

Somatic symptom disorder involves excessive worry about symptoms; here the disorder is a discrete motor deficit with positive neurological FND signs, not excessive symptom focus per se. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

Acute stress disorder requires a traumatic event and a different symptom profile of intrusive, avoidant, mood and arousal symptoms; not a discrete motor deficit. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

explanation.summary: Postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation and a plan, particularly with limited social support, is a psychiatric emergency requiring admission to a mother-baby unit where available. Sertraline is the SSRI of choice during breastfeeding due to minimal infant exposure. Fluoxetine is avoided because of its long half-life and active metabolite. Psychological therapy and community follow-up have a role only when safety is established.
key_points: EPDS >=13 plus active suicidal ideation = high risk; consider admission
Mother-baby units preserve bonding and breastfeeding
Sertraline preferred SSRI in breastfeeding; avoid fluoxetine (long half-life)
explanation.pearls: Item 10 of EPDS (thoughts of self-harm) endorsement always warrants direct safety assessment and explicit suicide risk evaluation, regardless of total score.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Active suicidal ideation with plan in the context of severe postpartum depression and limited social support warrants admission, not community follow-up; fluoxetine also has a long half-life and is not first-line during breastfeeding. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

Severe postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation and plan requires inpatient care; mother-baby units in Australia allow continued breastfeeding and bonding while ensuring safety. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

Psychological therapy alone is inadequate for severe postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation; safety must be addressed first via admission and pharmacotherapy. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)
Separation of mother and baby is harmful to bonding and breastfeeding; mother-baby units are preferred where available in Australia. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

Diazepam is not first-line for postpartum depression and crosses into breastmilk significantly; it does not treat the underlying condition and delays definitive care. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Lithium in early pregnancy is associated with a small absolute increase in Ebstein anomaly (background risk roughly 1 in 20,000; with first-trimester lithium roughly 1 in 1000-2000). This is detectable by fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks. In a patient with severe manic-predominant bipolar I and recent relapse off lithium, the maternal relapse risk on withdrawal far outweighs the small fetal cardiac risk. Continue lithium at the lowest effective dose, monitor levels monthly (then more frequently approaching term), maintain hydration, and reduce dose around delivery to avoid toxicity from volume contraction.
key_points: Continue lithium when manic-predominant illness and high relapse risk
Ebstein risk ~1:1000 with first-trimester lithium - screen at 18-20 weeks
Valproate contraindicated in women of childbearing age (10% major malformations)
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance increases in second and third trimesters then plummets after delivery; check levels weekly in final weeks and reduce or hold dose at labour onset to avoid maternal toxicity post-partum.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines: Bipolar disorder in pregnancy

options.rationale: Lamotrigine is more effective for depressive than manic episodes; her manic-predominant phenotype with severe manic relapses makes lamotrigine inadequate prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Valproate has the highest teratogenic risk of any mood stabiliser (around 10 percent major congenital malformations plus neurodevelopmental risk) and is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health
