options.rationale: Continuing lithium is appropriate given high relapse risk off lithium; absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is small (around 1 in 1000) and is screened with fetal echocardiography, with maternal benefit outweighing fetal risk in manic-predominant disease. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: First-trimester relapse risk is substantially higher than Ebstein risk; abrupt discontinuation also markedly increases relapse risk and has been associated with reduced response when lithium is restarted. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Quetiapine is a reasonable alternative when lithium cannot be continued, but switching introduces relapse risk unnecessarily in a patient already well-controlled with severe manic recurrence history. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised by motor (immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility), behavioural (mutism, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia) and autonomic features. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) supports recognition. First-line treatment is a lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM), with positive response within 30 minutes guiding scheduled lorazepam at 6-8 mg/day (sometimes higher). Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk progression to malignant catatonia or NMS. ECT is the definitive treatment in lorazepam non-responders and in malignant catatonia.
key_points: First-line: lorazepam 1-2 mg IV/IM challenge then 6-8 mg/day scheduled
Avoid antipsychotics in catatonia (risk of malignant catatonia/NMS)
ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia plus fever and autonomic instability) overlaps clinically with NMS and serotonin syndrome; immediate cessation of antipsychotics, supportive care, lorazepam and urgent ECT are required.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk progression to malignant catatonia or NMS; they should be reduced or paused while catatonia is treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

Lorazepam challenge is the first-line test and treatment for catatonia; a partial response within 30 minutes guides ongoing scheduled lorazepam dosing, with ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)
Haloperidol can precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS in a catatonic patient; antipsychotics should not be used to treat catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

Clozapine is used in treatment-resistant schizophrenia after multiple trials but is not the first-line agent for catatonia; lorazepam challenge precedes any antipsychotic change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

ECT is the next step after lorazepam challenge failure (or for malignant catatonia or rapid deterioration); lorazepam trial precedes ECT in non-malignant catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at the 12-week mark of treatment in Australia follows the RANZCP and Maudsley guidance: fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipid profile, body weight, body mass index, and waist circumference. Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-risk second-generation agents for weight gain, dyslipidaemia and glucose dysregulation. If metabolic parameters deteriorate beyond a 5% increase in weight or new metabolic syndrome criteria, options include lifestyle support, metformin add-on, and switching to lower-risk antipsychotics such as aripiprazole. Prolactin and ECG are reserved for specific agent profiles or clinical features.
key_points: 12-week panel: fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, weight, BMI, waist circumference
Olanzapine and clozapine are highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole lowest
Metformin add-on indicated for weight gain greater than 5% on antipsychotic
explanation.pearls: RANZCP suggests metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 6 months and annually thereafter; consider switching agent if BMI rises by 1 kg/m^2 or other metabolic criteria emerge.

options.rationale: HbA1c alone is insufficient; the recommended panel is fasting glucose (or HbA1c), fasting lipid profile, weight, BMI and waist circumference at 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

Thyroid testing is not indicated as routine antipsychotic monitoring without specific clinical features of thyroid disease; metabolic panel is the priority. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

RANZCP and Maudsley antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at 12 weeks comprises fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipid panel, weight, BMI and waist circumference. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

Olanzapine is not a high-prolactin antipsychotic; routine prolactin is for prolactin-elevating agents such as risperidone or amisulpride or when clinically symptomatic. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)
Olanzapine is low QTc risk; routine repeat ECG is not standard antipsychotic monitoring at 12 weeks unless QTc-prolonging factors are present. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes cardiotoxicity through sodium channel blockade leading to QRS prolongation, terminal R wave in aVR, hypotension and arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus is the antidote, working through both sodium loading and serum alkalinisation (target pH 7.45-7.55). The endpoint is QRS narrowing to under 100 ms. Intubation may be needed to maintain controlled ventilation and pH. Activated charcoal is reserved for ingestions within 1-2 hours of presentation; flumazenil and physostigmine are contraindicated; haemodialysis does not work due to high volume of distribution.
key_points: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg for QRS over 100 ms or hypotension; target pH 7.45-7.55
Endpoint is QRS narrowing under 100 ms
Flumazenil and physostigmine contraindicated; haemodialysis ineffective
explanation.pearls: Persistent hypotension despite sodium bicarbonate is treated with intravenous lipid emulsion 20% as a 1.5 mL/kg bolus and consideration of intra-aortic balloon pump or VA-ECMO in severe refractory cases.

options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate asystole or seizures; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

Activated charcoal beyond 1-2 hours post-ingestion has limited benefit and risks aspiration; cardiac stabilisation with sodium bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg is the antidote for TCA-induced QRS prolongation and hypotension; aim for pH 7.45-7.55 with narrowing of QRS as the endpoint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose where TCA is involved due to seizure risk and has no role in TCA toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

TCAs have a large volume of distribution and high protein binding so are not effectively cleared by haemodialysis; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treatable, with structured psychotherapy as first-line care according to RANZCP and NHMRC guidance. Dialectical behaviour therapy (Linehan), with weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group, between-session coaching and therapist consultation team, has the strongest evidence base, reducing self-harm, emergency presentations and hospitalisation over 12-month courses. Other evidence-based therapies include mentalisation-based therapy, schema therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy. Pharmacotherapy is not first-line and is reserved for short-term management of comorbid depression, anxiety or psychotic features.
key_points: DBT is first-line for borderline personality disorder
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, not core treatment
Prolonged inpatient admission worsens outcomes; outpatient structured psychotherapy preferred
explanation.pearls: Brief crisis admissions of 1 to 3 days for acute risk are acceptable but should be structured with a clear discharge plan back to outpatient psychotherapy to avoid iatrogenic regression.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first-line for core borderline personality disorder symptoms; structured psychotherapy such as DBT is first-line per RANZCP guidance. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

Prolonged psychiatric admission for borderline personality disorder is associated with worse outcomes and regression; outpatient structured psychotherapy is preferred. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

Standard CBT is less evidence-based for borderline personality disorder than dialectical behaviour therapy or other structured personality-disorder-specific therapies. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

Dialectical behaviour therapy is first-line evidence-based treatment for borderline personality disorder per RANZCP and NHMRC, reducing self-harm and ED presentations over 12 months. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

Borderline personality disorder is treatable with structured psychotherapy; declining specialist referral underestimates evidence base for therapeutic response. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder requires abstinence and observation for at least 4 weeks before assigning a primary psychotic illness diagnosis. Inpatient admission supports cessation, monitoring and family education. Antipsychotic medication (low-dose olanzapine, risperidone or aripiprazole) is added if symptoms persist beyond 1 to 2 weeks or are severe. Early psychosis intervention services in Australia (such as headspace and EPPIC) provide structured follow-up; approximately 25 to 50% of cannabis-induced psychotic episodes transition to a primary psychotic illness, with younger age, longer duration of use and family history increasing risk.
key_points: Cease cannabis and observe 4 weeks before committing to primary psychotic illness diagnosis
Low-dose antipsychotic if symptoms persist or are severe
Approximately 25-50% transition to primary psychotic illness; early psychosis service follow-up
explanation.pearls: Synthetic cannabinoids (such as Spice and K2) cause severe agitation, seizures, hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis, with longer-duration psychotic symptoms than natural cannabis and resistance to standard urine drug screens.

options.rationale: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder is managed with abstinence and observation; antipsychotic is started for persistent symptoms with planned weaning; early psychosis service follow-up captures transition to primary psychotic illness. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials; it is not first-line for any psychosis presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)
He is engaging voluntarily without acute risk, so involuntary detention is inappropriate; ECT is not first-line for substance-induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

SSRI is not indicated for psychosis; the presentation requires psychiatric assessment, abstinence support and possible antipsychotic, not outpatient SSRI alone. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)
Schizoaffective diagnosis requires sustained mood episodes alongside psychotic symptoms; presenting picture is acute substance-induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis is clinical and based on DSM-5 criteria. Stimulant medications (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) are first-line per RANZCP and the Australian ADHD Professionals Association guidelines, with non-stimulant atomoxetine or guanfacine as second-line, and clonidine third-line. Pre-treatment workup includes baseline BP, HR, ECG, and screening for cardiac and psychiatric risk factors. Driving is generally improved by stimulant treatment but patients should be counselled to take their dose before driving once tolerability is established. Comorbid depression, anxiety and substance use disorders are screened for and treated alongside.
key_points: Methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine first-line per RANZCP
Atomoxetine and guanfacine second-line; clonidine third-line
Pre-treatment: baseline BP, HR, ECG; screen for cardiac and psychiatric comorbidity
explanation.pearls: Schedule 8 stimulant prescribing requires state-based authority (e.g. NSW Pharmaceutical Services Branch) for adults newly diagnosed with ADHD; clinicians must verify their state's authority requirements before prescribing.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Stimulants generally improve, not impair, driving performance in adult ADHD; they remain first-line. Atomoxetine is second-line per RANZCP and Australian Practice Standards. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)

Stimulants such as methylphenidate are first-line for adult ADHD per RANZCP; titration with side-effect monitoring is standard; driving advice is to take dose before driving once tolerated. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)
Diagnosis of adult ADHD is clinical per DSM-5 criteria; neuropsychological testing is an adjunct, not required to start treatment once diagnosis is established. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)
SSRIs are not effective for core ADHD symptoms; pharmacotherapy targets ADHD with stimulants or atomoxetine, with SSRI reserved for comorbid depression or anxiety. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)
Clonidine is third-line for ADHD, mainly used in children with tic disorders or sleep onset; not first-line in adult ADHD per Australian practice. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance for moderate-severe adolescent depression that has not responded to 6 to 8 weeks of psychological therapy recommends fluoxetine as the first-line SSRI, with weekly initial reviews because of a small absolute increase in suicidal ideation in the first month of treatment. Sertraline and escitalopram are reasonable second-line SSRIs if fluoxetine is not tolerated. Combining medication with continued CBT or interpersonal therapy improves response. TCAs and MAOIs are not used in adolescents.
key_points: Fluoxetine is the only SSRI specifically approved in Australian adolescents
Combine pharmacotherapy with continued psychological therapy
Weekly review in the first month to monitor suicidal ideation and side effects
explanation.pearls: Black-box warnings for suicidal ideation with SSRIs in under-25s reflect a small absolute risk increase confined mostly to the first 1 to 4 weeks; weekly review during that window mitigates the risk.

options.rationale: Sertraline is a reasonable second-line SSRI in adolescent depression but does not have the same level of trial evidence as fluoxetine, which is the only SSRI approved for under-18s in Australia. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)
Mirtazapine is not first-line in adolescent depression; its sedating and weight-gain effects are not preferred, and SSRIs have stronger paediatric evidence. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI in adolescent moderate-severe depression with the strongest efficacy evidence and is the only SSRI specifically approved in this age group in Australia. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)
SNRIs are not first-line in adolescent depression and carry a higher discontinuation syndrome and blood-pressure burden; SSRIs are preferred initially. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)
Tricyclic antidepressants have not shown efficacy in adolescent depression and carry significant overdose risk, so are not recommended in this age group. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: PTSD requires symptoms for at least 1 month after a Criterion A traumatic exposure, with intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions/mood and hyperarousal clusters. Australian Phoenix guidelines and RANZCP recommend trauma-focused CBT or EMDR as first-line treatment for adult PTSD. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) and venlafaxine are second-line, used when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined, or insufficient. Prazosin is an adjunct for nightmares. Critical incident debriefing is no longer recommended.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first-line for adult PTSD
SSRIs (especially sertraline) are second-line pharmacotherapy
Single-session debriefing is not recommended and may worsen outcomes
explanation.pearls: Phoenix Australia recommends 8 to 12 weekly sessions of trauma-focused CBT for adult PTSD; a typical course incorporates psychoeducation, in-vivo and imaginal exposure, and cognitive restructuring.

options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling without trauma-focused techniques is inferior to trauma-focused CBT or EMDR for PTSD symptom reduction. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)
Single-session psychological debriefing is not effective for PTSD prevention or treatment and may worsen outcomes; it is no longer recommended. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

Sertraline has evidence in PTSD but Australian guidance positions it as second-line after trauma-focused psychological therapy in patients who can engage with therapy, and the patient prefers a non-pharmacological start. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

Trauma-focused CBT is a Phoenix Australia and RANZCP first-line recommendation for adult PTSD, with consistent strong evidence across military and civilian populations. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

Prazosin is an adjunct for trauma-related nightmares but is not a stand-alone PTSD treatment; primary therapy is trauma-focused psychological intervention. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

explanation.summary: Acute on chronic lithium toxicity classically follows the addition of an ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide or NSAID to a chronic lithium user. Renal lithium retention plus dehydration tips levels into the toxic range. Early features are coarse tremor, GI upset, ataxia and confusion; severe toxicity includes seizures, coma and arrhythmia. Initial management is to stop the precipitant, hold lithium, give intravenous crystalloid, and check lithium and renal function. Haemodialysis is reserved for severe toxicity (level above 4 mmol/L, severe symptoms, renal failure).
key_points: ACEi, ARB, thiazide and NSAID raise lithium levels
Early features: tremor, GI symptoms, ataxia
Haemodialysis if level above 4 mmol/L or severe symptoms with renal impairment
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic lithium range is 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance and up to 1.2 mmol/L for acute mania; symptoms generally appear above 1.5 mmol/L and dialysis is considered above 4 mmol/L or above 2.5 mmol/L with renal failure.

options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium meaningfully and is not used in lithium toxicity. (Source: AMH: Lithium)
Continuing lithium in a symptomatic patient with rising creatinine and a likely toxic level worsens neurological injury; the precipitant must be withdrawn. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

Haemodialysis is indicated for severe lithium toxicity (level above 4 mmol/L, level 2.5 to 4 with severe symptoms or renal failure, or impaired clearance) but is not first-line for mild-moderate toxicity that may respond to fluid resuscitation. (Source: AMH: Lithium)
Thiazides also raise lithium levels by reducing distal tubular sodium delivery; switching to a thiazide worsens lithium retention rather than helping it. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

Acute on chronic lithium toxicity from ACE-inhibitor-induced renal lithium retention and dehydration is treated with stopping the precipitant, lithium hold and IV crystalloid to enhance renal excretion. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the rapid intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium that follows reintroduction of carbohydrate in severely malnourished patients, classically those with BMI under 14 or rapid weight loss. Manifestations include hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, thiamine deficiency (Wernicke), peripheral oedema, cardiac arrhythmia and acute heart failure. Management is electrolyte replacement (intravenous if severe), thiamine 100 to 200 mg daily, reduction in caloric load (not cessation), and twice-daily biochemistry monitoring during the high-risk window of the first week.
key_points: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark electrolyte derangement
Replace phosphate, magnesium, potassium and give thiamine; reduce calories, do not stop
Twice-daily electrolytes for the first 5 to 7 days of refeeding in high-risk patients
explanation.pearls: ANZAED guidance recommends starting refeeding at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with twice-daily electrolytes and pre-emptive thiamine 100 mg, increasing calories cautiously by 10 kcal/kg/day if biochemistry stays stable.

options.rationale: This is biochemical refeeding syndrome with hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia; standard practice is IV replacement of the three electrolytes plus thiamine, with reduced (not stopped) caloric load. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)

Stopping nutrition risks further metabolic collapse and reverses the gains of feeding; the correct response is to reduce caloric load and aggressively replace electrolytes, not zero feeding. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)
Refeeding oedema is from sodium and water retention plus reduced oncotic pressure; loop diuretics worsen electrolyte derangements and are contraindicated in this context. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)
Increasing calories during active refeeding syndrome will accelerate metabolic complications; the correct move is to reduce caloric load while replacing electrolytes. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)
Beta blockers in severe anorexia carry hypotension and bradycardia risks and do not address the underlying electrolyte problem driving the tachycardia and QT prolongation. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Clozapine tolerance to hypotension, sedation and respiratory depression is lost after 48 hours without dosing. Australian product information and Clopine Connect mandate retitration as if commencing from scratch: a 12.5 to 25 mg test dose followed by daily incremental increases (50 mg, 100 mg etc.) targeting the previous maintenance dose. Concurrent enzyme inducers (smoking, carbamazepine) and inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) affect plasma levels significantly. Re-baseline FBC and ECG before re-initiation when restarting after prolonged interruption.
key_points: More than 48 hours off clozapine = retitrate from 12.5 mg test dose
Tolerance loss applies to hypotension, sedation and respiratory effects
Re-baseline FBC and ECG before extended re-initiation
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation during hospitalisation can double clozapine plasma levels because tobacco induces CYP1A2; a clozapine plasma level 2 weeks after admission is mandatory when a smoker is admitted to a non-smoking ward.

options.rationale: After more than 48 hours off clozapine, tolerance is lost and restarting at the previous full dose risks severe orthostatic hypotension, sedation and respiratory depression. (Source: Clopine Connect / Australian Clozapine Treatment Guidelines)

After 48 hours or more of missed clozapine, retitration is mandatory from a low test dose (12.5 to 25 mg) with day-by-day escalation, as if starting clozapine from scratch. (Source: Clopine Connect Prescribing Information)

Halving the dose for one night is insufficient to manage lost tolerance; the patient remains at risk of hypotension and over-sedation with any dose larger than the test dose. (Source: Clopine Connect Prescribing Information)
Long-acting olanzapine is not used as a bridge in clozapine-eligible patients and carries its own post-injection syndrome risk requiring 3 hours of supervised observation. (Source: AMH: Olanzapine)

Skipping the test dose at restart bypasses the safety check for hypotension and over-sedation in someone who has lost tolerance; Australian product information mandates test-dose retitration after 48 hours. (Source: Clopine Connect Prescribing Information)

explanation.summary: Capacity requires the person to understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision. In severe depression with suicidal intent the weighing limb is typically the one that fails, so refusal of life-saving treatment is not competent. In NSW the pathway is a mental health certificate, Schedule 1, completed by a medical practitioner or accredited person who has examined the person, authorising detention in a declared mental health facility. An authorised medical officer must then examine her as soon as practicable and within 12 hours. The Act authorises her care and treatment for mental illness; the antidote itself is given under the duty of care and must not wait on legal process.
key_points: Severe depression most often impairs the weighing limb of capacity.
NSW detention starts with a mental health certificate, not an assessment order.
Detention requires that no less restrictive care is appropriate and available.
Paracetamol toxicity is time-critical: do not delay N-acetylcysteine for paperwork.
explanation.pearls: Scheduling and treating are separate decisions. The schedule secures her psychiatric care; the N-acetylcysteine goes up on the duty of care while the paperwork is still being written.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: initial detention and transport

options.rationale: Severe depression with active suicidal intent distorts the appreciating and weighing limbs of capacity even when the patient can recite the facts, so this refusal is not a competent one. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

The Supreme Court is for enduring or contested incapacity questions. Where mental illness is driving an acute refusal the Mental Health Act 2007 and the duty of care are the working mechanisms. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

A medical practitioner who has examined her may complete a mental health certificate, Schedule 1, so she can be detained in a declared mental health facility: she is a mentally ill person under section 14, or at least mentally disordered under section 15, and no less restrictive care is appropriate and available. The Act carries the psychiatric care while the antidote is given without delay under the duty of care. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: initial detention and transport)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: initial detention and transport

options.rationale: Guardianship consent is for enduring incapacity and takes days to arrange. It is neither quick enough for paracetamol toxicity nor the right instrument for refusal driven by acute mental illness. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

Delaying N-acetylcysteine beyond 8 hours from ingestion sharply raises the risk of hepatic failure, and capacity impaired by acute suicidal depression rarely returns within hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Polyuria and polydipsia in a long-term lithium-treated patient with reduced urine osmolality after fluid restriction indicate lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Joint psychiatric and renal review is needed to consider dose reduction, switching to an alternative mood stabiliser, or adding amiloride. Fluid restriction is dangerous and desmopressin is largely ineffective because the defect is tubular resistance.
key_points: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI by reducing aquaporin-2 expression in collecting ducts
Long-term lithium also causes chronic interstitial nephritis and reduced eGFR
Joint psychiatric and renal review is required before dose change or switching
explanation.pearls: Amiloride 5 to 10 mg orally daily reduces lithium uptake in the principal cell and improves nephrogenic DI; thiazides can be used cautiously but raise lithium levels.

options.rationale: Polyuria with reduced urine osmolality after fluid restriction in a lithium-treated patient indicates lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; psychiatric review is needed to balance ongoing mood stabilisation against renal toxicity and consider dose reduction or switching. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus occurs in long-term lithium use regardless of therapeutic level and signals nephron damage; ignoring symptoms risks irreversible decline. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

Fluid restriction is dangerous in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and risks hypernatraemic dehydration; treatment is to reduce or stop lithium under specialist supervision. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)
Desmopressin is largely ineffective in nephrogenic DI because the defect is renal tubular resistance, and specialist input is required before commencing. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

Increasing the lithium dose worsens renal effects; the current level is therapeutic and increasing it without reason is contraindicated, especially with emerging nephrogenic DI. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD is treated first-line with a long-acting stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate modified release in Australia. Pre-treatment cardiovascular assessment includes history, BP and ECG; ongoing monitoring tracks BP, pulse and weight. Non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are reserved for stimulant contraindication or intolerance.
key_points: Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate MR) are first-line in adult ADHD
Pre-treatment cardiovascular history, BP and ECG are required before stimulant initiation
Non-stimulants are reserved for stimulant contraindication or substance use risk
explanation.pearls: Diversion risk should be discussed at every visit; in Australia, stimulant prescribing for adults is restricted and requires authority from the relevant state regulatory body.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Bupropion has limited evidence in adult ADHD and is not endorsed as first-line in Australian guidelines. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)
Atomoxetine is an alternative non-stimulant agent and is reserved for stimulant intolerance, substance use risk, or comorbid anxiety; it is not first-line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)
Immediate-release stimulants are second-line in adults because of multiple daily doses and diversion risk; long-acting forms are preferred. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)
Clonidine is used as augmentation in paediatric ADHD; it is not a first-line monotherapy in adults. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

Long-acting stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine are first-line for adult ADHD in Australia, offering once-daily dosing and lower abuse potential than immediate-release amphetamine. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk among mood stabilisers. The risk is approximately 10 percent for major malformations and 30 to 40 percent for impaired cognitive development. Women of reproductive potential must be on a pregnancy prevention program. Women planning pregnancy are cross-titrated to a safer agent (lithium or lamotrigine) under cover of effective contraception before stopping contraception.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no effective alternative exists
Lithium and lamotrigine are the preferred mood stabilisers in pregnancy planning
Cross-titration occurs under cover of effective contraception, not abrupt cessation
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine requires slow titration (25 mg/day increments) over 6 weeks to minimise the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome; pre-conception planning should allow this lead time.

options.rationale: Valproate has the highest teratogenic potential of mood stabilisers (about 10 percent major malformations, dose-related neurodevelopmental impact); women planning pregnancy are switched to a safer agent under cover of effective contraception. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)
High-dose folate does not offset the malformation and neurodevelopmental risk of valproate; switching to a safer agent before conception is required. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)
There is no safe dose of valproate in pregnancy; even reduced doses carry a substantial risk of structural and neurodevelopmental harm. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)
Abrupt cessation risks relapse of bipolar disorder; cross-titration under cover of contraception is the safer pathway. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)
While the pregnancy prevention program requires effective contraception, the woman is planning pregnancy and a switch is required, not indefinite continuation. (Source: TGA Valproate)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, cause weight gain, dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose metabolism. Australian RANZCP guidance schedules a metabolic screen at baseline, 12 weeks and 6-monthly comprising fasting glucose, lipid profile, weight, waist circumference and BP. Early identification at 12 weeks allows lifestyle intervention or antipsychotic switch before sustained metabolic disease develops.
key_points: 12-week metabolic screen on antipsychotic - fasting glucose, lipids, weight, waist, BP
Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest cardiometabolic burden
Weight gain over 5 percent in 12 weeks should prompt lifestyle and medication review
explanation.pearls: Metformin can be added to mitigate antipsychotic-induced weight gain (around 3 kg average effect) when lifestyle measures are insufficient and switching is undesired.

options.rationale: LFTs, TFTs and creatinine are baseline and yearly tests rather than the 12-week metabolic screen, which focuses on glucose, lipids, weight and BP. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)
Olanzapine has relatively low prolactin-raising effect; the 12-week screen is metabolic and DEXA is not part of routine 12-week monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)
Clozapine levels are irrelevant on olanzapine; FBC is mandatory for clozapine but not for olanzapine, and annual ECG is not the 12-week tool. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

Australian RANZCP guidance recommends a fasting metabolic screen (glucose, lipids, weight, waist circumference, BP) at 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic, then 6-monthly. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)
Symptom and EPS rating are important but do not substitute for metabolic blood and anthropometric monitoring which is the highest yield at 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian NHMRC guidance for borderline personality disorder prioritises a structured, evidence-based psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy) with continuity of care. Acute presentations with non-life-threatening self-harm are managed by validating distress, supporting the patient's existing safety plan, and rapid follow-up with the primary clinician. Admission and involuntary measures are reserved for acute psychiatric emergency.
key_points: Continuity with the primary therapist is the highest-leverage acute intervention
Routine inpatient admission for self-harm in BPD does not improve outcomes
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive and lacks BPD-specific efficacy in the long-term
explanation.pearls: Brief admission of 24 to 72 hours may be useful in acute suicidal crisis to prevent imminent harm; planned and time-limited stays reduce reinforcement of crisis presentations.

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy has limited evidence in BPD and as-needed sedative-antipsychotic use risks dependence; first-line management is psychological. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

Routine admission for self-harm in BPD often reinforces help-seeking via crisis and disrupts therapeutic work; admission is reserved for acute psychiatric emergency or comorbid acute condition. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

Evidence-based BPD care prioritises continuity with the primary therapist, validation, brief crisis interventions and use of the patient's existing safety plan; routine hospital admission for self-harm in BPD does not improve outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
BPD without acute serious risk does not warrant involuntary admission; her presentation is non-life-threatening and she has insight, capacity and a safety plan. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
Discharge is appropriate but should be coordinated with the usual treating team and include rapid follow-up rather than disengaging from acute care. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia presents with mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility and posturing and may complicate psychotic or mood disorders. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment at 5 to 10 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Lack of fever, autonomic instability and severe rigidity argues against NMS. ECT is reserved for benzodiazepine non-responders, malignant or recurrent catatonia.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is first-line diagnostic and therapeutic test for catatonia
NMS requires fever, autonomic instability and significant rigidity with marked CK rise
ECT is reserved for non-response, malignant or recurrent catatonia
explanation.pearls: Excited catatonia (hyperkinetic variant) presents with frenzied motor activity rather than stupor; lorazepam still works but the differential broadens to include serotonin syndrome and acute psychosis.

options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis warrants investigation in atypical or refractory cases, but does not delay urgent treatment of the catatonic state; lorazepam is safe and aids diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)
NMS requires fever, autonomic instability and significant rigidity with a markedly elevated CK; their absence here makes catatonia more likely than NMS. (Source: RANZCP NMS Position)

ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is reserved for lorazepam non-response, life-threatening features (malignant catatonia) or recurrent catatonia; trial of lorazepam comes first. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

Increasing antipsychotic dose may worsen catatonia (and could precipitate NMS); catatonia in psychosis is treated by stopping or reducing antipsychotic and adding benzodiazepine. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV) is the diagnostic and first-line treatment step for catatonia; partial or full response within minutes confirms the diagnosis and guides further benzodiazepine dosing. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

explanation.summary: Moderate alcohol withdrawal (CIWA-Ar 10-20) is managed with symptom-triggered or front-loaded diazepam, parenteral thiamine 300 mg daily before any carbohydrate, hydration, magnesium and folate replacement, and monitoring for delirium tremens and seizures. In hepatic failure, shorter-acting benzodiazepines such as oxazepam are preferred.
key_points: Diazepam is first-line in alcohol withdrawal without significant hepatic impairment
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg daily prevents Wernicke encephalopathy
Oxazepam or lorazepam are preferred in significant liver disease
explanation.pearls: Always give thiamine before glucose in malnourished alcohol-dependent patients to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; oral thiamine has poor absorption when intake is poor.

options.rationale: Haloperidol does not treat the underlying GABA-glutamate imbalance and lowers seizure threshold; benzodiazepines are first-line in alcohol withdrawal. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)
Beta-blockers mask tachycardia without preventing seizures or delirium tremens and are not adequate as monotherapy. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)

Single-dose chlordiazepoxide without titration or symptom-triggered repeat dosing under-treats moderate withdrawal; structured symptom-triggered or front-loaded regimens are recommended. (Source: RACP: Management of alcohol withdrawal)
IV chlormethiazole is no longer recommended for alcohol withdrawal in Australia due to respiratory depression risk and abuse potential. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)

Symptom-triggered diazepam loading (20 mg orally every 1-2 hours guided by CIWA-Ar) with parenteral thiamine 300 mg daily for at least 3 days is the Australian first-line regimen for moderate alcohol withdrawal. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is recognised by the triad of neuromuscular excitability (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis) and altered mental status, in the setting of serotonergic drug exposure. Tramadol combined with SSRIs is a common trigger. Management is drug cessation, IV fluids, benzodiazepines, active cooling and cyproheptadine if severe.
key_points: Hunter criteria identify serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor)
Tramadol plus SSRI is a high-risk combination
Differentiate from NMS by rigidity and rate of onset
explanation.pearls: NMS develops over days to weeks with rigidity and bradyreflexia; serotonin syndrome develops over hours with clonus and hyperreflexia; getting this distinction right changes management to dantrolene/bromocriptine in NMS or cyproheptadine in serotonin syndrome.

options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome from SSRI plus tramadol is managed by ceasing all serotonergic agents, supportive care with IV fluids, benzodiazepines for agitation and hyperthermia, active cooling and oral cyproheptadine 12 mg loading if symptoms persist. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)
Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome; serotonin syndrome lacks rigidity and is managed differently. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)
Bromocriptine is used in NMS where there is dopamine antagonism; it is not indicated in serotonin syndrome where the issue is excess serotonin. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)
Continuing the serotonergic drug perpetuates the syndrome; cessation of all serotonergic agents is essential to recovery. (Source: AMH: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors)

Sepsis is a differential and cultures should be sent but the clinical syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperthermia, serotonergic drug exposure) fits serotonin toxicity, which is treated by drug cessation and supportive care. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

explanation.summary: First-line treatment of moderate to severe generalised anxiety disorder is an SSRI or SNRI combined with cognitive behavioural therapy. Benzodiazepines are limited to short-term use due to dependence risk. Antipsychotics and beta-blockers are not first-line. Treatment effect for SSRIs is typically seen at 4 to 6 weeks with dose titration as needed.
key_points: SSRI plus CBT is first-line for moderate-severe GAD
Benzodiazepines are short-term adjuncts only due to dependence risk
Treatment response is typically assessed at 4-6 weeks
explanation.pearls: Counsel patients about possible initial worsening of anxiety in the first 1-2 weeks of SSRI initiation; lower starting doses (sertraline 25 mg) may reduce activation symptoms.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line in GAD due to tolerance, dependence and impaired psychomotor function; SSRIs or SNRIs and CBT are preferred. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Generalised anxiety disorder)

An SSRI such as sertraline combined with cognitive behavioural therapy is first-line treatment for GAD per Australian guidelines; expected onset of benefit is 4 to 6 weeks. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Generalised anxiety disorder)
Antipsychotics are not first-line in GAD and carry significant metabolic and motor side effects. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders

options.rationale: Propranolol may help performance anxiety but is not first-line for GAD where SSRIs and CBT address core cognitive and worry symptoms. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Generalised anxiety disorder)

GAD-7 of 16 is severe but does not by itself indicate admission; outpatient pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy is appropriate given employment and absence of suicidality. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically presents in the first 4 weeks of titration with persistent tachycardia, fever, elevated troponin and constitutional symptoms. Mandatory monitoring includes baseline and weekly CRP, troponin and FBC for the first 4 weeks. Suspected myocarditis requires immediate clozapine cessation, urgent cardiac assessment with echocardiogram, and lifelong avoidance of rechallenge.
key_points: Suspect clozapine myocarditis in weeks 1-4 with fever, tachycardia and high troponin
Immediate cessation and cardiac assessment is mandatory
Rechallenge with clozapine is contraindicated after myocarditis
explanation.pearls: Monitoring during titration includes baseline echocardiogram, weekly CRP and troponin for 4 weeks, and weekly FBC for 18 weeks then monthly for the duration of treatment.

options.rationale: Persistent tachycardia, fever and elevated troponin in the first 4 weeks of clozapine titration is suggestive of clozapine-induced myocarditis and requires immediate cessation. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)
Dose reduction is inadequate when myocarditis is suspected; immediate cessation and urgent cardiac assessment are required given the mortality risk. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)

Clozapine-induced myocarditis presents in the first 4 weeks of titration with tachycardia, fever and elevated troponin; immediate cessation, cardiology referral with echocardiogram, and avoidance of any future clozapine rechallenge is required. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)
Symptomatic beta-blockade does not address the underlying myocarditis and continued exposure increases mortality risk. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)
Outpatient management is unsafe in suspected myocarditis; admission for cardiac assessment is required before any switch is made. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Clozapine)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is best managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, which is a partial D2 agonist. Cabergoline carries a risk of precipitating psychotic relapse. Long-term untreated hyperprolactinaemia leads to hypogonadism and reduced bone mineral density.
key_points: Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing due to partial D2 agonism
Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are high-prolactin agents
Untreated hyperprolactinaemia causes hypogonadism and bone loss
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine, quetiapine and clozapine are also relatively prolactin-sparing options if aripiprazole is unsuitable; baseline prolactin should be checked before commencing any antipsychotic with high prolactin liability.

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists may precipitate psychotic relapse in schizophrenia and are not the preferred approach when an alternative antipsychotic option exists. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Antipsychotic adverse effects)
Stopping the antipsychotic without substitution risks psychotic relapse; hormonal therapy alone does not address the underlying dopamine D2 blockade. (Source: AMH: Risperidone)
Combination dopamine agonist plus antipsychotic risks psychotic relapse and is less preferred than switching to a prolactin-sparing agent. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Antipsychotic adverse effects)

Risperidone is a strong dopamine D2 antagonist causing prolactin elevation; aripiprazole is a partial dopamine D2 agonist and is prolactin-sparing, making it the preferred switch when antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is symptomatic. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Antipsychotic adverse effects)

The patient is symptomatic with amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and reduced libido; long-term hyperprolactinaemia also raises concerns about hypogonadism and reduced bone density. (Source: AMH: Risperidone)

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia nervosa meeting MARSIPAN medical instability criteria requires medical admission with continuous cardiac monitoring, slow refeeding from 5-10 kcal/kg/day, electrolyte and thiamine supplementation, daily bloods and clinical review for refeeding syndrome. Outpatient and standard ward management without monitoring are unsafe.
key_points: MARSIPAN criteria identify need for medical admission in severe AN
Refeeding starts at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with daily phosphate monitoring
Cardiac monitoring is required for QTc prolongation or bradycardia
explanation.pearls: Family-based therapy, CBT-ED and specialist outpatient eating disorder programs are evidence-based long-term treatments but only after medical stabilisation; involve mental health services early to plan post-admission care.

sources.label: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

options.rationale: Outpatient management is unsafe when patients meet MARSIPAN medical instability criteria; inpatient medical admission is required. (Source: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa)
source_refs: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

options.rationale: FBT is an appropriate longer-term therapy but does not address acute medical instability which requires immediate medical admission. (Source: ANZAED: Eating disorder medical management)

Full caloric refeeding from day 1 in severe anorexia nervosa risks refeeding syndrome including hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmia and Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa)
source_refs: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

options.rationale: CBT-ED is an evidence-based outpatient therapy in less severe disease; it is not appropriate when MARSIPAN criteria for medical instability are met. (Source: ANZAED: Eating disorder medical management)

MARSIPAN medical instability criteria (BMI under 13, HR under 40, postural BP drop above 20, hypothermia, K under 3.0, hypoglycaemia, prolonged QTc) require medical admission with cardiac monitoring, slow refeeding from 5-10 kcal/kg/day, electrolyte correction and daily monitoring for refeeding syndrome. (Source: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa)
source_refs: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring in a stable patient is at 6-monthly intervals and covers a 12-hour trough lithium level (target 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance), eGFR, TSH and calcium. Additional levels are drawn around dose changes, new interacting medications (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides), and intercurrent illness. Toxicity risk rises with dehydration, infection and renal injury. Annual cardiometabolic review and review of contraception remain relevant.
key_points: Stable lithium: 6-monthly lithium, eGFR, TSH and calcium
Trough lithium 12 hours post dose; therapeutic 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance
Monitor more frequently around dose changes, new interacting drugs and intercurrent illness
explanation.pearls: Maintenance lithium trough 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L drawn 12 hours post dose with 6-monthly eGFR, TSH and calcium balances relapse prevention with the risks of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney injury and hyperparathyroidism.

options.rationale: AU practice on stable lithium recommends 6-monthly serum lithium, renal, thyroid and calcium monitoring with trough levels 12 hours post dose, and additional levels around dose or interacting-medication changes. (Source: RANZCP clinical practice guidelines on mood disorders; AMH lithium monograph)
Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney injury and hyperparathyroidism; renal and calcium monitoring is mandatory. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)
Lithium toxicity, renal injury and thyroid disease can develop silently; long intervals miss reversible harms. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)
Stable disease on lithium is a reason to continue lithium with monitoring, not to switch agents. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)
Monthly testing is reserved for initiation, dose change or instability; routine stable monitoring is at 6 to 12 monthly intervals. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

explanation.summary: First-line AU pharmacotherapy for tobacco use disorder is varenicline (12 weeks at 1 mg twice daily after titration), combination NRT (patch plus short-acting formulation for 8 to 12 weeks), or bupropion sustained-release. Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates compared with pharmacotherapy alone. Quitline and brief intervention models support adherence. Vaping is a second-line aid considered when first-line pharmacotherapies fail. Bupropion is contraindicated in active eating disorders and seizure disorders.
key_points: Varenicline 12 weeks with behavioural support is AU first-line
Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) doubles quit rates over patch alone
Bupropion is contraindicated in active eating disorders or seizure history
explanation.pearls: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks (titrated over the first week) achieves around 25 percent abstinence at 6 months, roughly double the rate of NRT patch monotherapy.

options.rationale: RACGP positions vaping as a second-line cessation aid, considered only when first-line approved pharmacotherapies fail; not first-line. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)

Varenicline plus behavioural support is the AU first-line pharmacotherapy for tobacco use disorder, with the licensed titration to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation; AMH varenicline)
Standard NRT is 8 to 12 weeks at full dose combining a patch with short-acting formulation; 3 days is sub-therapeutic. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)
Bupropion is contraindicated in active eating disorders and is not first-line here; behavioural support is also needed. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)
Naltrexone is not an approved nicotine cessation pharmacotherapy in Australia. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 symptoms beginning before age 12, persisting into adulthood with functional impairment across more than one setting, after exclusion of competing diagnoses. Corroborative childhood history (parent, school reports) strengthens diagnostic confidence. Comorbidity with mood, anxiety, substance use and learning disorders is the rule rather than the exception. Treatment is multimodal: psychoeducation, environmental modification, and pharmacotherapy (stimulants first-line in non-substance-use comorbidity, atomoxetine for substance use risk). Stimulant initiation is restricted to psychiatrists and paediatricians under Australian state authorities.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 symptoms from childhood persisting into adulthood
Corroborative childhood history strengthens the diagnosis
Stimulants are initiated by a psychiatrist or paediatrician under AU state authorities
explanation.pearls: The AADPA 2022 guideline anchors adult ADHD diagnosis in structured DSM-5 interviewing with corroborative childhood history; GP-initiated stimulants are not legal in any Australian state.

options.rationale: Australian regulations require psychiatrist or paediatrician initiation of stimulants for ADHD; GPs cannot initiate. (Source: RACGP ADHD position; Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
SSRIs are not first-line for ADHD; they may treat comorbid depression or anxiety but do not address core ADHD symptoms. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)

Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 symptoms in childhood and adulthood with corroborating history; comorbidity screening guides management. Stimulant initiation must be by a psychiatrist (or paediatrician) under state authority and PBS rules. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)
CBT is adjunctive in moderate to severe ADHD; pharmacotherapy remains the most effective core treatment. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)
Lithium has no role in primary ADHD pharmacotherapy. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose produces sodium channel blockade with QRS prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia, seizures, anticholinergic and alpha-blocker effects. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated as needed) reverses sodium channel blockade by both pH alkalinisation and sodium loading, targeting QRS under 100 ms and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55. Adjuncts: airway protection, crystalloid plus noradrenaline for hypotension, benzodiazepines for seizures, lipid emulsion in refractory shock. Haemodialysis is ineffective due to high protein binding and large volume of distribution.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms in TCA overdose indicates sodium channel blockade
Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the first-line antidote
Target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS narrowing
explanation.pearls: QRS over 100 ms in suspected TCA overdose predicts seizures and arrhythmia and is the trigger for sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus; an R wave over 3 mm in aVR is corroborative.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a salvage option for refractory toxicity; it is not the first-line for QRS widening. (Source: NSW Health Poisons Information Centre TCA monograph; Murray Toxicology 4e)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.rationale: Activated charcoal at 4 hours after an ingestion of a slow-absorbed drug is of marginal benefit and does not address the cardiotoxicity. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines treat seizures but do not address the sodium channel blockade driving QRS widening and hypotension. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity from fast sodium channel blockade is reversed with hypertonic sodium bicarbonate aiming for QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55; airway and circulation support continue alongside. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.rationale: TCAs are highly protein-bound with a large volume of distribution; haemodialysis is not effective. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

explanation.summary: Catatonia presents with mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism and stupor; the Bush-Francis scale aids diagnosis. After exclusion of medical mimics (infection, NMS, encephalitis, hypoactive delirium, drug effects), the first-line treatment is a lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment within 10 minutes), followed by scheduled lorazepam typically 6 to 24 mg per day. ECT is the most effective second-line treatment when lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics are deferred unless psychotic features require treatment with concurrent benzodiazepines.
key_points: Bush-Francis catatonia rating helps quantify response to treatment
Lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV reverses catatonia in 60 to 80 percent within minutes
Antipsychotic monotherapy risks neuroleptic malignant syndrome in catatonic patients
explanation.pearls: A 1 to 2 mg IV lorazepam challenge with reassessment at 5 to 10 minutes confirms benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia in around 70 percent and titrates to scheduled lorazepam 6 to 24 mg per day.

options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for catatonia but follows a lorazepam challenge in most pathways and requires informed consent or substitute decision-maker authorisation. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource; Australian ECT guidelines)
SSRI initiation does not address acute catatonia and may delay effective treatment. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)

Antipsychotics, especially typical agents, can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome in catatonic patients; they are reserved for psychotic catatonia under specialist guidance after a benzodiazepine trial. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)
Anticholinergics have no established role in catatonia. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)

A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment within 10 minutes) confirms benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia in 60 to 80 percent of cases; ECT follows for non-responders. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires DSM-5 criteria of an uninterrupted period of illness with a major mood episode (manic or depressive) concurrent with schizophrenia A criteria, plus at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of a major mood episode. Mood episodes are present for the majority of the active and residual phases. Differentiation from bipolar I with psychotic features rests on persistence of psychosis outside of mood episodes; from MDD with psychotic features on the same point; from schizophrenia on the prominence and duration of mood symptoms.
key_points: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis for 2 weeks or more in the absence of an acute mood episode
Mood episodes must be present for the majority of the illness's active and residual phases
Mood-congruent psychosis confined to mood episodes points to MDD or bipolar I with psychotic features
explanation.pearls: Schizoaffective disorder is identified longitudinally: at least 2 weeks of psychosis without an active mood episode, with mood symptoms across the majority of the total illness duration distinguishing it from primary psychotic disorders.

options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires major mood episodes during a substantial portion of the illness with at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of an acute mood episode. (Source: DSM-5; RANZCP schizoaffective disorder clinical resource)
He has had no manic or hypomanic episodes and psychosis persists between mood episodes; bipolar I does not fit. (Source: DSM-5)
Brief psychotic disorder is by definition under 1 month and does not recur over years. (Source: DSM-5)
MDD with psychotic features requires psychosis to occur only during depressive episodes; persistent psychosis between episodes excludes this. (Source: DSM-5)
Schizophreniform applies for psychotic episodes lasting 1 to 6 months in total; the longitudinal course here exceeds this. (Source: DSM-5)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed by a stepped pathway: assess for medical or substance causes, attempt verbal de-escalation and environmental measures, offer oral medication (olanzapine, lorazepam or risperidone), then escalate to intramuscular olanzapine or droperidol if refused or unsafe. Monitoring includes airway, conscious level, SpO2, BP, HR, ECG (for QT), temperature and post-restraint review. Mechanical restraint is a last resort and time-limited. Specific AU pathways (NSW Health, Victorian DHHS, Queensland Health) operationalise this approach with consistent agents and review timing.
key_points: De-escalation and oral medication precede parenteral options where safe
IM olanzapine or droperidol is the preferred parenteral option with monitoring
Mechanical restraint is a last resort, time-limited and requires ongoing medical review
explanation.pearls: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg or droperidol 10 mg with airway, SpO2 and ECG monitoring is the AU-preferred parenteral rapid tranquillisation when oral medication is refused or unsafe.

sources.label: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG
RANZCP guideline on management of acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: A low oral benzodiazepine dose alone is sub-therapeutic for severe acute behavioural disturbance and lacks a planned escalation pathway. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.rationale: AU stepped pathway prioritises de-escalation and oral options before parenteral therapy; IM olanzapine or droperidol is the preferred parenteral option with monitoring of airway and ECG. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.rationale: High-dose haloperidol risks dystonia, QT prolongation and torsades, especially with stimulant intoxication; not recommended as a first-line single dose. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.rationale: IV midazolam infusion outside a high-acuity bed risks respiratory arrest; IM benzodiazepines or olanzapine are safer first-line parenteral choices. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.rationale: Mechanical restraint without pharmacotherapy and ongoing medical review is unsafe and ethically untenable; it is a last-resort short-term measure with chemical and behavioural alternatives. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis to persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms within a course that also includes mood episodes meeting major depressive or manic criteria for a substantial part of the illness. Bipolar disorder with psychotic features confines psychotic symptoms within the duration of mood episodes. Treatment for schizoaffective bipolar type usually combines a mood stabiliser with an antipsychotic; clozapine is considered for treatment resistance. The diagnosis often requires longitudinal data because of significant overlap with bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
key_points: Schizoaffective requires 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms
Mood episodes must be present for a substantial part of the illness
Treatment combines mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic; consider clozapine for resistance
explanation.pearls: Longitudinal collateral history outperforms cross-sectional assessment for distinguishing schizoaffective from bipolar with psychotic features.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis without prominent mood symptoms for at least 2 weeks alongside mood episodes meeting full criteria over the illness course. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia Clinical Practice Guideline)

Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis to occur only within mood episodes; persistence of psychosis after mood remits points to schizoaffective. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia Clinical Practice Guideline)
Schizophreniform disorder does not include episodes meeting full mania or major depression criteria during the course of psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia Clinical Practice Guideline)

Methamphetamine is undetectable in urine after 72 to 96 hours; substance-induced psychosis would also be expected to remit fully within weeks of cessation. (Source: RANZCP: Psychostimulant Position Statement)

Major depression with psychotic features requires the psychosis to occur during a current depressive episode, which this presentation lacks. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Varenicline is a partial nicotinic agonist that is started 1 to 2 weeks before the planned quit date with a standard titration to allow tolerance. Standard duration is 12 weeks; an additional 12 weeks may be considered to consolidate abstinence. Australian post-acute coronary syndrome guidance still considers varenicline first-line because cardiovascular safety is established. Common adverse effects include nausea, vivid dreams, and insomnia; severe psychiatric adverse effects are rare and historic boxed warnings have been substantially revised.
key_points: Set the quit date 1 to 2 weeks after starting varenicline
Titrate over 7 days then continue 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
Cardiovascular safety after acute coronary syndrome is established
explanation.pearls: Nausea peaks in the first 2 weeks of varenicline; taking the dose with food and a full glass of water reduces it markedly.

options.rationale: Varenicline requires a 1 week titration from 0.5 mg daily to 1 mg twice daily and the quit date is set within that first or second week, not immediately at first dose. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)
Beta-blockers do not interact pharmacologically with varenicline; both are continued and metoprolol is essential after recent myocardial infarction. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)
Recent meta-analyses show no excess cardiovascular events with varenicline; it remains a first-line option after acute coronary syndrome. (Source: RACGP: Smoking Cessation)
The standard quit date is set 1 to 2 weeks after starting, not 6 weeks; the dose of 2 mg daily is also non-standard. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)
Standard titration is 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily; the quit date is set 8 to 14 days after starting for 12 weeks. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychosis and first episode schizophrenia can be indistinguishable cross-sectionally. Australian early intervention practice favours admission to a specialist youth early psychosis service, low-dose oral antipsychotic to manage acute symptoms, structured cannabis cessation support, and longitudinal review. Approximately 40% of cannabis-induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia within 5 years, particularly with high-potency cannabis exposure, family history, and prodromal functional decline. Early intervention reduces transition rates and improves outcomes.
key_points: Admit acute psychosis with command hallucinations regardless of substance use
Use low-dose oral antipsychotic plus structured cannabis cessation
Up to 40% of cannabis-induced psychosis converts to schizophrenia within 5 years
explanation.pearls: Family history of schizophrenia and prodromal functional decline strongly raise transition risk after cannabis-induced psychosis; track these explicitly.

options.rationale: Premature labelling and depot initiation before observing the post-substance withdrawal trajectory is not best practice; substance-induced psychosis often resolves with abstinence. (Source: RANZCP: First Episode Psychosis Guideline)
Acute psychosis with command hallucinations requires admission for safety and observation regardless of substance use cause. (Source: RANZCP: First Episode Psychosis Guideline)

Australian early intervention practice supports admission, low-dose oral antipsychotic, structured cannabis cessation, and longitudinal review because up to 40% of cannabis-induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia. (Source: Orygen: First Episode Psychosis)
Antipsychotic medication relieves distressing symptoms and reduces risk during active psychosis even when substance use is implicated. (Source: RANZCP: First Episode Psychosis Guideline)

Acuphase is reserved for severe acute behavioural disturbance unresponsive to oral therapy; oral first-line antipsychotic is preferred when the patient can engage. (Source: NSW Health: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant unipolar depression after two adequate antidepressant trials benefits more from augmentation than a third sequential monotherapy switch. Atypical antipsychotic augmentation with aripiprazole or quetiapine has the strongest evidence base and is preferred in current Australian guidance. Lithium augmentation remains an option, particularly with comorbid suicidal ideation. Electroconvulsive therapy is considered for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression unresponsive to augmentation. Monitor metabolic side effects, akathisia, and movement disorders during augmentation.
key_points: After two adequate antidepressant trials, augment rather than switch
Aripiprazole and quetiapine have the strongest augmentation evidence
Monitor for metabolic syndrome and akathisia during antipsychotic augmentation
explanation.pearls: Quetiapine extended release has additional sedative benefit in middle insomnia; aripiprazole is more activating and may worsen insomnia in some patients.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: A third sequential antidepressant monotherapy switch has lower remission rates than augmentation after two adequate antidepressant trials. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Atypical antipsychotic augmentation, typically aripiprazole or quetiapine, has the strongest evidence base for treatment-resistant unipolar depression in current Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Combining serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor with tricyclic antidepressant has significant serotonergic and cardiovascular risk and is not a routine augmentation. (Source: AMH: Antidepressants)
Pramipexole augmentation has limited evidence and is not first-line in current Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is appropriate for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression but is generally considered after augmentation trials in non-psychotic moderate cases. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive Therapy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Clozapine haematological monitoring uses a traffic light system. Absolute neutrophil count over 2.0 x10^9/L is green and continues routine monitoring. Counts between 1.5 and 2.0 x10^9/L are yellow with twice-weekly bloods and physician review. Counts between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L are amber with twice-weekly bloods, continued clozapine, and clozapine program notification. Counts below 1.0 x10^9/L are red and clozapine is ceased; granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and intravenous antibiotics are considered if febrile.
key_points: Green over 2.0, yellow 1.5 to 2.0, amber 1.0 to 1.5, red below 1.0 x10^9/L for absolute neutrophil count
Cease clozapine in red zone and consider granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
Notify the clozapine program for amber or red zone events
explanation.pearls: Benign ethnic neutropenia in some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, African, and Middle Eastern patients warrants program-approved lower thresholds rather than clozapine cessation.

options.rationale: An absolute neutrophil count below 1.5 x10^9/L requires increased haematological surveillance regardless of asymptomatic status. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)
Permanent cessation is reserved for the red zone with absolute neutrophil count below 1.0 x10^9/L or other evidence of agranulocytosis. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor is reserved for the red zone with severe neutropenia, not amber zone monitoring; clozapine should be ceased in the red zone. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

Absolute neutrophil count between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L is the amber zone; continue clozapine, increase monitoring to twice weekly, and notify the clozapine program. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)
Dose reduction does not reverse clozapine-induced neutropenia; increased monitoring frequency is required and routine 4-weekly bloods are inadequate. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

explanation.summary: Lithium causes thyroid dysfunction in around 15 to 20% of patients on long-term therapy, predominantly hypothyroidism, and a smaller minority develop hyperparathyroidism. Australian best practice is to monitor TSH, calcium, creatinine, and lithium level every 6 to 12 months. When lithium-induced hypothyroidism develops in a patient with sustained mood stability, levothyroxine replacement is preferred over lithium cessation. Renal monitoring is for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic interstitial nephritis; baseline and annual eGFR are standard.
key_points: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism affects approximately 15 to 20% of long-term patients
Manage with thyroxine; do not stop lithium if mood stability has been hard-won
Annual monitoring: TSH, calcium, creatinine, lithium level, weight
Lithium also causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic interstitial nephritis
explanation.pearls: In a patient stable on lithium who develops hypothyroidism, add levothyroxine rather than stopping lithium - bipolar relapse risk after lithium cessation is approximately 50% within 12 months, far exceeding the morbidity of treated hypothyroidism.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation is associated with high rates of bipolar relapse, especially in a stable patient. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is reversible with thyroxine while continuing lithium. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism affects up to 20% of patients on long-term lithium and is managed with levothyroxine replacement rather than lithium cessation, given the lithium is providing effective mood stabilisation. Starting dose of 50 micrograms is appropriate in a woman without cardiovascular disease. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Subtherapeutic lithium risks bipolar relapse without reversing the autoimmune component of lithium-induced hypothyroidism, which is more reliably treated with thyroxine. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.rationale: She has clear clinical hypothyroidism with fatigue, constipation, and dry skin alongside a TSH of 18 and low T4. Delaying replacement worsens symptoms unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
